How to use

Two ways to read. The monograph can be read in order or chapter by chapter; the lookbook is for browsing freely. The two work together: each look links to the pieces and silhouettes it illustrates, and each piece entry links to the looks that show it.

Quotes. Each quote is given in English, followed by its original version when that original is in Japanese.

Facts and interpretations. The facts come from the sources listed in Chapter 09. When a passage is a matter of interpretation, the text says whose it is: a quoted author or the monograph itself.

Prices. Given as rounded ranges in euros, as an order of magnitude. Actual prices change quickly and vary by shop and country.

Images. Tap an image to enlarge it. The photos belong to their authors and are gathered here for personal use.

はじまりはアメリカ

Chapter 01 · History

01

America, seen from Tokyo

Before it was a way of dressing, the city boy (literally, a boy from the city) was a way of seeing. It belonged to young Japanese people who discovered America through books, films and catalogs. They wrote about it in Popeye, a Japanese men's magazine founded in 1976, which made the “city boy” its ideal reader. This history runs from the photo book Take Ivy (1965) to the magazine's fiftieth anniversary in 2026.

1954–1965 · Before Popeye

Ivy, Japanese style

A garment, then a system

It all began with a brand, a magazine and a handful of men who decided to dress Japanese youth like American college students.

In Osaka, Kensuke Ishizu opened a small shop in 1951, which became the clothing company VAN Jacket in 1954. Founding dates vary depending on whether one counts the shop or the company. Also in 1954 came Otoko no Fukushoku (“men's dress”), a magazine that would later become Men's Club. Ishizu turned it into VAN's mouthpiece: he wrote for it under pen names and bought up most of its print run.

It was in this magazine that Toshiyuki Kurosu, a future VAN executive, came across the word “Ivy.” It referred to the style of students at the elite American universities of the Ivy League.

In 1963, Kurosu launched a street photography column in Men's Club, “Ivy Leaguers on the Street.” For author W. David Marx, it was probably the first street-snap column in the Japanese press. An American based in Tokyo, Marx traced the history of American style in Japan in his book Ametora (2015). That same year, Ishizu set out the TPO principle: dress according to the Time, the Place and the Occasion.

Japanese Ivy then became a very precise code. It fixed the width of the tie at 7 cm. It laid down rules for the placket, the strip of fabric that carries the buttons, and for the vent at the back of the jacket.

W. David Marx's conclusion. He speaks of a “tyranny of details.” In his view, Japanese fashion has kept this taste for rules ever since.

The style was not without risk. In September 1964, with the Tokyo Olympics approaching, police in the Ginza district rounded up teenagers dressed in Ivy. They were nicknamed the “Miyuki-zoku,” the “Miyuki tribe,” after the street where they hung out.

東京

Tokyo goes Ivy

Seen by a high school student in 1964

“We hate being called members of the Miyuki Tribe—we’re Ivy.”

Words of a 16-year-old high school student reported in the press at the time, quoted by W. David Marx · the journal Lapham's Quarterly, 2015

1965 · The founding book

“Take Ivy,” a film first

Eight campuses, some despair and a cult book

To lend legitimacy to what it sold, VAN sent a team to film American campuses. It brought together Toshiyuki Kurosu, Hajime “Paul” Hasegawa, photographer Teruyoshi Hayashida and director Kyō Ozawa. They were joined by Shōsuke Ishizu, who had worked on the editorial staff of Men's Club. The team left for Boston on May 23, 1965.

The project was first a film, shown on August 20, 1965. The photo book followed, from the publisher Fujingahōsha. It came out on September 30, 1965, according to Ivy Style, or in “late 1965,” according to the American magazine The New Yorker.

On the campuses, the team was in for a rude surprise. At Harvard, students wore frayed shorts and flip-flops, a far cry from the impeccable Ivy that VAN was selling in Tokyo.

The book found a second life forty years later. In May 2008, blogger Michael Williams posted scans of it on his blog, A Continuous Lean, and they spread across the Internet. The English edition came out on August 31, 2010, from powerHouse Books, a Brooklyn publisher. It sold more than 50,000 copies.

The book, better known than the film

“Way more people have seen the book than the film. If you say ‘Take Ivy,’ people think of the book — but it was really a film.”

Toshiyuki Kurosu, 2013 interview with W. David Marx, published by Ivy Style in April 2026

Ivy in the lookbook

1967–1977 · Ivy heads for the mountains

Heavy Duty and the “Made in U.S.A. catalog”

Yasuhiko Kobayashi, the man who links it all

An illustrator for Men's Club since 1962, Yasuhiko Kobayashi began producing “illustrated reports” from abroad for Heibon Punch in 1967. The idea came from Jirō Ishikawa, a young editor at the magazine, and was backed by his superior, Yoshihisa Kinameri.

In 1969, in New York, Kobayashi and Ishikawa discovered the Whole Earth Catalog at the Doubleday bookstore. It was a huge American catalog of objects and tools for living differently. Its format would inspire the Made in U.S.A. catalog, and then Popeye.

As a child, Kobayashi had learned the phrase “heavy duty” (sturdy, built to last) from catalogs of the American brand L.L.Bean. They had been left behind by American officers lodging in the houses his mother rented out in Yokohama. In 1975, he gave his series of articles in Men's Club the subtitle “HEAVY-DUTY SURVEY.”

Then he invented “Heavy Duty Ivy,” or “hebi-ai” in Japanese. It paired the oxford shirt with the mountain parka, Levi's 501 jeans and hiking boots. He himself presented it as a parody of Ivy's rules, born just as that style was running out of steam. He launched it in Men's Club with a “declaration of the Heavy Duty Ivy party.” Sources disagree on the date: November 1976 according to Kobayashi, September 1976 according to Marx. His Heavy Duty Book came out in 1977.

アメリカ

A catalog as a warm-up

By the mid-1970s, Kinameri and Ishikawa had left Heibon Shuppan, the publisher of Heibon Punch. Marx describes them as “in exile” at a subsidiary of the publisher that made playing cards. There they produced the ski magazine Ski Life. Then the major daily Yomiuri Shimbun offered them a “mook,” half magazine, half book (a blend of magazine and book).

The result was the Made in U.S.A. catalog (1975), 274 pages long: Madison Avenue ties, Pendleton cardigans, Zephyr skateboards, garage tools. It even reproduced 56 pages from a camping store's mail-order flyer. A second volume, Scrapbook of America, followed in 1976.

A shock for the future head of BEAMS

Yō Shitara discovered the catalog a year before BEAMS, the clothing store founded by his father, opened in Tokyo. “It came as a real shock, and at the same time I was sure that what we were setting out to do was right.”

衝撃的でショックを受けたと同時に、自分たちがやろうとしていることは間違いないと思ったんです。

Yō Shitara, president of BEAMS · The Fashion Post, a Tokyo-based online fashion magazine, August 2017

Heavy Duty looks in the lookbook

1976 · The founding

“Magazine for City Boys”

Two staffers, thirty students and California

The first issue of Popeye came out in June 1976 from Heibon Shuppan, which would take the name Magazine House in 1983. English-language Wikipedia gives July, which may be the month printed on the cover. Kinameri was the editor-in-chief; Ishikawa, the magazine's “director.” Art director Seiichi Horiuchi designed the logo.

Kinameri refused to have staff assigned to him: “to start with, Ishikawa and I will make it, just the two of us.” Around them worked some thirty people: young outside talent and students paid by the article. Sales took a year and a half to take off. After that, each issue sold twenty to thirty thousand more copies than the one before.

The magazine nearly had a different name. Ishikawa wanted to call it “City Boys,” a fashionable expression at the time. But Kinameri saw the name of the sailor Popeye, the cartoon hero, written in English. He read it as “pop eye”: an eye on pop. The rights to the character were negotiated with the American agency King Features Syndicate.

For this first issue, part of the editorial team spent nearly two months in Southern California. In the issue: skateboarding, surfing, hang gliding and jogging. On top of that came thirty-one pages on the UCLA campus and seventy-eight sneaker models, with their American prices. Kobayashi drew a map of Westwood, the university's neighborhood. One story visited Jeff Ho, the maker of Zephyr boards.

“City Boys”: the word existed before the magazine!

年表

Issue No. 1 in six numbers

  1. 01

    Nearly 2 months

    Spent in Southern California preparing the issue, according to Takahiro Kinoshita, Popeye's editor-in-chief from 2012 to 2018. About fifty days, according to the Los Angeles Times, an American daily.

  2. 02

    31 pages

    Devoted to the UCLA campus. After the issue came out, the university bookstore had to put up signs in Japanese.

  3. 03

    78 sneakers

    Shown with their American prices, at a time when Japanese students had hardly more than two kinds of sneakers, according to Kinameri.

  4. 04

    2 staffers

    Kinameri and Ishikawa, surrounded by some thirty freelancers and students.

  5. 05

    The circulation that was enough, according to Kinameri, to create “a completely different medium”: no need to sell a million.

  6. 06

    0 nudes

    Kinameri's manifesto: no nudes, no gekiga (realistic comics for adults).

Two dubious stories. The magazine's impact was so swift, Marx recounts, that some claimed the CIA was secretly funding it. It is a rumor, nothing more. Another uncertain story, reported by Japanese-language Wikipedia: the American tourism office supposedly backed the launch.

An editorial invention

Shopping before you shop

What was really new about Popeye was not its subject but its layout. It lined up hundreds of photographed objects, with their prices and where to find them. The content changed with the times. In the mid-1970s, it was campus wear; by the end of the decade, the preppy style of American private schools. Then came European and Japanese designers in the 1980s, and street fashion in the 1990s. But, Marx notes, the magazine always stayed focused on consumerism.

Success soon drew mockery. In the early 1980s, critics sneered at the “catalog culture” (カタログ文化) of the readers of Popeye and of another Japanese magazine, Mono Magazine. The jibe arose in the wake of Nantonaku, Crystal, a 1980 novel by the writer Yasuo Tanaka that is packed with brand names.

Marx also sees distant descendants of Popeye: the American magazine Complex and, “arguably,” fashion blogs. They too let people shop before going to a store.

Harajuku, 1976

BEAMS and the invention of the “select shop”

In February 1976, four months before Popeye, the “American Life Shop BEAMS” opened in Tokyo's Harajuku district. The shop measured 25 square meters and was made to look like a Californian student's room. Its founder, Etsuzō Shitara, Yō Shitara's father, had been running a cardboard box factory hit by the oil crisis. The manager was Osamu Shigematsu.

A select shop is a store that makes nothing: it picks pieces from several brands and puts them together for the customer. According to Shigematsu, the format was invented by a vice president of SHIPS, another store, founded in 1975. The “big three” of the genre would be SHIPS, BEAMS and United Arrows. Shigematsu founded United Arrows on October 2, 1989, leaving BEAMS with some thirty managers.

The magazine and the store grew together. According to Japanese-language Wikipedia, the only source to tell this story, Popeye's editors tipped BEAMS off about new products, BEAMS bought them, and then the magazine featured them. Around 1979, at the height of the preppy boom, logo sweatshirts made up half of BEAMS's sales.

The style was expensive from the start. According to Yō Shitara, in 1976 BEAMS sold shoes for around ¥50,000, at a time when a starting salary was about ¥60,000.

The takeaway. The catalog magazine and the select shop do the same job: sorting the world and presenting it in order. Fifty years later, Popeye would say that a city boy knows how to “edit” his life, choosing what he needs (Chapter 02).

1978–2011

Olive, amekaji, then the slump

From preppy to the bubble

VAN went bankrupt on April 6, 1978. Two months later, on June 10, Popeye ran the headline “VAN was our teacher.” The idea came from Ishikawa, and the issue revived Ivy with the stylist Katsuhiko Kitamura. In 1979, the publisher Kodansha launched Hot-Dog Press, a near-carbon copy of Popeye. In 1982, an issue of Hot-Dog Press devoted to Ishizu outsold Popeye for the first time.

In 1980, Kinameri launched another magazine, Brutus. In the 1980s, Popeye rode the wave of “American Casual,” relaxed American clothing, shortened in Japan to “amekaji.” British style followed, then the boom in Japanese designer brands. According to Japanese-language Wikipedia, Popeye also ran articles about sex during those years, to set itself apart from Heibon Punch.

Circulation figures from the period remain uncertain. English-language Wikipedia gives 700,000 copies in 1991, citing the Wall Street Journal. magCulture, a London site about magazines, says “over 800,000” at its peak, without citing a source.

“Olive,” the French-style little sister

Olive first appeared as a supplement to Popeye on November 5, 1981. It became a magazine in its own right on June 3, 1982, with the slogan “Magazine for City Girls.” In 1983 it switched to “Magazine for Romantic Girls” and took the French schoolgirl as its model. Suspended in 2000, it ceased publication in 2003.

Amekaji, shibukaji, decline

In the late 1980s, the yen soared against the dollar. Anyone could then bring back stocks of American clothing and resell them at twice the price in Shibuya, Tokyo's youth district. Around 1989 came “shibukaji” (“Shibuya casual”), the relaxed style of Shibuya's young people.

In the mid-1990s, Popeye and Hot-Dog Press went into decline: young people no longer wanted magazines telling them what to buy. By 1999, Popeye's print run was down to 220,000 copies.

From 2007 to 2012, Magazine House's online archives show a monthly that followed trends. It ran street-snap rankings and put celebrities on its covers.

2012–2018

Takahiro Kinoshita's relaunch

“The ABCs of the city boy”

Born in 1968 in Shizuoka, Takahiro Kinoshita read Popeye as a teenager. After a spell at Men's Club, he joined Magazine House in 1997. There he worked on the women's magazine an·an, then on Brutus, where he put together the fashion issues. He took over Popeye in 2012 and relaunched it around the city boy.

His first issue, No. 782, came out on May 10, 2012: “シティーボーイのABC,” the ABCs of the city boy. The slogan “Magazine for City Boys” returned; the format, the binding and the culture pages changed. Kinoshita hired the stylist Akio Hasegawa as fashion director, a post Hasegawa held until the fall of 2018.

The issue themes sketch out the new program. Cities: New York, Paris, Portland, London, and Tokyo almost every year. Ideas: the classics, “cheap chic” (elegance on a budget), “How to be a man.” Passions: vintage clothing and watches, endangered bookstores, craftsmanship.

As early as January 2013, students interviewed in Shibuya said they followed Popeye's city boy features. They were answering questions from ACROSS, a street fashion observatory published by the Japanese retailer PARCO.

The conclusion of Kumiko Takano, editor-in-chief of ACROSS (2013). In her view, Popeye's classic pieces do not encourage readers to follow trends or to please others, which she calls “other people's point of view.” Instead they encourage readers to judge the material, the cut and the craftsmanship for themselves: “one's own point of view.”

Akio Hasegawa's “big silhouette”

Loose silhouettes in the lookbook

June 2016 · Forty years

No. 831, “40年後の西海岸” (the West Coast, forty years on), was sold with a complete reprint of No. 1. Around the issue: an archive exhibition in Omotesandō subway station, a public conversation between Ishikawa and Kinoshita, and a TV documentary. In this issue, Kinameri wrote that with Kinoshita, Popeye had “finally returned to its original course.”

木下孝浩・編集長の登場で『ポパイ』はやっと本来の軌道に戻った

2018

From Popeye to Uniqlo

On January 24, 2018, Magazine House announced Kinoshita's departure. Tōru Matsubara, editor-in-chief of Casa Brutus, another of the publisher's magazines, took over from him. On May 1, Kinoshita joined Fast Retailing, Uniqlo's parent company. There he took charge of creative communications: messaging, brand, stores, product design. In August 2019, he launched LifeWear magazine, a free magazine published twice a year.

In 2015, he said he was “not into digital at all”: as long as he ran Popeye, the magazine would have no digital edition. The POPEYE Web site would not launch until 2021, after he had left.

A lineage with caveats. People like to tell the story of an unbroken line from VAN to Uniqlo. Each link exists, but only taken on its own. The father of Tadashi Yanai, Uniqlo's founder, ran a VAN shop. According to Kinoshita, Yanai had been reading Popeye since the 1970s and found the spirit of those early days in the magazine relaunched in 2012. As for the story of Ishizu exclaiming “This is what I wanted to make!” in a Uniqlo store, it is known only second-hand. The overall narrative remains a construction.

2019–2026

POPEYE Web and the fiftieth anniversary

Yūji Machida, deputy editor-in-chief of Brutus, was appointed to head Popeye on July 26, 2019. In March 2021, Popeye became the last of Magazine House's print magazines to get a website: POPEYE Web. It is run by Ken Miyamoto, who has written for the magazine since 2012. In September 2022, No. 906 returned to the theme “the ABCs of the city boy.” According to a second-hand source, Magazine House published English editions of Popeye and Brutus in September 2025, which were reprinted within two weeks.

Yoshihisa Kinameri, the founder of Popeye, died on July 13, 2023, at the age of 93. Men's Club, the magazine of Ivy, stopped regular publication in October 2024.

2026 · Fifty years

No. 950 (on sale May 9, 2026): “Made in U.S.A. catalog 2026,” a tribute to the 1975 catalog, subtitled “our style began in America.”

No. 951 (on sale June 9, 2026), the fiftieth-anniversary issue: “Whole City Boy Catalog.” It gathers everything the editors mean by “city boy,” in three parts: fashion, lifestyle, city guide. Alongside it, POPEYE Web launched “50 X 50 Interviews”: fifty people, each asked fifty questions.

No. 954 (on sale September 9, 2026): “This is London.”

シティボーイ

Chapter 02 · Definition

02

What is a city boy?

A style, yes, but not only that. Popeye, a Japanese men's magazine founded in 1976 by the publisher Magazine House, made the “city boy” its ideal reader. Over fifty years, it has defined him in many ways. He is a savvy consumer, a boy who gives up his seat on the train, someone who knows how to enjoy his city. Here are those definitions, the life that goes with them, and the criticism they draw.

Setting the record straight

A word older than the magazine

This monograph began with a video by fashion YouTuber Percia Verlin: “City Boy starter pack” (April 2024). In the very first seconds, she states that the term “city boy” was coined by Popeye. The idea is very widespread, but it is wrong.

despite what you often read!

What we can say

  1. 01

    The slogan, yes

    “Magazine for City Boys” appears on Popeye from No. 1, in 1976. The slogan disappeared when Popeye became mainly a fashion magazine, then returned with the 2012 relaunch.

  2. 02

    The word, no

    “City boys” was already in circulation in the mid-1970s. According to W. David Marx, Ishikawa even wanted to make it the magazine's title.

  3. 03

    An uncertain lead

    According to a 2021 post by bxjp on the Japanese blogging platform note.com, the expression came from the Japanese magazine Takarajima. That magazine was already presenting American West Coast culture before Popeye. Its January 1975 issue reportedly used the word for a “tribe”: young people who see themselves first and foremost as children of the city. This origin rests only on a second-hand source.

“Americana,” “ametora”

“Americana” refers to typically American imagery and objects. In Japan, the word “ametora” is short for “American traditional,” following the Japanese habit of cutting foreign words down to four syllables. W. David Marx used it as the title of his book.

The Kinoshita era: a state of mind

2026: knowing how to “edit” one's life

The editors base this definition on a sentence from No. 1 (1976): “If you live in the city, a single week away is enough to make you miss its air” (都会に住んでいる人なら、一週間も街を離れるともう、あの空気が恋しくなってしまうでしょう).

The takeaway. In 1976, being a city boy meant knowing where to buy American goods. From 2012 to 2022, for Kinoshita, it was an ethic and a taste for the classic: he explicitly set clothing aside. In 2026, it is a list of ways to live. Yet clothing remains at the heart of the magazine, of its advertising and of its street-photo issues. This contradiction is what the critics target.

The basic wardrobe

What he almost always wears

着こなし

Popeye's editors may keep saying that the city boy is not just a style, but they open their fiftieth-anniversary issue (No. 951) with fashion. This is not, they write, “because fashion is the most important thing for a city boy,” but for the poise one wants around town. City boy fashion is meant “for enjoying the city freely and making life comfortable.” And when asked for the typical city boy wardrobe, the list comes right away.

The composite portrait that gets passed around

In 2016, the blog God Meets Fashion attributed a “concept” of the ideal reader to the May 10, 2012 issue, the first of the relaunch. He would be a white boy from a good family, introverted, from suburban New York State. He would love reading and music, and would rather watch sports than play them. This attribution comes from a second-hand source: treat it with caution.

Lifestyle

A way of living in the city

東京

For its fiftieth anniversary, Popeye sorted “the whole city boy” into three blocks: fashion, lifestyle, city guide. Fashion therefore takes up only one part out of three. The themes below come from the magazine's tables of contents. They show what Popeye chooses to highlight, not the detailed content of its articles.

The city, on foot and by bike

Popeye has published a Tokyo issue almost every year since 2013. These issues talk more and more about the neighborhood, and less and less about tourist sights. Examples include “My Town, Tokyo” (2019), “An Everyday Guide to Tokyo” (2021) and “Hello, Tokyo!” (2025). The 2021 guide proudly admits to being “a bit plain compared with a tourist guide.” The 2025 one gives the instruction: where the trains are inconvenient, “walk, walk.”

Cycling follows the same logic. “Buy a bike and ride all over Tokyo,” the magazine's headline urged in 2018. In 2020, it photographed the bikes of forty-four people in Tokyo and around the world.

In short. Here the bike is not a technical sport, but a way of exploring the city at street level.

Café, record store, bookstore

Cafés and kissaten. A kissaten is an old-fashioned Japanese coffee house and tearoom. It came back into fashion in the 2020s, along with nostalgia for the Shōwa era (1926–1989). Popeye keeps coming back to it: Tokyo's jazz cafés (2016), late-night cafés in Kyoto (2017), the kissaten with the girl you like (“Girlfriend” issue, 2017). In 2021, its “Coffee and Travel” issue sums it up. What matters is not the perfect cup, but “the time and place where there's coffee by my side.” Kinoshita recommends the café Meikyoku Kissa Lion, in Tokyo's Shibuya district.

Records. In 2021, Popeye presented vinyl and cassettes as a counterpoint to streaming platforms. In 2023, a whole issue paired “records and watches,” with fifty Tokyo stores.

Books. “If the bookstores disappeared from your town, that would be terrible!” the magazine's headline warned in 2017, with a guide to Jinbōchō, Tokyo's second-hand booksellers' district. In 2023, its headline read “The bookstore is our wonderland,” with thirty-seven stores listed. And this observation from 2013: “Towns with a good bookstore somehow have a lot of good curry restaurants.”

What about film?

The city boy is often associated with the analog film camera. Since 2023, Popeye's tables of contents have indeed included a regular “photography class” column. But from 2012 to 2026, they show no feature devoted to film photography. Nothing, then, confirms this cliché.

Travel, home, cooking

The short trip. “My rules for short trips” (“Short Trips and Packing” issue, 2023) begins by looking at what seasoned travelers take with them. The article then suggests journeys by train, bus or boat. There are also solo trips in Asia (2024, 2025) and “100 things to do abroad” (2026).

In short. The typical trip is short, solo or for two, slow and planned: packing a suitcase becomes a style topic in its own right.

The weekend. “What you do on your days off is a matter of style too,” says the 2020 “Weekend Life Catalog.”

The room. Almost every winter since December 2012, an issue has visited people's homes, often under the title “部屋とシティボーイ” (the room and the city boy). In 2026: “What matters is not expensive furniture, or space, or a neat-looking interior. Above all, it is knowing what kind of interior you like.”

Cooking. Curry, sandwiches, pizza, hamburgers: the food issues keep coming, and in 2021 Popeye summed up its doctrine: “Tasty! Easy! And kind of stylish!”

The city boy's little rules

The most telling list comes from the fiftieth-anniversary issue. It says nothing about clothes.

  • See films in a movie theater whenever possible.
  • Have tea once a day.
  • Don't look at your phone during meals.
  • Be a regular at the neighborhood bookstore.
  • Take notes by hand.
  • When possible, take the local train that stops at every station.
  • Drink bottled beer from a small glass.
  • Drink tea from a big mug.

Making this way of life your own

A synthesis, not a quotation. The advice below puts in order the themes that keep coming back in Popeye's tables of contents.

  1. 01

    A neighborhood

    Choose one and explore it on foot or by bike.

  2. 02

    A regular café

    Take your time there, rather than just drinking a coffee.

  3. 03

    Real things

    Be a regular at a bookstore, a record store; prefer objects you can hold in your hand.

  4. 04

    Second-hand clothes

    Hunt through thrift stores and flea markets, and mend your things.

  5. 05

    Your room

    Look after it like a self-portrait.

  6. 06

    Simple cooking

    Aim for the “tasty, easy, kind of stylish” that Popeye champions.

  7. 07

    The short trip

    Travel light, with a well-thought-out packing list.

  8. 08

    A list

    Keep a list of films, books and exhibitions to see.

  9. 09

    One foot outdoors

    Run, walk, camp: the outdoors “for indoor people.”

Issues cited: Tokyo (2013–2026), cycling (2018, 2020), coffee and travel (2021), records and watches (2023), bookstores (2017, 2023), second-hand clothes (2017, 2021, 2024, 2025), the room (every year), cooking (2021), short trips (2023), the outdoors for indoor people (2025).

Debates and criticism

What critics hold against the city boy

1. A consumer culture

As early as the start of the 1980s, the culture of Popeye's readers was mocked as “catalog culture.” They were accused of buying whatever the magazine listed. W. David Marx points out that the magazine changed style every decade, but that its focus on consumerism remained. Kinoshita responds by defending buying to last: “buy something good and wear it for a long time.”

2. A boys' magazine, for boys

In 2020, a post on the Japanese blogging platform note.com criticized the “Girlfriend” issues, published almost every December since 2014. It accused them of assuming that all readers are heterosexual, of reducing women to their smiles and of running a dating column. It also reported that a 2019 recruitment video claimed there were no women editors at Popeye. This information is second-hand.

Counterpoints. In 2015, Kinoshita claimed a 30% female readership in Monocle, and said there is “no boundary between men and women.” For its part, Olive, a magazine for young women launched in 1982 by Popeye's publisher, encouraged its readers not to try to please men. The essayist Junko Sakai, who wrote a column for it in the 1980s, highlights this point. Yokogao Magazine even sees city boys as “rewriting” masculinity.

3. A very white model?

The heaviest accusation also rests on the weakest source. According to the blog God Meets Fashion, the concept of the 2012 relaunch described a white boy from suburban New York State. The style was supposedly established through simple outfits worn by white models. The claim is second-hand: treat it with caution. The charge of cultural “appropriation,” for its part, does not seem to have been leveled at the city boy in the Western press.

4. A uniform?

Ivy is the style of Ivy League students, from the elite universities of the American East Coast. In Japan, it was built on strict rules. In 1976, in the Japanese men's magazine Men's Club, the illustrator Yasuhiko Kobayashi invented Heavy Duty Ivy to poke fun at it. It is a mix of Ivy and rugged outdoor clothing. Readers took the parody seriously. Kinoshita, for his part, embraces his own uniform, the striped shirt. And Percia Verlin worries that chinos can quickly look like a uniform.

5. An expensive style?

In 1976, a pair of shoes at BEAMS, a store opened that year in Tokyo's Harajuku district, cost almost as much as a starting monthly salary. But Popeye also publishes “cheap chic” issues (2013, 2024): style with well-made, affordable clothes. Kinoshita notes that Uniqlo is the brand most worn in the magazine's street photos. And Marx considers Heavy Duty Ivy more accessible than preppy, a younger and sportier version of Ivy. The price of the style, however, does not seem to have drawn direct criticism.

2015–2026

Seen from abroad

The design and independent press discovered Popeye in the mid-2010s. First came magCulture, a London website and shop devoted to magazines, then Monocle, Kinfolk, Inventory and the Studio Nicholson journal.

The menswear and streetwear press followed. In 2016, the book Ametora was discussed by the streetwear site Hypebeast and by Put This On. It was also covered by Heddels, an American site about denim and workwear. Then came the American luxury magazine Robb Report on Heavy Duty Ivy (2022), the Tokyo online magazine sabukaru and the newsletter Blamo. The mainstream press takes an occasional interest. The Los Angeles Times covered the magazine's fortieth anniversary, and the American weekly The New Yorker wrote about Take Ivy.

Many foreign readers look through the magazine without being able to read its texts, Marx notes.

On YouTube, Percia Verlin sums up the English-speaking world's version of the style, which she calls “Japanese Americana.” It features blues and greens worn together, green fatigue pants, chinos, and a striped or loose shirt. Add New Balance sneakers, a bandana and a tote bag.

影響

Chapter 03

03

Influences

The city boy invents almost nothing: he borrows from American students, workers, the army, surfers, Breton sailors and Tokyo's vintage dealers. His whole art lies in the mix.

A style built by assembly

Borrowed pieces, mixed together

In Japan, “city boy” describes not so much a uniform as a curious young city dweller who pays attention to the details of his life.

When it comes to clothes, the city boy style reinterprets mostly American influences in a Japanese way. It draws on campus style, workwear, the outdoors, college sports, skateboarding and surfing. On top of that come European borrowings, from French blue work jackets to English classics. Everything is worn loose.

This logic of assembly was already visible in the 1970s. The Japanese illustrator Yasuhiko Kobayashi presented the outdoor craze, Heavy Duty, as the outdoor version of Ivy, the style of American college campuses. In other words, a mountain parka can be worn with an oxford shirt (a button-down in slightly heavy cotton).

The takeaway. Popeye, a Japanese men's magazine founded in 1976 by the publisher Magazine House, made the “city boy” its ideal reader. Fifty years later, it still works the same way: it pairs a piece from one world with a piece from another.

How to read this chapter

Each entry explains where the influence comes from, what the city boy keeps from it and what he changes. The photos come from the lookbook, the site's gallery of outfits: tap a photo to find out what to look for in it.

Influences · 1

Campus America

It all starts with students at the great universities of the American East Coast, photographed in 1965 for the Japanese book Take Ivy. Then come their more relaxed cousins: preppy style and college sportswear.

01

Ivy and Take Ivy

Ivy Style · アイビールック (aibī rukku) · American Traditional

Definition
The style of students at East Coast universities, which became widespread in the 1950s. Instead of a suit, they wore more relaxed British and American clothes every day: blazer, oxford button-down shirt, sweater, chinos (cotton cloth pants).
Origin
The campuses of the Ivy League (Harvard, Yale and the other great East Coast universities), from the 1920s to the 1940s. In Japan, Kensuke Ishizu, founder of the VAN brand, brought the style over in the early 1960s. Around 1964, young people dressed this way on Miyuki Street, in Tokyo's Ginza district, were nicknamed the “Miyuki-zoku” (the “Miyuki tribe”). In 1965 came Take Ivy, a Japanese book of photographs taken on American campuses.
What the city boy keeps
The basic pieces: oxford shirt, navy blazer, chinos and loafers. The imagery of campus life, which Popeye revisits regularly: a “Take Ivy 2016” feature, then a report that went as far as the universities of Oxford and Cambridge in 2022. And the habit of studying a garment, its origin and its details, which took hold in Japan as early as the 1960s.
What changes
In 2022, Popeye said it wanted to think about classic American style “a little more freely”: it mixes it with sportswear (athletic clothes worn every day), workwear and bright colors. Cuts become loose instead of fitted. The strict rule, a set outfit you simply had to follow, gives way to a personal mix.
Pieces
Oxford button-down shirt, Relaxed blazer (unstructured navy blazer, Ivy three-button), Chinos (khakis), Loafers / penny loafers, Crewneck sweater (Shetland, fisherman/guernsey, cable-knit/Aran)

02

Preppy

prep · プレッピー (pureppī)

Definition
The style of current and former students of private schools in the northeastern United States, which prepare them for the top universities: hence the word “prep.” It is an even more relaxed and younger version of Ivy, with the polo shirt, the rugby shirt and boat shoes. It remains associated with well-off families.
Origin
The prep schools and universities of the Northeast, in the first half of the 20th century. The style made a strong comeback in 1980 with The Official Preppy Handbook, a largely tongue-in-cheek guide. According to W. David Marx, in the mid-1970s Popeye showed campus outfits from the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA). By the end of the decade, it had moved on to preppy outfits.
What the city boy keeps
The pieces: rugby shirt, polo shirt, boat shoes and the Boat and Tote canvas bag by the American brand L.L.Bean. It is the bag that fashion YouTuber Percia Verlin sees most often in this style. Her video “City Boy starter pack,” published in April 2024, was the starting point of this monograph. Then there is a taste for L.L.Bean catalogs, which inspired Popeye's layout, according to Marx. Finally, the summer classics Popeye presented in 2021: boat shoes, sunglasses, straw hat.
What changes
The social-class dimension fades away; what remains is the portrait of a cultured young city dweller. Preppy pieces are often bought second-hand and mixed with workwear. WardRove, a Japanese fashion advice site, notes that in Japan Ivy and preppy blur together under the label “American trad” (classic American style).
Pieces
Polo shirt (piqué and knit), Rugby shirt, Boat shoes, Canvas tote (structured, Boat and Tote type)

03

College sportswear

collegiate · カレッジ (karejji) · スタジャン (sutajan, stadium jacket)

Definition
The training and fan clothing of American universities. It includes the sweatshirt, gray or in campus colors, sometimes printed with the university's name, and the football jersey. Add athletic shorts and the “varsity” jacket (the one worn by college teams), embroidered with a letter.
Origin
The sweatshirt was born in 1920. A University of Alabama football player, tired of itchy wool jerseys, had a cotton practice jersey made. In the mid-1970s, Popeye showed campus outfits from UCLA.
What the city boy keeps
The sweatshirt and hoodie bearing a university's name, the bright team colors. The imagery of campus and game day: “It’s game day y’all!” was the title of a Popeye feature in 2019. The campus can be Japanese, too: in 2024, Popeye paired Japan's Waseda University with its color, a deep carmine red.
What changes
There is no need to have attended the university on the logo: the garment is bought for its look, often second-hand. In 2021, Popeye encouraged readers to wear sportswear in the city, freely and with style.
Pieces
Crewneck sweatshirt, Hoodie

Influences · 2

Working America

Clothes designed to last and to do a job: the clothes of work, the army and the mountains.

04

Americana and workwear

American heritage · アメリカーナ (amerikāna) · ワークウェア (wākuwea)

Definition
Americana means the clothes born of manual labor, the army, sports and rural life in the United States: jeans, heavy canvas pants, work shirts, sweatshirts, boots. They are valued for their toughness, their practicality and their authenticity.
Origin
American work clothes of the 19th and 20th centuries. In Japan, Popeye itself dates their discovery. First came the Made in U.S.A. catalog, a catalog of American goods published in 1975 by the magazine's future founders. Then the first issue of Popeye, devoted to the West Coast, in 1976. According to the magazine, this craze for anything made in the USA gave birth to amekaji, the Japanese abbreviation of “American casual.”
What the city boy keeps
The cult of practical, sturdy American goods: when it comes to shoes, Popeye wrote in 2026, “style is born from function.” The pieces: jeans, canvas work pants, sweatshirt, baseball cap, watch cap, work boots, tote bag. And the catalog format, which Popeye borrowed from the American Whole Earth Catalog and from L.L.Bean catalogs, according to Marx.
What changes
In 2016, Marx noted that Popeye was trying to do “something very different than just historical Americana.” So the point is not to recreate a worker's outfit, but to take one piece and mix it with preppy clothes, European vintage or a Japanese brand. Silhouettes are looser, colors softer.
Pieces
Straight or wide jeans, Work pants and painter pants, Crewneck sweatshirt, Baseball cap, Short cuffed beanie (watch cap, short “fisherman” beanie), Boots (moc toe, hiking boots…), Canvas tote (structured, Boat and Tote type)

David Marx; Bandana, essay by W. David Marx, 2024-09-19.

05

Military surplus

army surplus · ミリタリー (miritarī) · fatigues

Definition
The clothing and equipment the army sells off when it has too much, sold through surplus stores. By extension, any military-style piece: fatigue pants, field jacket, peacoat, watch cap.
Origin
In the United States, surplus has existed since the end of the Civil War. In the late 1940s, veterans who went to college brought the army's khaki chinos into Ivy style. In Japan, according to Marx, the hippies of Tokyo's Shinjuku district wore surplus in the late 1960s. Surplus is also part of the amekaji wardrobe.
What the city boy keeps
Green fatigue pants, straight-cut and often vintage: the piece Percia Verlin sees again and again. The US Navy peacoat, the watch cap, the field jacket. And a taste for clothing designed for real use.
What changes
One piece is enough: in 2021, Popeye noted that wearing a single military piece makes an outfit more stylish. It is mixed with a shirt, knitwear or preppy pieces, never worn as a full uniform. Nothing warlike or political is emphasized: military clothing becomes simply raw material for style.
Pieces
US Army fatigue pants (OG-107), M-65 field jacket (US Army), Cargo pants, Short cuffed beanie (watch cap, short “fisherman” beanie)

06

From Heavy Duty to gorpcore

ヘビーデューティー (hebī dyūtī) · urban outdoor · gorpcore

Definition
Outdoor clothing and gear worn in the city: mountain parka, down jacket, 60/40 parka (a cloth blending cotton and nylon), hiking shoes, fleece, waterproof jacket. “Heavy Duty” is the Japanese name for the great outdoor craze of the 1970s. “Gorpcore,” an English word coined in 2017, refers to a related trend: wearing technical outdoor gear as streetwear.
Origin
In the 1970s, Yasuhiko Kobayashi launched Heavy Duty in Men's Club, a Japanese men's magazine, then in Popeye. The phrase “Heavy Duty Ivy” comes from a parody article he published in Men's Club in 1976; his book on the subject came out in 1977. Popeye revived “Urban Outdoor Life,” the outdoors in the city, in July 2012. The word “gorpcore” first appeared in 2017, coined by the writer Jason Chen. He was then writing for The Cut, the fashion blog of the American magazine New York Magazine.
What the city boy keeps
Kobayashi's founding idea: Heavy Duty is “the outdoor version of Ivy,” so the parka goes with the oxford shirt. The pieces: mountain parka, down vest and down jacket, fleece, fanny pack, technical sandals, wool socks. As early as 2012, Popeye considered this “urban outdoor” style a classic of city dress.
What changes
Kobayashi's young readers mainly wanted to know which parka to wear out in Ginza, Marx reports. Like them, the city boy wears the gear in town and mixes it with ordinary clothes, instead of putting on a full technical outfit. Gorpcore in the English-speaking world tends to show off the big outdoor brands and sometimes loud colors. Popeye's version favors the mix and keeps the link to Ivy.
Pieces
60/40 mountain parka, Anorak / pullover smock, Fleece jacket, Down jacket, Down vest, Sport sandals

Influences · 3

The West Coast

In 1976, the first issue of Popeye was devoted to California: surfing and skateboarding have been part of its identity from the start.

07

Surfing and California

West Coast · 西海岸 (nishi-kaigan) · Summer Boy

Definition
The lifestyle of the American West Coast: outdoor sports (surfing, skateboarding, jogging, hang gliding), beach and athletic wear, sneakers, an easygoing attitude.
Origin
Surf culture flourished in Southern California in the 1950s and 1960s. In 1976, according to Marx, Popeye's founders built the magazine around the athletic lifestyle of West Coast teenagers. They began with a research trip to Los Angeles.
What the city boy keeps
The West Coast is the magazine's very identity. Popeye returned to it for its 40th anniversary, in 2016 (“The West Coast, forty years on”), then in 2018 in an issue about surfing and summer. In 2026, it summed up what its first issue had revealed to readers: functional clothing and cheerful, unpretentious fashion. Summer becomes the season of style: shorts, T-shirt, sandals.
What changes
The wonder of 1976, when everything was new, gives way to a well-researched nostalgia. California becomes one reference among others, alongside London, Paris or Copenhagen. Surfing becomes a city dweller's hobby, something to try one day more than an identity: “this summer, I’m taking it up,” Popeye wrote in 2018.
Pieces
Shorts (chino, fatigue, baggies), Heavyweight T-shirt, Crewneck sweatshirt, Sport sandals, Baseball cap

08

Skateboarding

skateboarding · スケート (sukēto)

Definition
The culture born of the skateboard, itself invented by surfers so they could “surf” on pavement. As for clothes: loose, worn-in pieces, sneakers, caps, beanies.
Origin
Southern California, as an offshoot of surfing. In its very first issue, Popeye ran a story on the Zephyr surf shop. The shop sponsored the Z-Boys, skaters who became legends in skateboarding history.
What the city boy keeps
An attitude more than a uniform: in 2023, Popeye declared that “there’s no such thing as skater fashion.” A few details: beanie, sneakers, loose pants. Popeye's issues on outfits photographed in the street also feature skaters from Venice Beach, in Los Angeles, or from London.
What changes
Skateboarding serves as a cultural reference and a breeding ground for creative people, rather than as a catalog of streetwear brands. Popeye's “& Skate” issue thus cites the director Spike Jonze and the artist Tom Sachs. Logos are kept in the background, and skate pieces are mixed with classic ones.
Pieces
Canvas sneakers, Baseball cap, Short cuffed beanie (watch cap, short “fisherman” beanie), Heavyweight T-shirt

Influences · 4

Europe

Since its 2012 relaunch around the city boy, Popeye has also looked to Paris, London and Copenhagen. This is what sets the city boy apart from a mere copy of America.

09

The French work jacket and the Breton shirt

chore coat · Breton shirt · バスクシャツ (basuku shatsu)

Definition
French workers' and sailors' clothes that became classics. On one side, the blue work jacket and pants known as “bleu de travail” (literally “work blue”); on the other, the blue-and-white striped marinière of the French Navy.
Origin
In the 19th century, blue became the color of workers, and the expression “bleu de travail” appeared. The marinière became part of the official uniform for seamen through a regulation of March 27, 1858.
What the city boy keeps
The blue work jacket, bright or faded, worn as an everyday city jacket. The Breton shirt, which Percia Verlin herself counts as workwear, since it was what sailors wore. A taste for blue faded by use.
What changes
Percia Verlin distinguishes two Breton shirts. One, with a French cut, has a boat neck (wide and straight, from shoulder to shoulder) and a slightly flared hem. The other, sold by the Japanese chain Uniqlo, is thinner, bigger and longer. The garment leaves any worker or sailor context behind to become a colorful basic. Popeye places it within a broader image of Paris: in 2013, the “Basque Shirt,” one of the Japanese names for this striped knit, appears in its Paris ABC.
Pieces
Work jacket (bleu de travail, chore coat), Breton striped shirt (marinière)

10

Practical Parisian chic

French Ivy · Parisian chic · 実用とシック (jitsuyō to shikku)

Definition
The Parisian way of mixing classics (Ivy style, shirt, trench coat) with practical clothes, as Popeye describes it in its reports from Paris. The magazine speaks of “French Ivy” and practical chic rather than “French casual.”
Origin
Popeye's reports from Paris since its 2012 relaunch. First came “City Boy Goes to Paris!” in 2013, then “French Ivy” in 2020. These were followed by a feature on practicality and chic in Paris and New York (2022), “What is the Real Parisian Chic?” (2025) and “Parisian Classics” (2026).
What the city boy keeps
The idea of classic clothes worn in a practical, mixed way. Vintage clothes and books, which Popeye presented in 2013 as the specialties of Paris, and taking care of old things. The pieces: Breton shirt, trench coat, blue work jacket, shirt.
What changes
Paris serves as a second point of reference alongside New York, which moves the city boy away from a purely American amekaji. That does not mean imitating “the Parisian”: Popeye asks what real Parisian chic is rather than laying down its rules.
Pieces
Breton striped shirt (marinière), Trench coat, Work jacket (bleu de travail, chore coat), Loafers / penny loafers, Thick-soled derbies (leather)
Sources

Sources: Popeye 2020年2月号 (released 2020-01-09), Fujisan table of contents; Popeye No. 900 “実用とシック” (2022-03-09), magazineworld.jp table of contents; Popeye No. 798 (2013-09-10), magazineworld.jp table of contents; Popeye No. 934 “STYLE SAMPLE ’25” (2025-01-09), magazineworld.jp table of contents; Percia Verlin, “City Boy starter pack (Japanese Americana),” YouTube, 2024-04-29 (section on the shirt brand S.H. Shirt).

11

Workwear and English classics

British workwear · donkey jacket · 英国トラッド (eikoku torado)

Definition
British work clothes: the “donkey jacket” (the English laborer's jacket), corduroy, heavy boots, the flat cap. More broadly, English classics (tweed, duffle coat, trench coat, country clothing), which Popeye reinterprets in its issues devoted to London.
Origin
In Britain, from the mid-19th century until the 1970s, dustmen, coalmen and navvies (manual laborers) wore flat caps, corduroy, heavy boots and donkey jackets. Popeye published “City Boy in London” as early as fall 2012, then another London issue in 2015 and “This is London” in 2026.
What the city boy keeps
The pieces: trench coat, tweed, Royal Navy work pants, duffle coat, rugby shirt. For the trench coat, Percia Verlin names the English brand Burberry first. British craftsmanship, which Popeye has highlighted since 2012. Since Ivy itself drew on English country clothing, the mix comes naturally.
What changes
In 2012, Popeye wanted to learn how to be “more English than the English” in Tokyo: a reinterpretation, not a copy. English workwear is worn loose, in a soft palette, with no reference to the working class.
Pieces
Trench coat, Balmacaan coat (with a turn-down collar and raglan sleeves), Rugby shirt
Sources

Sources: Wikipedia (en), “Workwear”; Popeye No. 201209 (2012-08-10), Fujisan table of contents; Popeye No. 201211 (2012-10-10), Fujisan table of contents; POPEYE Web, “若きシティボーイに必要な服。”; Robb Report (republished on Yahoo Finance), “‘Heavy Duty Ivy,’ Winter’s Leading Menswear Look, Explained”; Percia Verlin, “City Boy starter pack (Japanese Americana),” YouTube, 2024-04-29.

12

The Scandinavian influence

北欧 (hokuō) · Nordic

Definition
At Popeye, Scandinavia matters through lifestyle (everyday objects, ceramics, furniture, cycling) and Nordic outdoor life. It matters less as a codified way of dressing.
Origin
It has been there since 2012: the magazine's relaunch issue included Scandinavian pottery in its ABC. In fall 2012, the issue on classics gave it a “Scandinavia” section. Then came “Nordic Outdoor” in 2013, followed by reports on cycling in Copenhagen.
What the city boy keeps
Object design and furniture: WardRove describes “Nordic furniture” in the city boy's room. Cycling as a way of living in the city. Percia Verlin also mentions Breton shirts by the Danish brand Norse Projects, often found second-hand, and sneakers by Karhu, a brand of Finnish origin.
What changes
It is a diffuse influence, felt through everyday life more than through a silhouette of its own.
Pieces
Breton striped shirt (marinière), Retro running sneakers, Crewneck sweater (Shetland, fisherman/guernsey, cable-knit/Aran)
Sources

Sources: Popeye No. 201211 (2012-10-10), Fujisan table of contents; Popeye No. 201206 “シティボーイのABC” (2012-05-10), Fujisan table of contents; Popeye 2020年2月号, Fujisan table of contents; WardRove, 2025-05-23; Percia Verlin, “City Boy starter pack (Japanese Americana),” YouTube, 2024-04-29.

Influences · 5

Japan

What remains is what Japan made of all this: amekaji, vintage culture and a generation of minimalist brands.

13

Amekaji

アメカジ · American casual · 渋カジ (shibukaji, Shibuya casual)

Definition
The Japanese abbreviation of “American casual.” In the broad sense, American-style clothing and the way it is worn. In Japan, mainly a casual outfit made of American pieces: jeans, chinos, sweatshirt, sneakers, varsity jacket, western boots, bandana, surplus. Add the chambray shirt, in a cloth born in the French town of Cambrai, woven with blue and white threads.
Origin
In the 1980s and 1990s, youth gangs in Tokyo's Shibuya district launched “shibukaji.” The word “amekaji” spread as the style reached the whole country. It was later applied to older American fashions as well. For Popeye, amekaji was born from the craze for the Made in U.S.A. catalog (1975) and for its own first issue (1976).
What the city boy keeps
Almost the entire basic wardrobe: jeans, chinos, sweatshirt, sneakers, cap, bandana, surplus. In 2026, Popeye claimed this lineage and invited seven commentators, including W. David Marx, to say what amekaji is.
What changes
The city boy adds Europe, minimalist Japanese brands and a way of life. He does not try to reproduce the original pieces faithfully, whether replica jeans (copies of old models) or boots. In short, amekaji is a category of clothing; the city boy is a way of living in which these clothes find their place.
Pieces
Straight or wide jeans, Chinos (khakis), Crewneck sweatshirt, Baseball cap, Chambray shirt, Bandana, Boots (moc toe, hiking boots…)
Sources

Sources: Wikipedia (ja), “アメリカンカジュアル”; Popeye No. 950 (2026-05-09), magazineworld.jp table of contents; Popeye 2026年6月号 / No. 950, Fujisan table of contents.

14

Vintage

古着 (furugi) · vintage · デッドストック (deddo sutokku, old stock never worn)

Definition
Clothes that have already been worn, put back on sale. In Japan, furugi (literally “old clothes”) ranges from cheap everyday second-hand to collector's pieces. Wear and fading count as qualities.
Origin
In Japan, used American clothing arrived in bulk right after the war: about 800,000 pieces in 1950 alone. In the 1980s and 1990s, Japanese people traveled to the United States to hunt for vintage, Marx recounts. Popeye devoted entire issues to it in 2017, 2021, 2024 and 2025.
What the city boy keeps
Vintage as the main source of American and European pieces. In 2021, Popeye highlighted everyday, affordable American vintage, but also European pieces with character. A taste for fading and wear. And the search itself, the “dig,” as both a hobby and a body of knowledge.
What changes
RushOut, the blog of a Japanese vintage store, advises against pieces in poor condition: the city boy stays neat. So a vintage piece is paired with a new one. In 2025, Popeye acknowledged that vintage had become a mass trend, but turned this into an argument: such abundance makes it possible to find a value all one's own.
Pieces
Straight or wide jeans, Oxford button-down shirt, Crewneck sweatshirt, US Army fatigue pants (OG-107), Bandana

Sources

David Marx; RushOut (blog); Percia Verlin, “City Boy starter pack (Japanese Americana),” YouTube, 2024-04-29.

15

Japanese minimalism

ミニマル (minimaru) · big silhouette

Definition
A wave of Japanese brands that emerged in the 2010s. They offer understated clothes in fine materials, without logos, loose and made to last, conceived as a continuous wardrobe rather than a series of trends.
Origin
Tokyo brands of the 2010s: Graphpaper, for example, was founded in Tokyo's Aoyama district in February 2015. In the late 2010s, according to Marx, Popeye stylist Akio Hasegawa launched the “big silhouette” look. It was made up of loose sweat suits and sportswear.
What the city boy keeps
Looseness: Graphpaper wants to leave “space” between the person and the garment. Material and longevity rather than logos, a restrained palette. The Japanese online store prips, devoted to city boy style, lists the Japanese brands Auralee, Comoli and Graphpaper among its references.
What changes
The reference is no longer an American original but a Japanese creation. The city boy combines this minimalism with vintage and touches of color. These brands are expensive. At the same time, Popeye champions cheap chic (style on a budget), and WardRove names the Japanese chains Uniqlo and Muji among the affordable options.
Pieces
Loose shirt worn untucked (including band collar), Wide pleated trousers (balloon cut), Crewneck sweater (Shetland, fisherman/guernsey, cable-knit/Aran), Heavyweight T-shirt, Balmacaan coat (with a turn-down collar and raglan sleeves)

Influences · 6

Ideas more than clothes

Two influences are not visible at first glance: they are ways of thinking about a wardrobe.

16

Normcore

ノームコア (nōmukoa) · unFASHION

Definition
A unisex trend for ordinary clothes with no distinguishing features: jeans, T-shirt, sweatshirt, shirt, sneakers. For the collective that launched the word in 2013, it was an attitude: “finding liberation in being nothing special.” In 2014, a New York Magazine article reduced it to dressing neutrally so as not to stand out.
Origin
The report Youth Mode: A Report on Freedom, published in 2013 by K-Hole, a trend-forecasting collective. Then the article by the writer Fiona Duncan in New York Magazine, on February 26, 2014. Popeye devoted pages to it as early as its “unFASHION” issue of October 2014.
What the city boy keeps
A taste for anonymous basics. POPEYE Web, Popeye's website, recommends for instance an “anonymous” sweatshirt that also works under other layers. In 2016, a Japanese blog even saw the city boy as the basis of normcore in Japan.
What changes
The city boy is not “nothing special,” though: he chooses each basic for its history, its material and its provenance. His outfit also keeps personal touches. Popeye itself raised the question as early as 2014: “Not normcore, but acting basic?”
Pieces
Heavyweight T-shirt, Crewneck sweatshirt, Straight or wide jeans, Chinos (khakis), Polo shirt (piqué and knit)
Sources

Sources: Wikipedia (en), “Normcore”; Popeye No. 811 “un FASHION” (2014-10-10), magazineworld.jp table of contents; God Meets Fashion, 2016-04-29; Popeye No. 858 (2018-09-07), magazineworld.jp table of contents.

17

Cheap chic

チープシック (chīpu shikku)

Definition
The idea that one can be stylish in well-made, practical clothes, often cheap or second-hand, rather than in luxury fashion. It covers basics, workwear, military clothing, sportswear and pieces from all over the world.
Origin
The American book Cheap Chic, by Caterine Milinaire and Carol Troy. Popeye interviewed both authors in 2013. The magazine drew two issues from it: “Cheap Chic ’13” in 2013, then a new issue on cheap chic in 2024.
What the city boy keeps
The very categories of the wardrobe: basics, sportswear, workwear, denim, outdoor, military, classics, trad (traditional classic style), ethnic, preppy. In 2024, Popeye looked to it for well-tailored clothes in fine materials that you can live with for a long time, or for practical, affordable clothes.
What changes
At Popeye, cheap chic became a recurring editorial principle rather than a dated reference. It shows up in a “Mr. Cheap Chic” column and in a 2017 report from Berlin titled “The city boy goes cheap chic.”
Sources

Sources: Popeye No. 797 (2013-08-10), magazineworld.jp table of contents; Popeye No. 930 (2024-09-09), magazineworld.jp table of contents.

Not to be confused

Neighboring styles

The city boy is often confused with similar styles. This table sums up what they share and what sets them apart. The last column separates what the sources establish from what is interpretation.

The city boy and its neighbors
StyleWhat they shareWhat sets them apartStatus
AmekajiThe same basic American wardrobe (jeans, chinos, sweatshirt, sneakers, surplus). Popeye presents itself as one of the birthplaces of amekaji.Amekaji is defined by the American origin of the clothes and extends to the most distinctive pieces (western boots, varsity jacket). Its purists seek out replica denim, faithful copies of old jeans. The city boy adds London, Paris, minimalist Japanese brands and a cultured way of life.Sourced definitions; the comparison is an interpretation
Heritage, pure workwearA taste for sturdy work clothes, for things made in the USA, for signs of wear.Heritage style seeks authenticity in each piece, and often a consistent head-to-toe outfit. The city boy takes a single work piece. For city life, WardRove notes that an outfit made head to toe of outdoor clothes looks out of place day to day.Interpretation based on WardRove and Popeye
Classic preppyOxford shirt, chinos, blazer, boat shoes, L.L.Bean tote.Preppy is tied to a social class (elite schools, old money) and to sharp cuts. The city boy is a cultured young city dweller who readily buys vintage and wears things loose; Popeye wants to think about classic American style more freely.Sourced definitions; the comparison is an interpretation
GorpcoreOutdoor clothes worn in the city: waterproof jacket, fleece, technical shoes, fanny pack.Gorpcore (2017) wears technical gear as streetwear, often head to toe and with the big outdoor brands. At Popeye, urban outdoor was already a classic of city dress in 2012 and is worn as part of a mix. It descends from the Heavy Duty of the 1970s, conceived as the outdoor version of Ivy.Sourced dates and definitions; the difference in use is an interpretation
Quiet luxuryNo logos, muted colors, quality materials that age well.Quiet luxury signals wealth without ostentation and remains associated with old money. The city boy champions cheap chic and vintage, bright touches of color and a youthful spirit. His own luxury is curiosity, not price.Sourced definitions; the comparison is an interpretation
Japanese AmericanaA Japanese reinterpretation of Americana. Percia Verlin uses the phrase in the very title of her video, “City Boy starter pack (Japanese Americana).”“Japanese Americana” is an English-language label. It largely covers amekaji and what W. David Marx calls “ametora” (Japanese shorthand for “American traditional”). The city boy belongs to it without being limited to it: he adds European influences. Popeye also gives lifestyle a central place (cities, books, cafés, bedrooms).Interpretation

定番

Chapter 04

04

The pieces

Fifty-nine garments and accessories, from fatigue pants to the keychain. For each one: where it comes from, how the city boy wears it, what it costs, where to find it new or second-hand, and the mistakes to avoid.

How to use this chapter

A basic wardrobe, then everything else

The city boy has no uniform, but he does have his classics. The Japanese magazine Popeye, which made the city boy its ideal reader, sums them up in a single sentence.

In June 2026, for its fiftieth anniversary, the magazine published a “Whole City Boy Catalog.” The fashion section opens with the clothes worn “almost always.” Asked about the typical wardrobe, the editors answer that “you can picture it right away”: an Oxford shirt, chinos, jeans, a T-shirt, a sweatshirt, a hoodie, white sneakers, a sweater, a duffle coat.

This chapter starts from these basics and goes much further: pants borrowed from the army and from work clothes, campus shirts, outdoor jackets, shoes, accessories. The entries draw on Popeye, on the Japanese and English-language fashion press, and on brand websites. They also draw on “City Boy starter pack” (2024), the video by fashion YouTuber Percia Verlin. That video was the starting point of this monograph.

How to read an entry

At the top: the number, the piece's name, then its other names, in English and Japanese, useful for looking it up online.

The photos come from the lookbook, the site's gallery of outfits: tap a photo to find out what to look for in it. When there is one, a photo of the piece on its own opens the series.

Origin: where the piece comes from. The city boy way: how to choose it (cut, fabrics, colors, details). Wear it with: what to pair it with.

The fold-out panels: the brands, with their range and a rough price bracket; where to buy it, new or second-hand; what is best avoided; the sources.

Source: POPEYE Web, presentation of No. 951 “WHOLE CITY BOY CATALOG,” June 8, 2026.

The pieces · 1

Pants

01

US Army fatigue pants (OG-107)

fatigue pants · OG-107 utility trousers · army fatigues · ファティーグパンツ · ユーティリティーパンツ

Origin
These are the US Army's utility pants, named OG-107 after the code for their shade, “Olive Green 107.” The first specification is dated November 21, 1952. They are cut from cotton sateen (a smooth-faced fabric) weighing 8.5 ounces, about 290 g/m². That is lighter than the herringbone twill (a zigzag-patterned fabric) uniforms of World War II. All branches of the US armed forces wore them from 1952 to 1989. The BDU, a camouflage uniform adopted from 1981 on, gradually replaced them. At the end of 1964, “small, medium, large” sizes gave way to real measurements (32 × 30, for example). The adjustment tabs, small tabs that tighten the waist, disappeared at the same time. In 1975 came a wrinkle-resistant poly-cotton version, called “durable press,” in shade OG-507 with a zip fly. Sold off as surplus, the pants won over hikers, climbers and hippies with their toughness and low price.
The city boy way
Cut. Choose them straight and loose, the leg falling straight down, as fashion YouTuber Percia Verlin describes them. Go for a fairly high rise (the distance from the crotch to the waistband). The hem has a slight break (the fold it makes over the shoe) or is turned up once.
Fabrics. Cotton sateen, which develops a patina as it ages. They also come in twill (a fabric with fine diagonal ribs) or ripstop (a fabric reinforced with a tear-resistant grid).
Colors. Mostly olive green, sometimes khaki.
Details. Large rectangular patch pockets on the front, meaning they are sewn onto the fabric: this is their signature feature. Back pockets with button flaps. Adjustment tabs at the waist on early models, until 1964.
Wear it with
Wear them with a blue top, a pairing Percia Verlin often sees in this style, or with a big shirt worn untucked. On the feet, New Balance-type sneakers or brown leather shoes. Despite their military look, they are a basic piece that is easy to pair, according to the Japanese magazine Begin. The American site Heddels also finds them just as comfortable dressed up as dressed down.

Good to know

“Treillis” (the French word for fatigues), “fatigue” and “baker pant” largely refer to the same pants. The official designation was “utility trousers,” and soldiers said “fatigues.” “Baker pant” is a name that came from Japanese fashion, with no military basis, according to Heddels. This sheet follows the regulation model and its surplus; the “Baker pants” sheet gathers the reproductions sold under that name. Second-hand, search under all three names.

See also: Baker pants — the same pants, under the name Japanese fashion gives them, and their reproductions.

See also: Cargo pants — the military pants with pockets on the thighs, which fatigue pants lack.

See also: Shorts — the short version of the OG-107 fatigues, reproduced by Buzz Rickson's and Stan Ray.

Where to buy, second-hand

In store or online

  • Cultizm — online store

Second-hand

  • Vinted: Search for “pantalon og107”: expect about €100–150 for a vintage pair, and around €50 for a reproduction, such as those from the brand Pike Brothers. Percia Verlin advises typing the exact name of the piece: it is cheaper and more eco-friendly. (source)
  • eBay / Etsy / Grailed: According to Percia Verlin, eBay and Etsy are full of genuine vintage military pants. (source)
  • Local military surplus store: Percia Verlin also recommends the nearest army surplus store, which often has genuine fatigues. (source)
  • JAM Trading (Japanese vintage store): This vintage store publishes a guide to dating a piece. 1950s models have brown urea buttons (an early plastic) and adjustment tabs. In the 1960s, the tabs disappear and the cut slims down at the end of the decade. The zip fly arrives in the 1970s. Expect about €70–140 a pair. (source)
Avoid
  • The poly-cotton “durable press” versions (OG-507), if the aim is the patina of cotton sateen: check the label.
  • More recent surplus that is not OG-107: BDUs, French F2 and F3 fatigues, camouflage. On Vinted, a search for “treillis US Army” brings up a lot of camouflage (Multicam, OCP, woodland).

02

Baker pants

baker pants · ベイカーパンツ · fatigue pants · OG107 utility pants

Origin
“Baker pant” is not a military name. American soldiers said “fatigues,” and the official designation was “utility trousers.” These are the pants of the OG-107 uniform, named after the code for its olive-green shade and adopted by the US Army in 1952. For the American site Heddels, “baker pant” is an invention of Japanese fashion, with no historical basis. The word “baker” points to bread-making, but the dictionary of the Japanese site Fashionsnap considers the origin of the name unknown. The Japanese vintage store JAM Trading puts forward two theories: pants worn by bakers, or front pockets that look like a slice of sandwich bread. According to the store, the 1950s model is made of cotton sateen (a smooth-faced fabric), with brown urea buttons. It also has adjustment tabs, small tabs that tighten the waist. It loses them in the 1960s and slims down at the end of the decade. The 1970s, the last decade in cotton sateen, bring the zip fly. Some Japanese reproductions go back further. The brand Jelado copies the herringbone twill (zigzag-patterned) pants issued to the US Army in 1947; the brand FOB Factory copies models from the 1940s.
The city boy way
Cut. Choose them loose, with a straight or slightly tapered leg, meaning narrower toward the hem. The rise, the distance from the crotch to the waistband, is often deep, according to Fashionsnap. The hem has a slight break (the fold it makes over the shoe) or is turned up once.
Fabrics. Cotton sateen, which gains character with wear, according to the Japanese magazine Begin. Cotton herringbone twill at Jelado. “65/35” cloth, a blend of cotton and polyester, on the model shown by the magazine Popeye.
Colors. Mostly khaki, according to Fashionsnap, but also olive. Sellers also offer them in black, navy or indigo.
Details. Large L-shaped front pockets and flapped back pockets, all of them patch pockets, meaning sewn onto the fabric, according to Fashionsnap. A button fly on reproductions of old models.
Wear it with
Wear them every day, as a basic piece. Despite their military look, they are easy to pair, according to Begin. The Japanese magazine points out that they were designed for work, not combat. In 2022, Popeye shows them with a parka in the same 65/35 cloth, in an article on The North Face Purple Label, the Japanese line of The North Face.

Good to know

Brands use both names, baker and fatigue, for the same pants. orSlow, for instance, sells “US Army Fatigue Pants,” and Stan Ray an “OG Loose Fatigue.” Some also copy the US Air Force utility pants worn by ground mechanics (Buzz Rickson's, The Real McCoy's). The classic models to know are therefore the same as for fatigue pants.

See also: US Army fatigue pants (OG-107) — the history of the regulation OG-107 model, how it changed, and tips for finding vintage surplus.

See also: Cargo pants — the other great military pants, born from the British combat uniform of 1938.

03

Chinos

chinos · khakis · chino pants · チノパン · チノパンツ

Origin
Chinos descend from the khaki uniform. The Corps of Guides, a military unit raised in India in December 1846, was the first to wear the color. Its khaki uniform, introduced in 1848, was made of a tightly woven linen or cotton cloth. The US Army adopted khaki during the Spanish–American War of 1898. Twill pants (twill is a fabric with fine diagonal ribs) spread across the United States when soldiers came home from the Philippines with theirs. According to the dictionary of the Japanese site Fashionsnap, the name may come from fabric bought in China: “chino” means “Chinese.” English-language Wikipedia considers this etymology uncertain. After 1945, khaki chinos entered the civilian wardrobe.
The city boy way
Cut. Choose them wider than classic chinos, with pleats (folds sewn in below the waistband), or even in a balloon cut that narrows at the ankle. That is the advice of fashion YouTuber Percia Verlin. The magazine Popeye, for its part, favors a cut that is “neither too tight nor too wide.” The hem has a slight break (the fold it makes over the shoe), or is left unfinished so it can be hemmed to the right length.
Fabrics. Fairly heavy, tightly woven cotton twill.
Colors. Khaki and ecru, according to Fashionsnap. Percia Verlin also sees a lot of beige and white in this style.
Details. On Japanese reproductions of military chinos: US Army metal buttons at Pherrow's. At The Real McCoy's, based on a 1945 model: urea buttons (an early plastic) and piped back pockets, edged with a thin trim.
Wear it with
Wear them with a blazer, choosing a heavy pair, as Popeye does. They also go with a blue top or a big shirt worn untucked.

Good to know

See also: Wide pleated trousers — the wide pleated cut Percia Verlin recommends for chinos, in other fabrics.

See also: US Army fatigue pants (OG-107) — the style's other basic military pants, olive green, with large patch pockets.

04

Wide pleated trousers

pleated wide trousers · double pleated trousers · balloon pants · ワイドパンツ · 2タックパンツ · タックパンツ

Origin
They descend from “Oxford bags,” the loose trousers worn by Oxford students. They appeared in the mid-1920s and were worn until the 1950s. Their leg opening grew from 22 or 23 inches (56–58 cm) to 44 inches (110 cm), or even more. The fashion returned in 1970s Britain among fans of northern soul, a British music movement, for the ease of movement it gave on the dance floor. According to the dictionary of the Japanese site Fashionsnap, pleated trousers owe a lot to 1980s fashion. The waist is often high, with one to three pleats, folds sewn in below the waistband. In May 2024 (No. 925), the magazine Popeye celebrates a pair of wide Giorgio Armani trousers, tapered (narrower toward the hem) and double-pleated. It admits to wanting trousers “like ’90s Armani.”
The city boy way
Cut. Choose them wide and high-waisted, with volume from the hips to the thighs and a narrower hem: Popeye finds this shape beautiful. Wear them long, with a break (the fold the hem makes over the shoe), and, like Popeye, sitting a little low on the hips rather than at the waist.
Fabrics. Cupro and viscose, fluid man-made fibers, for the Armani pair celebrated by Popeye. Brands also offer them in cotton twill (a fabric with fine diagonal ribs), herringbone (a zigzag pattern), linen-cotton or wool.
Colors. Beige, sand, navy or black, based on the brands' models.
Details. At the Japanese brand NEAT: two pleats, a deep rise (a long distance from the crotch to the waistband) and an unfinished hem, to be taken up to the wearer's length.
Wear it with
Casual pieces, to avoid looking like a suit: a T-shirt or a shirt worn untucked, and sneakers.

Good to know

The “wide pleated chino” recommended by fashion YouTuber Percia Verlin belongs both to this sheet and to the chinos sheet. NEAT's Standard Chino is an example. According to Fashionsnap, chinos are defined by their cloth, a sturdy cotton twill; pleated trousers, by their cut.

See also: Chinos — khaki chinos, also best chosen wide and pleated to avoid looking like a uniform.

05

Straight or wide jeans

jeans · denim · 501 · selvedge jeans · ジーンズ · デニム

Origin
On May 20, 1873, Levi Strauss and the tailor Jacob Davis received US patent No. 139,121. It covered work pants reinforced with copper rivets at the points of strain. In 1890, the patent entered the public domain and Levi's began numbering its models: “501” designated the “waist overall,” the riveted work pants. In 1936, the small red label, the Red Tab, appeared on the right back pocket. During World War II, to save metal, the crotch rivet, the watch-pocket rivets and the cinch strap (which tightens the waist) were removed. “Selvedge” denim, with a finished edge, comes from old shuttle looms. They weave cloth about 76 cm wide, compared with 150 cm or more on modern looms. This denim is associated with the high end of the market. The White Oak mill, opened in 1905 in Greensboro, North Carolina, long belonged to Cone Mills, the world's leading denim maker. It closed in 2017.
The city boy way
Cut. Choose them straight and relaxed, “without being overly baggy or too slim,” like model 105 from the Japanese brand orSlow. Or go for a properly loose pair, like the Stone Island jeans picked by the magazine Popeye. The hem has a slight break (the fold it makes over the shoe) or is turned up into a cuff that shows the selvedge.
Fabrics. 100% cotton denim, often selvedge, Japanese or American, raw (never washed) or washed once. Brands also reproduce old fabrics: Popeye presents the raw 1943 denim recreated in Japan by the brand Sugar Cane.
Colors. Indigo, raw or faded; faded black.
Details. Button fly, leather or paper patch, rivets. Some reproductions copy the model of a specific year, such as 1947 or 1955, or the World War II model (“大戦モデル”).
Wear it with
Wear them every day, without fuss: a Popeye reader says he wears and washes his every day. Pair them with big shirts, T-shirts and sneakers.

Good to know

See also: Work pants and painter pants — denim work pants, with double knees or a tool pocket.

06

Cargo pants

cargo pants · M-65 trousers · BDU trousers · six-pocket pants · カーゴパンツ

Origin
According to the American site Heddels, cargo pants were born in 1938 with battle dress, the British combat uniform. They were olive green, with one pocket on the left thigh and another on the right hip. In the 1940s, the American officer William P. Yarborough, a future lieutenant general, adapted them for paratroopers: he added pockets on both sides. In 1951, the M-51 model, adopted along with the field parka, went to six pockets and gained a drawstring at the waist. The M-65, adopted in 1965, was made of nylon or nylon-cotton so it could take a quilted liner. The BDU, a combat uniform issued on October 1, 1981, was made of half-cotton, half-nylon twill in woodland camouflage (a forest pattern). Reinforced at the knees, elbows and seat, it was retired in April 2008. In the 1990s, cargo pants spread to hip-hop, skateboarding and the counterculture.
The city boy way
Cut. Choose them loose, straight and high-waisted, like the 1940s US Army M-42 pants reproduced by the Japanese brand orSlow. The magazine Popeye also picks them in a lightweight version, in the style of paratrooper pants. Long, they sometimes gather at the ankle: with ties at the brand Carhartt WIP, with an elasticated hem on the French army's F2 fatigues.
Fabrics. Cotton herringbone twill (a zigzag-patterned fabric), ripstop (a fabric reinforced with a tear-resistant grid), cotton twill or nylon-cotton. The lightweight versions blend in polyester.
Colors. Olive and army green, black. Faded, surplus-style dyes, like the “faded surplus” cargo pants from the American brand Todd Snyder, cited by fashion YouTuber Percia Verlin. Popeye even shows cargo pants in tartan, the Scottish check.
Details. Flapped bellows pockets on the thighs, pleated pockets that expand as they are filled. Double-layered knees.
Wear it with
Lighten them with a simple top and sneakers, so they look less military.

Good to know

Cargo pants are recognizable by their bellows pockets on the thighs. OG-107 fatigues and “baker pants” have none: their large patch pockets are on the front. On second-hand sites, searches for “M65” or “treillis” mix the two models.

See also: US Army fatigue pants (OG-107) — OG-107 fatigues, and their 1975 poly-cotton version, the OG-507, which turns up in listings.

See also: Shorts — six-pocket cargo shorts.
