07

Shorts

shorts · bermuda shorts · baggies · ショーツ · ハーフパンツ · 短パン

Origin
The invention of Bermuda shorts is credited to Nathaniel Coxon, who ran a tearoom in Bermuda. In 1914, he shortened his employees' uniform trousers. The British Army adopted these shorts during World War I, for tropical and desert climates. Bermuda shorts stop about 2.5 cm above the knee; Vogue magazine first wrote “Bermuda shorts” in 1948. In 1982, the climber Mike Graham, a member of the Stonemasters, a group of Yosemite climbers, founded the brand Gramicci. Its shorts have a crotch gusset (an added piece of fabric) inspired by kung fu pants. Their nylon webbing belt adjusts with one hand. On the military side, the Japanese brand Buzz Rickson's reproduces the OG-107 shorts in cotton sateen (a smooth-faced fabric). They are the short version of the olive-green utility uniform worn by the US forces from 1952 to 1989.
The city boy way
Cut. Choose them loose, with a wide, straight leg, and long: to the knee, or down over the shin, as in the magazine Popeye. The classic military version stops just above the knee.
Fabrics. Cotton twill (a fabric with fine diagonal ribs), cotton sateen, denim. Ripstop (a fabric reinforced with a tear-resistant grid) at Engineered Garments, seersucker (puckered cotton) at All American Khakis. Nylon for outdoor shorts, like Patagonia's Baggies.
Colors. Olive, beige, navy, black, denim or checks, based on the brands' models.
Details. Fatigue-style patch pockets or six cargo-style pockets. An elastic waist or adjustment tabs, small tabs that tighten the waist.
Wear it with
Wear them in a “well-mannered” way, says Popeye: with a cashmere sweater, a polo shirt or a denim shirt. On the feet, socks and sneakers, or sandals.

Good to know

See also: US Army fatigue pants (OG-107) — the OG-107 pants that fatigue shorts derive from.

See also: Elastic-waist pants — the climbing pants from Gramicci, the brand behind the webbing-belt shorts.

08

Work pants and painter pants

painter pants · carpenter pants · double knee pants · work pants · ペインターパンツ · ダブルニーパンツ · bleu de travail

Origin
The American brand Stan Ray presents its OG Painter Pant as its founding model. It has made them in Texas since 1972, for painters and carpenters. The Japanese brand Warehouse & Co. traces its double-knee pants back to the Works Progress Administration (1935–1943). This Great Depression program employed seamstresses in public workshops. In France, Édouard Béerens registered the Vétra brand in Paris in 1927. He created men's workwear, starting from the family apron factory. The company moved to Lambersart, near Lille, in 1930. Le Laboureur, a manufacturer in Digoin (Saône-et-Loire), has made workwear since 1956, according to its website. It holds the Entreprise du patrimoine vivant label, a French state distinction for heritage craftsmanship.
The city boy way
Cut. Choose them straight and a little loose, for ease of movement, as the dictionary of the Japanese site Fashionsnap describes them. Wear them long, with a slight break (the fold the hem makes over the shoe), or with the hem turned up.
Fabrics. Sturdy fabrics, according to Fashionsnap: denim, or hickory, a finely striped cloth. Ecru cotton drill, a heavy twill (a fabric with fine diagonal ribs), at Stan Ray; cotton twill at Vétra.
Colors. Ecru, indigo, hickory stripe, workwear blue, black or brown, based on the brands' models.
Details. A long tool pocket and a hammer loop on the leg, as Fashionsnap describes. At Stan Ray, flat-felled seams stitched in three rows, which are very strong. Reinforced knees on the so-called “double knee” models.
Wear it with
Give them a light look, far from the roughness of old-time workwear, advises the magazine Popeye. They go with a French work jacket, like those from the brands Le Laboureur or Le Mont Saint Michel, cited by fashion YouTuber Percia Verlin.

Good to know

See also: Straight or wide jeans — jeans, the other denim work pants.

See also: Work jacket — the work jacket, French or American, which Percia Verlin places among the same influences.

09

Elastic-waist pants

easy pants · climbing pants · drawstring pants · Gramicci Pant · イージーパンツ · クライミングパンツ

Origin
On the outdoor side, the reference model comes from the brand Gramicci. The climber Mike Graham founded it in 1982, to make practical outdoor clothing. He belonged to the Stonemasters, a group of climbers active in Yosemite in the 1970s. At the crotch, a diamond-shaped gusset (an added piece of fabric), inspired by kung fu pants, gives 180 degrees of movement. A nylon webbing belt built into the waist adjusts with one hand. The name “Gramicci” comes from a nickname picked up during a supposed “all-Italian” first ascent of Half Dome, in Yosemite. None of the climbers was Italian. The Gramicci Pant keeps this gusset and this belt, on an elastic waist.
The city boy way
Cut. Choose them relaxed and tapered, meaning narrower toward the hem, like the Gramicci Pant. The British brand Universal Works adds a pleat, a fold sewn in below the waistband. Narrowed, the hem clears the shoe: it stops at the ankle or has a slight break (the fold it makes over the shoe).
Fabrics. Soft materials, according to the dictionary of the Japanese site Fashionsnap. Heavy 10-ounce cotton canvas (about 340 g/m²) from the brand Smoke T One, presented by the magazine Popeye. Also twill (a fabric with fine diagonal ribs), nylon, or the indigo cloth called “kendo” from the brand 3sixteen.
Colors. Olive, sand, rinsed denim and checks in the Gramicci collection presented by Popeye. Charcoal, olive or indigo at other brands.
Details. An elastic waist, with a drawstring or a built-in webbing belt. Fatigue-style patch pockets on some models.
Wear it with
Wear them casually every day, or dressed up with a jacket. They don't mind wrinkles, Fashionsnap notes.

Good to know

Easy pants are woven; knit tracksuit pants have their own sheet. Some models, like Universal Works' Pleated Track Pant, sit on the border between the two.

See also: Tracksuit — knit tracksuit pants and their matching jacket.

See also: Shorts — Gramicci shorts, the short version of the climbing pants.

The pieces · 2

Tops

10

Oxford button-down shirt

Oxford cloth button-down (OCBD) · button-down shirt · ボタンダウンシャツ · オックスフォードシャツ · BDシャツ

Origin
In 1896, in England, John Brooks, grandson of the founder of the American clothier Brooks Brothers, watched a polo match. The players fastened down their collar points so they would not flap in the wind. In 1900, Brooks Brothers brought out its button-down collar shirt in oxford, a cotton cloth with a basket weave. In October 2020 (No. 882), the magazine Popeye recalls this origin and tells the story of the shirt's arrival in Japan. In 1954, the first issue of the Japanese magazine Men's Club showed Ivy League looks, the style of the great universities of the American Northeast. In the late 1950s, the shirt was still almost unknown in Tokyo. In 1965, while shooting the Japanese photo book Take Ivy, the book's team bought some at Brooks Brothers in New York.
The city boy way
Cut. Choose it loose, like the Polo Ralph Lauren “Big Fit” oxford picked by Popeye in spring 2023, and wear it casually. Depending on the outfit, it is worn untucked or tucked in. Fashion YouTuber Percia Verlin points out that the loose version is made to be worn untucked.
Fabrics. Cotton oxford, worn soft and unstarched, as Popeye recommends: it gets better with washing and creasing.
Colors. Light blue and white first, then blue stripes. Percia Verlin notes that this style is dominated by blue and green.
Details. A button-down collar with a low collar stand, for a casual effect; the collar stand is the band that joins the collar to the shirt. According to Popeye, a true “button-down” can be recognized by three details. These are the placket (the strip that holds the buttons), a box pleat in the middle of the back and a topstitched collar.
Wear it with
Wear it with chinos, fatigue pants or work pants, with a sweatshirt over it.

Good to know

11

Loose shirt worn untucked

oversized button-down · big shirt · band collar shirt · grandad collar shirt · ビッグシャツ · オーバーサイズシャツ · バンドカラーシャツ

Origin
This is the classic dress shirt, made wider and worn over the pants. It also comes with a band collar: a standing, band-shaped collar that circles the neck with no turned-down part. It is usually less than 5 cm high at the front. It recalls 19th-century shirts, which had no fixed collar: a separate collar was attached to them. In Troy, New York, tradition credits Hannah Montague with inventing the detachable collar, in 1827. In spring 2023 (No. 912), the magazine Popeye lists the Polo Ralph Lauren “Big Fit” oxford among the essentials of the young “city boy,” the magazine's ideal reader. In March 2024, it features an oxford “big shirt” from the same brand.
The city boy way
Cut. Choose it very loose, wide especially toward the bottom, and wear it untucked, as fashion YouTuber Percia Verlin describes. Dropped shoulders, a slightly longer length and a rounded hem.
Fabrics. Oxford, poplin (a fine, tightly woven cloth) at Studio Nicholson, washed twill at Auralee. Cotton and rayon, a man-made fiber, for a soft fabric at Uniqlo × JW Anderson.
Colors. Blues and whites, or stripes. Percia Verlin notes that blue is often paired with green in this style.
Details. A classic collar or a band collar, which the Japanese brand Graphpaper, recommended by Percia Verlin, also offers. Side slits on some models.
Wear it with
Wear it with wide or balloon pants (narrowing at the ankle), fatigue pants or chinos. Popeye layers it with other basics.

Good to know

A loose-cut oxford button-down belongs to two sheets. This one covers the cut and how to wear it; “Oxford button-down shirt” covers the cloth, the collar and the history.

See also: Oxford button-down shirt — the Brooks Brothers button-down shirt and its details.

Flannel check shirt

flannel shirt · plaid shirt · check shirt · ネルシャツ · チェックシャツ · フランネルシャツ

Origin
In 1924, Pendleton Woolen Mills (Oregon) began producing wool sport shirts for men. By 1929, it offered a full line of wool sportswear. In 1937, the Scotch Plaid Flannel Shirt entered the catalog of the American brand L.L.Bean. In September 2024, the magazine Popeye points out that it has been a staple there for more than 85 years. In 1961, a band named itself the Pendletones, after the Pendleton shirt, before becoming the Beach Boys. Pendleton ties that name to its Board Shirt, worn by Southern California surfers in the 1960s.
The city boy way
Cut. Take it one size up, as Popeye advises, so a sweatshirt can slip underneath. L.L.Bean also offers a version with a shorter hem, to wear untucked.
Fabrics. Brushed cotton flannel, for a soft feel; at L.L.Bean it is Portuguese. Wool at Pendleton.
Colors. Tartans, the Scottish checks, as at L.L.Bean: red, green, navy blue.
Details. Two chest pockets and simple buttons.
Wear it with
Wear it over a zip-up hoodie, with slim pants for a sharp look, as in Popeye. Or with chinos.

Good to know

13

Chambray shirt

chambray shirt · chambray work shirt · シャンブレーシャツ · ワークシャツ

Origin
Chambray takes its name from Cambrai, in northern France, where the cloth was originally woven. It is a plain-weave cloth, in which the threads cross one over one. The warp threads, running lengthwise, are colored, often blue; the weft threads, running across, are white. In 1901, the US Navy officially authorized denim and chambray, which spread the cloth across the United States. Workers then adopted it, hence the expression “blue collar.” In September 2025 (No. 942), the magazine Popeye devotes an article to it. It calls it a “year-round starter,” to wear in every season, that gets better with age. It compares models from the 1970s and 1990s with recent ones.
The city boy way
Cut. Choose it straight, like a work shirt. Wear it untucked, or open over a white T-shirt.
Fabrics. Cotton chambray, for example in 6-ounce selvedge (cloth with a finished edge), about 200 g/m², from the brand Riprap. Or vintage poly-cotton, comfortable in every season, according to Popeye, writing about a 1970s shirt from the brand Big Mac.
Colors. Chambray blue, which takes on a patina in the wash; ecru or white as a variant.
Details. Triple stitching where the strain is greatest, flap pockets with a pen slot, and a neatly made placket (the strip that holds the buttons).
Wear it with
Wear it with khaki pants or fatigue pants.

Breton striped shirt

Breton stripe shirt · striped shirt · バスクシャツ · ボーダー · ボーダーTシャツ

Origin
First worn by fishermen in Brittany and Normandy, it became regulation dress on March 27, 1858. That day, a French Navy decree set out the sailors' uniform, including the striped knit top. It has 21 white stripes, each twice as wide as the 20 or 21 navy blue stripes. According to the brand Orcival, the blue stripes measure 10 mm. Based in Lyon since 1940, Orcival supplied the French Navy from the early 1940s. Being close to the naval base in Toulon helped. During World War I, the designer Coco Chanel drew on sailors' uniforms. She launched a “sailor style” in jersey, a soft knit, in her boutique in Deauville. In 1983, the designer Jean Paul Gaultier closed his “Boy Toy” show with a Breton striped shirt.
The city boy way
Cut. Choose it in a French cut, slightly flared at the hem, as fashion YouTuber Percia Verlin describes. Or take a bigger, longer striped T-shirt with a boxy silhouette.
Fabrics. Heavy cotton jersey for traditional Breton shirts (Orcival, Armor Lux), thinner jersey for striped T-shirts (Muji).
Colors. Ecru or white with navy stripes; also dark gray, black or light blue stripes.
Details. A boat neck, a wide, straight neckline. Percia Verlin likes more unusual models, for example with one sleeve in different stripes.
Wear it with
Wear it alone or as a base layer, as the magazine Popeye shows, with chinos, fatigue pants or jeans.

Good to know

See also: Heavyweight T-shirt — the boxy T-shirt cut, for the loose striped version.

Heavyweight T-shirt

heavyweight T-shirt · heavy tee · ヘビーウェイトTシャツ · 厚手Tシャツ · 肉厚Tシャツ

Origin
In 1913, the US Navy first issued the T-shirt, as an undergarment. The word entered American English in the 1920s. In the 1950s, the actor Marlon Brando wore one in “A Streetcar Named Desire,” which made it even more popular. At the American brand Champion, the heavyweight T1011 series has been improved several times since the 1930s. The magazine Popeye points this out in June 2026. Heavy Weight Collections was born in 1996 as an exclusive brand of the American department store JC Penney. According to Popeye, it has become a family business that still makes T-shirts.
The city boy way
Cut. Choose it boxy, as Popeye describes: roomy shoulders and body, and a fairly short length to balance the width.
Fabrics. Heavy cotton, from 6 ounces (about 200 g/m²) to over 10 ounces (about 360 g/m²). The American brand Lady White knits a tubular jersey, so there are no side seams, in North Carolina cotton. The French site BonneGueule offers a 250 g/m² jersey. The German brand Merz b. Schwanen uses loopwheel knit, made on old circular knitting machines.
Colors. At Champion, new colors every season, dyed after the garment is sewn. Popeye likes their worn look, which comes from pigment dyeing. Otherwise, white, heather gray, navy or black.
Details. A sturdy ribbed collar and reinforcing tape across the shoulders. Popeye likes models made in the United States.
Wear it with
Wear it alone in summer, or under an open shirt, with wide pants or fatigue pants.

Good to know

Pocket T-shirt

pocket tee · pocket T-shirt · ポケットTシャツ · ポケT

Origin
Its history comes down to a handful of brands. Velva Sheen, a maker of sweatshirts, T-shirts, jackets and gym shorts, was founded in 1932 in Cincinnati, Ohio. The brand makes heavy pocket T-shirts, pigment-dyed (a dye that gives a slightly worn look), in a “Vintage fit.” The German brand Merz b. Schwanen calls its own “1940sP,” after its 1940s silhouette. In January 2022, the American site Heddels presented the Max-Weight Pocket T-Shirt from the American brand Camber as a contender for the “perfect plain white tee.” It is made of 8-ounce cotton (about 270 g/m²), in the United States.
The city boy way
Cut. Choose it slightly boxy, of standard to short length. For a loose effect, the American brand Lady White advises going one size up.
Fabrics. Medium to heavy cotton jersey, from 4.6 to 8 ounces (about 155–270 g/m²). Loopwheel knit, made on old circular knitting machines, at Merz b. Schwanen. At Lady White, carded cotton jersey with a firm feel that softens in the wash.
Colors. White first: Heddels considers it the classic. Then colors, sometimes obtained through pigment dyeing.
Details. A chest pocket on the left, as on the models from the brands mentioned. A set-in, snug collar at Lady White.
Wear it with
Wear it under a shirt or with a cardigan, as the magazine Popeye shows, or alone with work pants.

17

Hawaiian shirt

aloha shirt · Hawaiian shirt · アロハシャツ · ハワイアンシャツ · 開襟シャツ

Origin
It was born in Hawaii, somewhere between the palaka work shirt and the kimono fabrics of Japanese immigrants. In 1904, the Japanese immigrant Chōtarō Miyamoto founded the Musa-Shiya shop in Honolulu. The term “aloha shirt” first appeared in one of its advertisements, on June 28, 1935, in the Honolulu Advertiser newspaper. Ellery Chun, a merchant at the King-Smith Clothiers store in Waikiki, registered “aloha sportswear” as a trademark in 1936. He registered “Aloha Shirt” in 1937, for twenty years. First made of silk, the shirt was mostly made of rayon, a man-made fiber, until the 1950s. Polyester arrived in the 1960s. Many of the fabrics came from Japan, notably from Kyoto. In 1961, Elvis Presley wore a red shirt by the designer Alfred Shaheen on the cover of “Blue Hawaii.” In 1966, “Aloha Friday” officially began: employers allowed men to come to work in aloha shirts on Fridays. In Japan, Toyo Enterprise, the company behind the reproduction brand Sun Surf, was founded in 1965 in Sumida (Tokyo). It succeeded Kosho & Co., a company created in the 1940s. In 1986, Patagonia launched its “Pataloha” surf line. In August 2024, the magazine Popeye recommends a second-hand one for summer.
The city boy way
Cut. Take it a little big: Popeye chooses a 2XL. Its hem is straight, and it is worn untucked.
Fabrics. Rayon for vintage models and Japanese reproductions. Poly-cotton printed on the reverse side (“reverse print”) for softened colors, as at Reyn Spooner.
Colors. Prefer discreet patterns and softened colors. Popeye likes those of the Pataloha line: simply drawn fish and plants, Japanese-inspired.
Details. An open collar, known as a Cuban collar. Popeye wears it wide open, to tone down the vacation effect.
Wear it with
In summer, with shorts and flip-flops, as in Popeye. In the city, over a white T-shirt, with wide pants.

18

Crewneck sweatshirt

crewneck sweatshirt · sweatshirt · スウェット · スウェットシャツ · トレーナー · reverse weave · loopwheel / 吊り編み

Origin
In 1920, Benjamin Russell Jr., quarterback of the University of Alabama football team, was fed up with itchy wool jerseys. He had his father's company make a practice jersey in heavy cotton: this was the birth of the sweatshirt and of the Russell Athletic brand. The Champion brand was born in 1919 in Rochester, New York, under the name Knickerbocker Knitting Mills. Its founders were Simon Feinbloom and his sons Abraham and William. In 1934, coaches complained that sweatshirts shrank in the wash. Champion then developed Reverse Weave: the fleece is cut crosswise, along its width. The patent, filed in 1938, was granted in 1952. In Japan, from the 1960s on, fast machines replaced the circular knitting machines imported from Europe in the early 20th century. Founded in 1999 by Satoshi Suzuki, the Japanese brand LOOPWHEELER has its fabric knitted in Wakayama on these old machines. They produce only about one meter of fabric per hour. Fleece knitted this way is called “loopwheel.”
The city boy way
Cut. A boxy cut, with a wide chest and unsloped shoulders, which rounds out the silhouette: that is how the magazine Popeye describes it. Choose it on the short side, to balance the width of the chest.
Fabrics. A thick, dry-feeling cotton that tightens up and gains body in the wash. For example a heavy jersey of about 8 ounces (around 270 grams per square meter), a loopwheel fleece or Reverse Weave.
Colors. Stick to the basic shades of the benchmark brands: heather gray (a mix of light and dark yarns), navy, ecru, black.
Details. Ribbed collar and cuffs. The body can be knitted as a tube, with no side seams, as at Loopwheeler. The German brand Merz b. Schwanen adds gussets, small triangular pieces sewn under the arms. The French site BonneGueule offers raglan sleeves, which run in one piece up to the collar. For decoration, just a university name or a small, discreet embroidery.
Wear it with
As a set, with matching pants in a relaxed but clean cut, as Popeye shows. Also wear it over an oxford shirt with roomy pants, or under a jacket in spring and fall.

Good to know

See also: Hoodie — the same knit, with a hood: same brands, same sizing advice.

See also: Tracksuit — for a matching jacket and pants, in knit trimmed with stripes.

Hoodie

hoodie · hooded sweatshirt · パーカー · フーディー · スウェットフーディ · sideline shirt

Origin
It appeared in the United States in the 1930s, first for workers in New York's cold-storage warehouses. According to Wikipedia, the Champion brand, based in Rochester, made the first ones. In the same decade, Champion also launched it for college sports, with the University of Michigan. It was then called the “sideline shirt,” the shirt worn on the edge of the field. In the 1970s, it gained visibility thanks to New York hip-hop, the designer Norma Kamali and the film “Rocky” (1976). The word “hoodie” came into common use in the 1990s. Tommy Hilfiger, Giorgio Armani and Ralph Lauren then offered them in their collections.
The city boy way
Cut. A roomy, boxy cut with a large hood, as the magazine Popeye describes it. Choose it on the short side or in a standard length, like the crewneck sweatshirt.
Fabrics. A heavy cotton fleece, brushed on the inside for extra softness. Popeye cites the one from the brand Los Angeles Apparel, which weighs 14 ounces, or about 475 grams per square meter.
Colors. Stick to basic shades: heather gray (a mix of light and dark yarns), undyed ecru, navy, black. Faded shades, obtained by pigment dyeing, also work.
Details. Double-layer hood, large kangaroo pocket on the front, drawcords.
Wear it with
As a set with matching pants, hood up on cool evenings, as Popeye suggests. Also wear it under a jacket or coat.

Good to know

See also: Crewneck sweatshirt — its history (Champion, Reverse Weave, loopwheel fleece) and its sizing advice.

Rugby shirt

rugby shirt · rugby jersey · rugger shirt · ラグビーシャツ · ラガーシャツ

Origin
It was first worn in the 1830s by schoolboys at Rugby, in Warwickshire, England. Everything about it serves the game: the dense cotton is tough yet allows movement, and the white collar stays easy to see. The rubber or plastic buttons do not cause injuries in tackles. Numbers on the back only arrived at the turn of the 20th century. In the United States, a Dartmouth College graduate (class of 1959) remembers seeing them on campus. The Dartmouth and Yale co-op stores sold a few, and the American clothier J. Press imported them from the United Kingdom. They then reached department stores. In the 1970s and 1980s, the American brands Gant (“Rugger” model), Lands' End, Brooks Brothers and L.L.Bean offered them. The Canadian brand Barbarian has been knitting and sewing them in Kitchener, Ontario, since 1981. In 1995, rugby union turned professional: on the field, collars shrank, sleeves got shorter and polyester replaced cotton. The cotton shirt lives on as a style garment.
The city boy way
Cut. A relaxed cut, in a standard length, worn over the pants. The London brand Drake's recommends going one size up to wear it over a shirt.
Fabrics. A heavy cotton jersey: up to 12 ounces at the brand Battenwear, or about 400 grams per square meter.
Colors. Choose wide stripes or color blocks: green, navy, burgundy, ecru, with a contrasting white or ecru collar.
Details. White shirt collar, made of woven fabric rather than knit like the body. Button placket below the collar; sometimes a chest pocket or felt college letters.
Wear it with
Pair it with chinos and a blazer or denim jacket, with loafers or sneakers, as the magazine Popeye shows. Slip a button-down shirt under or over it, as a discreet layer. The spirit stays preppy, that of students at private schools in the northeastern United States, without looking too sporty.

Good to know

Polo shirt

polo shirt · tennis shirt · knit polo · ポロシャツ · ニットポロ · 鹿の子ポロ · L.12.12

Origin
In 1926, the tennis player René Lacoste played the US Open in a white short-sleeved shirt of cotton piqué, a knit with a small raised texture. He called this fabric “jersey petit piqué”; the soft collar was unstarched. In 1933, retired from the courts, he teamed up with André Gillier to sell this shirt, embroidered with a crocodile, in Europe and North America. The first model was called the “L.12.12.” The name reads as follows: L for Lacoste, 1 for piqué, 2 for short sleeves, 12 for the twelfth prototype chosen. In 1972, Ralph Lauren sold a tennis shirt as a “polo shirt” in his Polo line, and the word stuck. In Japan, according to the magazine Popeye, the L.12.12s sold locally come from a Lacoste factory opened in 1988 in Akita.
The city boy way
Cut. A little roomy: Popeye even photographs an L.12.12 in size XXL. Knit polos, like the one from the Japanese store Beams, are worn relaxed and loose. Wear it untucked or tucked in, depending on the outfit.
Fabrics. Cotton petit piqué for the L.12.12. In spring and fall, a knit polo: merino wool, open-work knit or heavy cotton jersey.
Colors. Bold but classic colors. Popeye details the six permanent colors of the L.12.12, including black, burgundy and a deep green called “Lacoste green.” It also praises a lemon yellow with “French chic.”
Details. Clearly visible collar, two or three buttons, discreet embroidered logo: a crocodile for Lacoste, a laurel wreath for the British brand Fred Perry, also recognizable by its twin-tipped trim.
Wear it with
White jeans and leather shoes, Popeye suggests. For a preppy version, in the spirit of American private-school students, let the polo collar show and throw a sweatshirt over the shoulders. Also slip it under a rugby shirt.

Good to know

See also: Rugby shirt — a heavy cotton jersey shirt with a shirt collar, to wear over the polo.

Crewneck sweater

crew neck sweater · jumper · Shetland sweater · guernsey / gansey · Aran jumper · fisherman sweater · ニット · セーター · シェットランドセーター · ケーブルセーター · ガンジーセーター

Origin
It began as the wool sweater of fishermen and sailors from the British Isles and the Normandy coast. On Guernsey, knitting dates back to the late 15th century. The word “guernsey” appeared in a dictionary in 1851, and the sweater was widely issued to Royal Navy sailors in the 19th century. Contrary to legend, the Aran stitch, with raised cables, only appeared between the 1890s and the early 1900s. Sweaters from the west of Ireland were not exported to the United States until the early 1950s. According to the magazine Popeye, the Prince of Wales, the future Duke of Windsor, played golf in 1925 wearing a Fair Isle sweater. This multicolored patterned knit immediately won over golfers and young dandies. In Shetland, Jamieson's, founded in 1893, is one of the few knitting mills left on the island. In Normandy, Saint James, founded in 1889, still knits its striped sailor sweater with shoulder buttons. Its knit is so tight that it makes the sweater “almost waterproof,” according to the brand.
The city boy way
Cut. Wear it roomy and relaxed, like a sweatshirt, one size up: that is Popeye's advice. The traditional sailor sweater is longer, for better protection, Saint James explains. The others are worn untucked, in a standard length.
Fabrics. A rustic wool: Shetland (wool from the sheep of the Shetland Islands), brushed wool, tightly knitted virgin wool; cables in cotton or wool.
Colors. Royal blue, highlighted by Popeye in 2022. Also navy, ecru, green and sailor stripes.
Details. Ribbed crew neck. Depending on the model: cables (Aran sweater), shoulder buttons (sailor sweater), Fair Isle patterns, or bird's-eye (a small dotted pattern).
Wear it with
Over a T-shirt or an oxford shirt, with chinos, military pants or jeans; under a duffle coat or a navy blazer.

Good to know

Cardigan

cardigan · mohair cardigan · カーディガン · モヘアカーディガン · ケーブルニットカーディガン · gilet (en maille)

Origin
It owes its name to James Brudenell, 7th Earl of Cardigan. This British general led the Charge of the Light Brigade at Balaclava, during the Crimean War, in 1854. The garment spread after the war. In a 2025 column, the magazine Popeye recalls this origin: the buttoned opening is said to have made it easy to dress wounded soldiers. In the 1920s, Coco Chanel got women to adopt it. It is mostly associated with the students of the Roaring Twenties and the early 1930s; it came back in the 1950s, 1970s and 1990s. In the early 1990s, the musician Kurt Cobain wore a flannel shirt and a mohair cardigan, in a thrift-store style. This style was dubbed “grunge,” after his music, Popeye recalls in its issue No. 848 (2017). Founded in 1920 in Portland, Oregon, the knitwear house Dehen still knits its cardigans in worsted wool. It uses machines in service since the 1940s.
The city boy way
Cut. Close to the body at the London brand Drake's, slightly straight at the French site BonneGueule. Buy it in the usual size, or one size up to wear it over other layers. Choose a standard length or a little longer, to cover the waistband.
Fabrics. Mohair or brushed yarns, with a slightly fuzzy look; cotton cables; lambswool. It also comes in loopwheel fleece, knitted slowly on old circular knitting machines, with the comfort of a sweatshirt.
Colors. Greens (loden, lichen, forest), navy, heather gray, burgundy or ecru.
Details. Horn, mother-of-pearl or buffalo-horn-style buttons; patch pockets, sewn onto the front; V-neck. Nautical-inspired models sometimes have jacquard patterns, knitted into the fabric, or elbow patches.
Wear it with
Over an oxford or flannel shirt, with chinos or roomy jeans. In spring and fall, tie it over the shoulders, as in Popeye, or wear it as a light jacket.

Good to know

See also: Sweater vest — which also covers the sleeveless cardigan, buttoned and with pockets.

Sweater vest

sweater vest · slipover · tank top · sleeveless jumper · cricket vest · ニットベスト · スリップオーバー · チルデンニットベスト

Origin
Very common in the 20th century, especially in the United Kingdom in the 1970s, it came back into fashion in the 21st century. Cable-knit versions are traditionally worn by cricketers; golfers adopted it too. The British call it a “tank top” or “sleeveless jumper.” The site Ivy Style is devoted to Ivy style, that of the elite universities of the American East Coast. In 2015, it noted that tennis and cricket sweaters have been part of that style “for the last 100 years or so.” They are as traditional there as the Shetland crewneck, in wool from the Shetland Islands.
The city boy way
Cut. Take it one size up for a relaxed look, as the London brand Drake's advises; the English brand Universal Works cuts it roomy. It comes down to the waistband and is worn over a shirt, untucked or tucked in.
Fabrics. Lambswool, flecked recycled wool, cable-knit cotton in the manner of cricket sweaters; cotton and linen in spring and fall.
Colors. Navy, dark green, brown, ecru; Fair Isle patterns, multicolored geometric designs knitted into the fabric; contrasting trim, tennis- or cricket-style.
Details. V-neck, cables, and trim at the neck and armholes. There is a buttoned variant with pockets: the sleeveless cardigan.
Wear it with
Wear it over a T-shirt, with very light blue jeans, as in the magazine Popeye. In spring and fall, layer it over a shirt. Over an oxford shirt or a polo shirt, it adds a preppy touch, in the spirit of American private-school students.

Good to know

See also: Cardigan — the sleeved version, open and buttoned.

See also: Crewneck sweater — the Shetland crewneck, as traditional a piece of Ivy style as the cricket sweater.

Fishing vest

fishing vest · fly fishing vest · utility vest · フィッシングベスト · フライフィッシングベスト · ユーティリティベスト

Origin
It is a vest with many pockets, designed for fly fishing. It is short so it stays dry when wading into the water, and its pockets hold gear, explains the Japanese webzine Houyhnhnm. Lee Wulff (1905–1991) was an American fly fisherman. In spring 2008, the journal The American Fly Fisher presented him as the “innovator” of the fishing vest. In the 1980s, Setsumasa Kobayashi, founder of the Japanese brand Mountain Research, discovered the fishing vests of the brand Columbia. He had seen one on the artist Joseph Beuys and wanted the same. In 2017, he turned this into a collaboration between Columbia Black Label and Mountain Research. In 2023, the Japanese branch of the American brand L.L.Bean reissued one of its 1990s fishing vests, reports the magazine Popeye.
The city boy way
Cut. Roomy and unrestrictive, to go over a shirt or sweatshirt. Prefer it a little longer than the original, like the L.L.Bean reissue, lengthened for the city.
Fabrics. A very tightly woven nylon ripstop, like the one in the L.L.Bean reissue praised by Popeye. Ripstop is woven with a grid that stops tears from spreading. Utility versions also come in heavy cotton.
Colors. A vivid blue, or neutral shades: navy, black, beige, celadon green (a pale grayish green).
Details. Plenty of storage and an inner elastic belt that spreads the weight, on the Orvis fishing vests described by Houyhnhnm. Other common details: snap or flap chest pockets, a large back pocket, a D-ring to hang gear on.
Wear it with
Throw it on without fuss over a casual shirt, a plain T-shirt or a crewneck sweatshirt.

Good to know

See also: Down vest — the style's other sleeveless vest, filled with down.

Tracksuit

tracksuit · track jacket · track top · track pants · トラックジャケット · トラックトップ · トラックパンツ · ジャージ

Origin
In 1920, the French manufacturer Le Coq Sportif invented sweatpants, for athletes' comfort and freedom of movement. It then paired them with a matching top. In 1967, adidas created its first garment: a tracksuit launched with the soccer player Franz Beckenbauer. The flagship adidas Originals tracksuit is in fact named after this player, the “Emperor” of 1970s soccer, the magazine Popeye recalls. In the late 1970s, velour became the most common material. In 1986, the music video for “My Adidas” by the rap group Run-DMC tied the adidas tracksuit to hip-hop for good. In the late 1980s, the shiny triacetate or polyester tracksuit kept the trend going in the hip-hop and breakdance scenes.
The city boy way
Cut. Straight, relaxed pants, in the tradition of the adidas Beckenbauer model. The jacket is straight, with a stand collar, and stops at the waist. The pants can also be roomy and tapered at the ankle, full-length or slightly cropped, as at the English brand Universal Works.
Fabrics. Cotton-polyester knit for the Beckenbauer model; nylon for a 1990s feel. For a dressier version, loopwheel fleece, knitted slowly on old machines.
Colors. Retro 1970s colors, such as the dark green known as “college green,” navy or burgundy, or black, with contrasting white stripes.
Details. Piping or three white stripes, stand collar, zipper; period logos, like Umbro's double diamond or the adidas trefoil.
Wear it with
Push up the sleeves to highlight the white stripes, Popeye advises. Add a sleeveless leather vest on top, or a vintage piece from the period. Wear the jacket over a short-sleeved shirt, or pair it with pleated trousers to move away from head-to-toe sportswear.

Good to know

See also: Crewneck sweatshirt — the fleece sweatshirt, which Popeye also wears with matching pants, as long as the bottoms stay clean-cut.

See also: Elastic-waist pants — woven pants with an elastic waist, dressier than tracksuit pants.

Work jacket

chore coat · chore jacket · French work jacket · bleu de travail · coltin · veste de comptoir · カバーオール · フレンチワークジャケット

Origin
It appeared in France in the late 19th century, worn by factory workers, railwaymen and farmers. It was then made of coutil (a tightly woven cotton drill) or moleskin (a thick cotton that is soft to the touch). Its color earned it the name “bleu de travail,” literally “work blue”; the French army had already been dyeing its uniforms blue since the mid-19th century. Several French firms still in business claim early dates: Le Mont Saint Michel “since 1913,” Vetra founded in 1927. Le Laboureur has been based in Digoin since 1956; its work jacket is called the “coltin.” In the United States, the brand Pointer, founded in 1913 by L.C. King, was among the first makers of “chore coats,” jackets for farm chores. The first jacket of this kind from the brand Carhartt, in 1923, was made of blue denim; the brown canvas version came later. In Japan, the French work jacket is sought after: in 2024, the Japanese shop BIOTOP commissioned a goatskin version from Vetra.
The city boy way
Cut. Straight and fairly roomy, worn open as an outer layer. It stops at the hips, neither too long nor too short.
Fabrics. Moleskin, cotton twill (a weave with diagonal ribs), denim. For more fashion-forward versions: oiled cotton and linen, or leather.
Colors. Bright blue, known as cobalt, or faded blue: these are the two shades noticed by fashion YouTuber Percia Verlin. Also ecru, khaki, black.
Details. Three patch pockets (two at the bottom, one on the chest), turn-down collar, single-breasted front. Prefer models with few buttons, like those made in wartime, when materials were rationed.
Wear it with
A sweater, for instance a chunky-ribbed shaker style, vintage jeans and boots, as in an outfit shown by the magazine Popeye. Or work pants, or roomy chinos.

Good to know

See also: Relaxed blazer — Vetra and Universal Works also make blazers; the Bedford jacket by Engineered Garments sits halfway between a work jacket and a tailored jacket.

See also: Denim jacket — The other workman's jacket, cut from denim.

Coach jacket

coach jacket · coaches jacket · stadium jacket · コーチジャケット

Origin
It is the jacket worn by coaches on the sidelines of American sports fields. Sources disagree on when it first appeared. According to the English brand Universal Works, it was born in the stadiums of the 1960s and 1970s, hence its other name, “stadium jacket.” It was then made of nylon in team colors, with “COACH” in large capitals across the back. The Japanese brand The Real McCoy's places its appearance in the mid-20th century, before mass production in the 1970s. The French site BonneGueule dates it instead to 1980. In the 1990s, American streetwear took it up, with the rap groups Public Enemy and N.W.A, according to BonneGueule. In Japan, vintage college pieces are sought after.
The city boy way
Cut. Roomy and boxy, a little relaxed. It stops at the hips, with a drawcord that cinches the hem.
Fabrics. Nylon, sometimes ripstop, reinforced with a grid that stops tears from spreading; flannel or quilted lining for winter; corduroy variations.
Colors. Navy, black, olive. A bright color, yellow or cobalt, freshens up this ordinary piece, suggests the magazine Popeye.
Details. Snap buttons, pointed shirt collar, slanted pockets, drawcord at the hem; logo or lettering on the back.
Wear it with
A sweatshirt or hoodie, ripstop or cargo pants, sneakers. For a deliberate contrast, Popeye wears it over a shirt and tie.

M-65 field jacket

M-65 field jacket · M-1965 field jacket · field jacket · veste de campagne M65 · M-65フィールドジャケット

Origin
It is the US Army's field jacket, first issued in 1965. It succeeded the M-1951, itself derived from the M-1943 of World War II. Made to military specification MIL-C-43455, it switched in 1966 to a half-cotton, half-nylon fabric. It broke new ground with a hood rolled into the zippered collar and hook-and-loop tabs at the cuffs and collar. It has been made for the civilian market since at least the early 1970s. Vietnam veterans wore it at protests against the war. The French retailer De Toujours sees it as the jacket of young Americans in Vietnam, which became the emblematic multi-pocket military jacket of the counterculture.
The city boy way
Cut. A wide cut, worn roomy, true to military proportions. It stops at the hips, with a drawcord that cinches the waist.
Fabrics. Cotton-nylon sateen, or cotton sateen, a smooth, slightly shiny weave; removable quilted liner for winter.
Colors. Olive above all, the US Army regulation shade known as OG-107; also black or navy.
Details. Four flap pockets, and drawcords at the waist and hem.
Wear it with
Wear it over a sweatshirt or shirt, with chinos or roomy jeans. Without its liner in the fall, with it in winter: it lasts through several seasons.

Good to know

M-65 jacket or parka? The M-65 parka, known as the “fishtail,” is longer. Original pieces are getting rare, whereas they used to turn up in every vintage shop. In 2019, the Japanese webzine Houyhnhnm noted that their prices were rising every year, in Japan as in the United States.

See also: 60/40 mountain parka — Its cousin: the US Army mountain jacket, ancestor of the mountain parka, also derives from the M-1943.

Trench coat

trench coat · trench-coat · imperméable · トレンチコート

Origin
In 1853, John Emary, based on Regent Street in London, developed a waterproof wool cloth. He went into rainwear: this is the origin of the house of Aquascutum. In 1879, Thomas Burberry, whose house was founded in 1856 in Basingstoke, invented gabardine. This tightly woven fabric with diagonal ribs, breathable and waterproof, is the original trench coat fabric. The trench coat took shape around World War I, as a coat for British officers. The war added shoulder straps, for rank insignia, and D-rings, for map cases and equipment. Burberry and Aquascutum both claim to have invented it. After 1918, many veterans kept theirs, and it became a civilian garment. Film made it an icon, with actor Humphrey Bogart in “Casablanca” (1942). In Japan, it became a classic of men's winter wear from the 1930s, according to Japanese Wikipedia. The Japanese manufacturer Sanyo Shokai makes its “100-year coat” there, under the SANYOCOAT label.
The city boy way
Cut. Preferably choose it single-breasted, with the buttons hidden under a fly front. Buttoned up, such coats hang straight: “they kind of just look like a big tent,” says fashion YouTuber Percia Verlin. Long, below the knee, or short: both work.
Fabrics. Cotton gabardine, or coated cotton that water runs off.
Colors. Beige, green or dark blue, the shades Percia Verlin has noticed; also tobacco brown, worn on rainy days in the magazine Popeye.
Details. A tab under the collar that fastens to protect the throat; raglan sleeves, which run in one piece up to the collar. Straps at the cuffs; a back vent closed with a button.
Wear it with
Over workwear, for example a coverall from the American brand Dickies, as in Popeye, to mix workwear with military chic. Or with a turtleneck and roomy pants.

Good to know

Trench coat or balmacaan? Both are raincoats with raglan sleeves, often made by the same houses (Sanyo, Mackintosh, Grenfell). The balmacaan, named after a Scottish estate, has neither shoulder straps nor D-rings: it is a single-breasted coat with a small turn-down collar. The single-breasted trench with hidden buttons that Percia Verlin describes comes very close to it.

See also: Balmacaan coat — The other classic raincoat, more understated.

Balmacaan coat

balmacaan · balmacaan coat · raglan coat · mac · soutien collar coat · ステンカラーコート · バルマカーンコート

Origin
It takes its name from an estate near Inverness, in Scotland, on the west shore of Loch Ness. It is a single-breasted coat, often a raincoat, with a small rounded collar and raglan sleeves. It is made in tweed, a rustic woolen cloth, or in gabardine, a tightly woven waterproof fabric. The raglan sleeve, which runs in one piece up to the collar, is named after Lord Raglan, a British general in the Crimean War (1853–1856). The word “raglan” first referred to an overcoat. At American universities in the 1920s, students wore tweed raglan overcoats. The site Ivy Style, devoted to the style of the elite universities of the American East Coast, lists the balmacaan among the classics of that style. In Japan, the word “ステンカラーコート” (“soutien collar coat”), used for this kind of coat, is recorded as early as 1911. Released around 2008, the Soutien Collar Coat by the Japanese brand nanamica was still a hit in 2023, according to the Japanese webzine Houyhnhnm. It is lined with GORE-TEX, a waterproof, breathable membrane. The Japanese manufacturer Sanyo Shokai also keeps a Japan-made balmacaan in production.
The city boy way
Cut. Roomy and A-line, meaning wider at the bottom than at the top, and wide enough to go over a jacket or sweater. It is worn mid-length or down to below the knee.
Fabrics. Cotton gabardine or twill, cotton GORE-TEX, lightweight nylon; more fashion-forward versions in silk or wool.
Colors. Beige, navy, black; olive.
Details. Small turn-down collar that can be turned up; one-piece raglan sleeves; hidden button placket; tab under the collar, to close it at the throat.
Wear it with
Wear it around town over a jacket or sweater, thrown on casually.

Good to know

In Japan, the word “ステンカラーコート” (“soutien collar coat”) is often used for two different collars, which Japanese Wikipedia tells apart. The first is the balmacaan collar. The second is mounted on a collar stand, a band of fabric that holds it upright.

See also: Trench coat — Its military version: the same houses (Sanyo, Mackintosh, Grenfell), the same gabardines.

32

Relaxed blazer

navy blazer · unstructured blazer · sack blazer · 3/2 roll blazer · 紺ブレ · ネイビーブレザー · テーラードジャケット

Origin
The word “blazer” comes from the Lady Margaret Boat Club, the rowing club of St John's College, Cambridge, founded in 1825. Its oarsmen wore a red flannel jacket. In the 1860s, the blazer was a scarlet jacket for rowing and cricket. Founded at Yale in 1902, the clothier J. Press claims to have created the “Ivy League look.” This is the style of students at the elite universities of the American East Coast. In the 1920s, the navy blazer became a staple of that style, sold by the American clothiers Brooks Brothers and J. Press and worn at Harvard, Yale and Princeton. In the 1930s, the double-breasted navy blazer found its place between the casual tweed jacket and the dark suit.
The city boy way
Cut. A straight cut with natural shoulders and no stiff canvassing, the interlining sewn inside that gives a jacket its structure. Choose it on the wide side, with dropped shoulders, to wear it casually, as the Japanese webzine Houyhnhnm suggests. It keeps a classic length that covers the seat.
Fabrics. Navy wool, in flannel, serge or broadcloth; corduroy; cotton twill, workwear-style.
Colors. Navy first and foremost, the symbol of Ivy style and of preppy, its younger and sportier version, according to the magazine Popeye. As variations, brown, olive or tweed.
Details. Three buttons, with the lapel rolling down to the middle button, the only one fastened: this is called “3-roll-2” in English, 段返り in Japanese. Gold or horn buttons, patch pockets, a back vent known as a “hook vent,” whose top forms a small step.
Wear it with
Pair it with an oxford button-down shirt and chinos or gray flannel trousers. For a casual version, Popeye wears it with a knit vest, a T-shirt, light jeans and loafers.

Good to know

See also: Work jacket — Vetra and Universal Works also make work jackets; the Bedford jacket by Engineered Garments sits halfway between the two.

60/40 mountain parka

mountain parka · 60/40 parka · マウンテンパーカー · マウンパ

Origin
During World War II, the US Army produced a mountain jacket in small runs, derived from the M-1943, its field jacket. It was issued notably to the 10th Mountain Division. In 1968, Sierra Designs, a brand founded in 1965 in Berkeley, California, launched the “60/40 Parka,” in a fabric blending cotton and nylon. In 1976, the American brand The North Face released its Mountain Parka, which its Japanese line Purple Label reissues in 65/35 cloth. The company Goldwin has distributed The North Face in Japan since 1978; the city-oriented Purple Label line was born in 2003.
The city boy way
Cut. A straight, easy cut with raglan sleeves, which run in one piece up to the collar. The short version stops at the hips; there are also long models.
Fabrics. 60/40 cloth, meaning about 60% cotton and 40% nylon, or 65/35 cloth, polyester and cotton, at The North Face Purple Label. Also cotton-nylon ripstop, reinforced with a tear-resistant grid.
Colors. Moss green, sky blue, navy, green, olive; earth tones and khaki.
Details. Four flap pockets, heavy zippers, hook-and-loop cuffs, hand pockets, hood. Reissues of 1990s models keep their period paneling.
Wear it with
Over a synthetic shirt and a fleece, as in an outfit described by the magazine Popeye. Or simply thrown over everyday clothes, as the Japanese webzine Houyhnhnm suggests.

Good to know

Mountain parka or anorak? The anorak goes on over the head, with no full-length opening, and often has a large pocket on the stomach. The American brand L.L.Bean makes both.

See also: Anorak — Its pullover cousin, in lightweight nylon or cotton.

See also: Fleece jacket — The fleece, to slip underneath as a mid-layer.

See also: M-65 field jacket — The US Army field jacket, another descendant of the M-1943.

Anorak

anorak · smock · pullover parka · アノラック · アノラックパーカ

Origin
The word comes from the Greenlandic “annoraaq” and only entered the English language in 1924. In the early 1950s, the leisure anorak was made of nylon. It switched to poplin, a fine, tightly woven cloth, in 1959, the year Vogue magazine featured it. In France, Léon-Claude Duhamel created the K-Way in 1965: a coated nylon windbreaker that folds into a pouch worn at the waist. It sold 250,000 units in 1966. In 2023, the magazine Popeye showed an anorak from L.L.Bean Japan Edition, the Japanese line of the American brand L.L.Bean. It revives a 1984 model in fine, lightweight ripstop: a nylon woven with a tear-resistant grid.
The city boy way
Cut. Roomy, wide at the shoulders and chest. It stops at the hips, with a drawcord that cinches the hem.
Fabrics. Lightweight nylon ripstop; cotton in Indian madras (multicolored checks), plaid or poplin; Supplex, a windproof fabric that water runs off.
Colors. Bright colors or contrasting color blocks; madras, brown checks, red.
Details. No full-length front opening, only a half zip or a buttoned placket: it goes on over the head. Hood, large pocket on the stomach, drawcords at the waist and cuffs.
Wear it with
A high-neck top underneath, cargo pants or nylon shorts, and second-hand ankle boots, as in Popeye.

Good to know

Anorak or mountain parka? The mountain parka opens at the front with heavy zippers and has four flap pockets. The American site Heddels sums it up as “the iconic four pocket jacket.”

See also: 60/40 mountain parka — Its cousin in 60/40 cloth, a blend of cotton and nylon.

Fleece jacket

fleece jacket · fleece pullover · フリース · Synchilla Snap-T · Retro-X · Denali

Origin
The textile mill Malden Mills was founded in 1906 in Malden, Massachusetts, by Henry Feuerstein. In 1979, with the American brand Patagonia, it developed Synchilla (“synthetic chinchilla”), a lightweight synthetic pile meant to replace wool. Patagonia used it for its Snap-T pullover. Malden Mills, which later became Polartec, registered the PolarFleece trademark on October 6, 1981. Its boss, Aaron Feuerstein, chose not to patent the fabric, which spread to every manufacturer. In 2019, the American site Heddels noted that the Snap-T was still made of Synchilla. The Retro-X jacket was then widely worn on the streets of Tokyo.
The city boy way
Cut. Roomy and comfortable, often a pullover, with a snap collar like Patagonia's Snap-T, or full-zip like the Retro-X, from the same brand, or The North Face's Denali. It stops at the hips.
Fabrics. Polyester fleece (Synchilla) or curly pile (Retro-X). The North Face Purple Label, the brand's Japanese line, uses a wool-polyester boucle; there are also mohair versions.
Colors. Muted tones (charcoal, brown, natural) livened up by a contrasting detail: red zipper pull, blue piping (a thin sewn-in trim), colored panels. That is the case with a vintage fleece shown by the magazine Popeye.
Details. Snap collar and flap chest pocket on the Snap-T; chest pocket and windproof lining on the Retro-X; nylon panels on the Denali.
Wear it with
Wear it as a mid-layer, over a shirt and under a mountain parka, as in Popeye. In winter, it also works on its own over a shirt.

Good to know

See also: 60/40 mountain parka — In 60/40 cloth, a blend of cotton and nylon, to wear over the fleece.

Down jacket

down jacket · puffer jacket · down parka · ダウンジャケット · Nuptse · ヌプシ

Origin
The mountaineer Pierre Allain made down jackets from 1931 to 1964, in the workshop of his sporting-goods store in Paris. In the United States, Eddie Bauer founded the brand bearing his name in Seattle. In 1936, after a bout of hypothermia on a fishing trip, this outdoorsman developed a down jacket. In 1940, he patented the “Skyliner,” the country's first quilted goose-down jacket. From 1942, he produced more than 50,000 B-9 parkas for the US Army's air arm. Around the 1970s, the down jacket left climbing behind, and glossy lacquered-nylon models took over the cities. In Japan, it spread in the 1980s with amekaji, “American casual,” as a winter essential. Released in 1992, the Nuptse by the American brand The North Face became the archetypal “bubble” down jacket; the brand reissues its 1996 version.
The city boy way
Cut. Voluminous and short like the Nuptse, or straight in canvas like a parka, wide enough to slip a knit or a hoodie underneath. The “bubble” stops at the waist or hips; the down parka comes down to mid-thigh.
Fabrics. Goose or duck down; shell in nylon, in 60/40 cloth (about 60% cotton, 40% nylon) or in corduroy.
Colors. Black, khaki, olive, navy; bright touches are possible.
Details. Detachable hood, cargo or hand pockets, snaps under a flap. The quilting is stitched through, or built in boxes separated by fabric walls.
Wear it with
Over a sweatshirt or a hooded knit, with a big shirt, jeans or nylon cargo pants, and a cap or beanie. The magazine Popeye stresses its unisex side.

Good to know

Down jacket or down vest? The same fill, and often the same houses (The North Face, Pyrenex, Crescent Down Works, Rocky Mountain Featherbed). The down jacket is worn as the outer layer; the vest slips underneath.

See also: Down vest — Its sleeveless version, for layering.

Down vest

down vest · puffer vest · body warmer · ダウンベスト · インナーダウン

Origin
It is an outdoor piece from the 1970s. The workshop Crescent Down Works, whose products include the “Down Italian Vest,” has been making clothes in Seattle since 1974. In 2016, the American site Heddels cited a 1976 down vest by the brand The North Face. It inspired the brand Battenwear's Batten-Down Vest, with a half-nylon, half-cotton shell. In 2021, Heddels noted that the American brand Rocky Mountain Featherbed is known for its “Christy” vests. The Japanese company 35 Summers holds the license to reissue them.
The city boy way
Cut. A straight cut that stops at the hips. There are thin versions, made to slip under other layers.
Fabrics. Goose or duck down. Shell in 60/40 cloth (about 60% cotton, 40% nylon), in nylon and cotton, or in ultralight nylon taffeta.
Colors. Olive, navy, black, fawn and rust, khaki.
Details. Snaps or a two-way zipper, V-neck or padded stand collar, patch pockets; leather panels on some reissues.
Wear it with
Over a big shirt, with corduroy pants and a tie, as in the magazine Popeye. Or under a down jacket, with a shirt and chinos. Or simply thrown over a T-shirt, as Crescent Down Works suggests.

Good to know

Vest or down jacket? The magazine Popeye counts the vest among mid-layers, between the layers worn next to the skin and the jacket. The down jacket, for its part, is worn as the outer layer.

  • Buying without reading the fabric content: some outdoor vests, like The North Face's Aconcagua Vest, are filled with polyester, not down.

Denim jacket

denim jacket · trucker jacket · Type I / Type II / Type III · デニムジャケット · Gジャン

Origin
Levi Strauss & Co. launched the “Type I” jacket in 1905, then called the 506XX. In 1953, it was reworked and became the “Type II.” The Type III (model number 557), designed by Jack Lucier, came out in 1962, but was already in the October–December 1961 catalog. It dropped the pleats and rivets in favor of two V-shaped seams, and became model 70505 in 1967. In the 1980s, side pockets were added. It was around that time that collectors in the Japanese vintage clothing market coined the name “Trucker.”
The city boy way
Cut. Straight, a little roomy, worn open. Short, it stops at the waist.
Fabrics. 100% cotton denim, for example a Japanese selvedge of about 13.5 ounces (around 460 grams per square meter), raw or faded by wear. Selvedge is denim woven on old narrow looms, with finished edges.
Colors. Deep indigo or vintage fades, with orange topstitching that stands out, as the magazine Popeye points out.
Details. Pleats on the front and back, and two chest pockets, on the Type II; V-shaped seams on the Type III.
Wear it with
Slipped under a navy blazer with a turtleneck, and sandals to break up the look, as in Popeye. According to Levi's, it can be dressed up or down.

Good to know

39

Loafers

loafer · penny loafer · coin loafer · ローファー · コインローファー · Weejuns

Origin
A low slip-on shoe without laces. According to Wikipedia, a first “Wildsmith Loafer” may have been created in London in 1926 by Raymond Lewis Wildsmith, as a house shoe for King George VI. The American maker G.H. Bass, in Wilton, Maine, drew on the slip-on shoes worn by Norwegian farmers and fishermen. The company dates its “original penny loafer,” the Weejuns, to 1936. Wikipedia gives 1934, and the Japanese Wikipedia page points out the gap between the two dates. The strap is the band of leather set across the foot. In the 1950s, students at American private schools are said to have slipped a one-cent coin (a “penny”) into its slit. That would be the origin of the name “penny loafer,” according to one explanation among others. In 1946, the French house J.M. Weston created the “180” loafer, made entirely in its Limoges factory. According to the magazine Popeye, the house was founded in 1891 by Édouard Blanchard. In Japan, the Ivy wave of the 1960s, inspired by students on the American East Coast, made the loafer a staple shoe. It even turns up in school uniforms. The Japanese maker Regal has offered a Goodyear-welted penny loafer since 1972, a construction that allows the sole to be replaced.
The city boy way
Cut. A round, classic shape. The strap has a half-moon slit, or a seagull-shaped one at Weston. A low shoe.
Fabrics. Smooth leather, black or brown: calfskin (box calf) or glazed leather, with a shiny finish. Leather or rubber sole.
Colors. Black, burgundy, dark brown.
Details. Apron (the piece stitched on top of the foot) assembled by hand, raised seams along the sides. Blake construction (the sole stitched through the shoe) or Goodyear: both can be resoled.
Wear it with
Visible gray socks and pants that stop at the ankle, turned up once, as Popeye shows. The magazine presents Weston's 180 as a classic that goes with “any pants.”

Good to know

Loafer or boat shoe? Both share the same moccasin construction, with a hand-sewn apron. The boat shoe adds a leather lace that runs all around the shoe. It also has a non-slip rubber sole, invented by the American Paul Sperry in 1935. Several houses make both: Sebago, Paraboot, Quoddy, Yuketen.

See also: Boat shoes — The boat shoe, a laced moccasin with a non-slip sole.

See also: Clarks Wallabees and desert boots — The Clarks Wallabee is also a moccasin with an apron, on a crepe sole.

See also: Visible socks — Visible gray socks, which Popeye pairs with the black loafer.

Boat shoes

boat shoe · deck shoe · top-sider · デッキシューズ · ボートシューズ · スリーアイ（3eye）

Origin
In 1935, the American Paul A. Sperry, of New Haven, Connecticut, invented the modern boat shoe. He cut grooves into its sole with a knife after watching his dog run across ice without slipping. This was the birth of the Sperry Top-Sider brand. Its Authentic Original model follows that design: moccasin construction (the upper sewn by hand), rawhide lace, grooved sole. Sebago, a brand born in Maine in 1946, named its line of boat shoes Docksides. According to Wikipedia, the boat shoe moved from sailing gear to casual fashion in the 1970s. It became a trend in the 1980s. It came back in the late 2000s with the preppy style, the look of students at private schools in the northeastern United States.
The city boy way
Cut. A low moccasin, with a lace that runs all around the shoe. The city boy version is sturdier than the classic Sperry.
Fabrics. Oiled full-grain leather (the intact surface of the hide), or nubuck (sanded leather with a velvety feel). Rawhide lace, rubber sole.
Colors. Brown, light brown, navy in nubuck.
Details. Lug sole with chunky treads; hand-sewn apron (the top piece); two or three eyelets, the holes for the laces.
Wear it with
A canvas work jacket, for a slightly rugged East Coast look. That is the pairing shown by the magazine Popeye in content sponsored by Timberland.

Good to know

Thick-soled derbies

derby shoe · blucher · Tyrolean shoe · ダービーシューズ · チロリアンシューズ · 外羽根式プレーントウ · Paraboot Michael (ミカエル)

Origin
A sturdy walking shoe of Tyrolean inspiration, with open lacing: the two laced flaps are stitched onto the front of the shoe. The story of Paraboot begins in 1908, when Rémy-Alexis Richard, a farmer's son, left the shoe factory to set up on his own. In 1910 he married Juliette Pontvert, hence the company's name, Richard-Pontvert. In 1927 he registered the name Paraboot: “Pará,” an Amazon port that exported latex, and “boot,” a kind of shoe he had discovered in the United States. In 1945 came the Michael derby, named for the birth of Michel Richard, the founder's grandson. It is Norwegian-welted, with a very sturdy visible stitch that allows the sole to be replaced. Its rubber sole is called the Marche II. In 2025, for the Michael's 80th anniversary, the Japanese webzine Houyhnhnm recalled its roots as a Tyrolean shoe. In Japan, the maker Regal launched the 2504 plain-toe derby in 1969. It became a classic with the Ivy look, inspired by students on the American East Coast.
The city boy way
Cut. A round, generous shape that owns its volume. Plain toe, or Tyrolean, with an apron (an oval piece) stitched on top. A low shoe.
Fabrics. Oiled leather (fed with oils and waxes), smooth or in nubuck, a sanded leather with a velvety feel. Also Chromexcel, an oiled leather from the Horween tannery. Thick rubber sole.
Colors. Coffee brown, brown, black, cognac nubuck.
Details. Norwegian-welted construction, or Goodyear, another stitch that allows resoling. Rubber sole, like Paraboot's Marche II, or a lug sole from the maker Vibram.
Wear it with
Anything from a suit to shorts, and even sweatpants, according to Houyhnhnm. The magazine Popeye considers this kind of shoe ready to wear right away, with no break-in period for the leather.

Good to know

Retro running sneakers

retro running sneakers · dad shoes · ニューバランス · New Balance 990 / 996 / 1300 / 2002R / RC30 · Karhu Fusion · Diadora

Origin
Running shoes from the 1980s and 1990s, worn in the city. They combine suede, mesh (an open-weave synthetic fabric) and cushioned soles. In 1906, William J. Riley founded the New Balance Arch Support Company in Boston, which made arch supports. In 1960, its Trackster was the first running shoe offered in several widths. In 1982 came the 990 series, an all-terrain running shoe promoted with the slogan “990 points out of 1,000.” Its sixth version, the 990v6, arrived in Japan in 2022. Karhu, a Finnish brand founded in Helsinki in 1916, used three stripes as its emblem. In 1952, it sold them to Adidas for the equivalent of €1,600 and two bottles of whiskey. Karhu then adopted an “M” logo and launched the Fusion in 1996, since reissued as the Fusion 2.0. The Italian brand Diadora was founded in 1948 in Caerano di San Marco.
The city boy way
Cut. A bulky running silhouette, with a thick, cushioned sole. A low shoe.
Fabrics. Suede, including pigskin suede, and mesh.
Colors. New Balance gray above all, then neutral tones.
Details. A clearly visible midsole (the cushioning layer between the foot and the outsole), with New Balance's ABZORB or FuelCell cushioning. Made in the United States or the United Kingdom for the 900 and 1500 series.
Wear it with
Everyday clothes, in the city. Fashion YouTuber Percia Verlin notes that New Balance is still very present in Japanese menswear.

Canvas sneakers

canvas sneakers · キャンバススニーカー · Converse Chuck 70 · オールスター · Vans Authentic · Spring Court G2 · ヴァルカナイズ

Origin
Canvas basketball and tennis shoes, born in the early 20th century. Their sole is vulcanized: the rubber is baked in an oven, which hardens it and bonds it to the canvas. In 1908, Marquis Mills Converse founded the Converse Rubber Shoe Company in Malden, Massachusetts. In 1917, the brand created the forerunner of the All Star, sold under the name “Non-Skids.” In 2013, it launched the Chuck Taylor All Star '70, known as the Chuck 70, built like the All Star basketball shoes of the late 1960s. The G2, Spring Court's first tennis shoe, was born in Paris in 1936. It is made of cotton canvas, on a vulcanized sole pierced with four ventilation holes. Vans (Van Doren Rubber Company) was founded on March 16, 1966, in Anaheim, California. The model sold on opening day, a boat-deck shoe, would become the “Authentic.” The side stripe arrived in 1976 with the “Old Skool.” In Japan, Moonstar, based in Kurume, says it has been making shoes since 1873. It highlights vulcanization, which very few Japanese factories still practice.
The city boy way
Cut. An old-fashioned silhouette: a toe that barely turns up, classic proportions, like the All Star reissues or the G2. High-top or low.
Fabrics. Heavy cotton canvas, vulcanized rubber sole, cotton laces.
Colors. Ecru, off-white, beige; in spring, bold primary colors (red, yellow, blue).
Details. Glossy vulcanized sole, ankle patch. Converse Japan also sells a version made in Japan, the ALL STAR J.
Wear it with
Chinos, jeans, a student look: they are the canvas counterpart of running sneakers.

Clarks Wallabees and desert boots

Wallabee · ワラビー · Desert Boot · デザートブーツ · Clarks Originals · クラークス

Origin
Two suede shoes from the British brand Clarks, on a crepe sole, a thick, supple natural rubber. The brand was founded in 1825 by Cyrus Clark in Street (Somerset), where its headquarters still stand. The Desert Boot, designed by Nathan Clark, was officially released in 1950. During his military service in Burma, he had noticed suede ankle boots made in the bazaars of Cairo, which inspired him. Wikipedia dates the Wallabee to 1967: made in Kilkenny, Ireland, it was based on a moccasin called the Grasshopper. Clarks Japan gives 1966, and says it has been sold in Japan since 1971. According to Wikipedia, the rude boys, a Jamaican subculture, adopted Clarks in the late 1960s. The Desert Boot won over the mods, a British subculture. The Wallabee came back in the mid-1990s with the hip-hop group Wu-Tang Clan.
The city boy way
Cut. Wallabee: a moccasin with an apron (a piece stitched on top of the foot), wide and flat, low or high. Desert Boot: a two-eyelet boot that rises to the ankle.

Colors. The fawn shade called “maple” first, then dark brown and black.
Details. Thick crepe sole. The magazine Popeye advises slipping in a thick insole, for comfort.
Wear it with
Everyday clothes: it is an easy-to-wear leather shoe. In her 2024 video, fashion YouTuber Percia Verlin observed that Clarks were showing up more than boat shoes.

Birkenstocks

Birkenstock Boston · Birkenstock Arizona · ビルケンシュトック · ボストン · アリゾナ · cork footbed sandal

Origin
According to Wikipedia, Birkenstock was founded in 1774 by Johann Adam Birkenstock. Around 1896, Konrad Birkenstock developed the first contoured insole, shaped to fit the foot. In 1963, Karl Birkenstock launched the first sandal with a contoured footbed, the future Madrid model. The Arizona followed in 1973, and the Boston clog in 1976. The Japanese webzine Houyhnhnm confirms that date by celebrating the Boston's 50th anniversary in 2026, with a version made for the Tokyo store BEAMS. In 1966, the German-American dressmaker Margot Fraser discovered these shoes while taking a spa cure in Bavaria. She imported them to the United States, where they spread through health food stores and the counterculture.
The city boy way
Cut. Boston: a clog closed at the front, with one strap and a buckle. Arizona: a two-strap sandal. The London, which covers more of the foot, is for winter.
Fabrics. Suede or oiled leather, rather than Birko-Flor, the brand's synthetic material.
Colors. Taupe, mocha, tobacco brown; gray for the summer Arizona.
Details. Contoured footbed in Portuguese cork and latex, lined with jute and suede, made in Germany, according to the magazine Popeye.
Wear it with
Thick mohair socks in spring and fall. Popeye even shows the clog worn with a bathrobe, for a stroll around the neighborhood.

Good to know

46

Sport sandals

sport sandals · スポーツサンダル · Teva Hurricane (ハリケーン) · Teva Original Universal · SUICOKE (スイコック) · KEEN Newport · Chaco Z/1

Origin
Between 1982 and 1984, the geophysicist Mark Thatcher, a rafting guide, found that no shoe was suited to rivers. He created Teva in 1984: the first strapped sport sandal. The footwear company Deckers produced it under license from late 1985, then bought the brand in 2002. The Hurricane, released in 2002, became Teva's flagship model. In 2003, KEEN created the Newport, a sandal with a rubber-protected toe. The American brand Chaco, for its part, can repair its Classic sandal, with a single adjustable strap, in its Michigan workshop.
The city boy way
Cut. Two or three straps, a thick, cushioned sole. Some models are designed for the city, like the DEPA from the Japanese brand SUICOKE. A low, open shoe.
Fabrics. Polyester or nylon straps, neoprene (the synthetic rubber used in wetsuits). Rubber sole, made by the sole maker Vibram for SUICOKE.
Colors. Black, navy, chalk: neutral tones.
Details. Hook-and-loop closures or adjustable buckles, lug sole, molded footbed (the surface the foot rests on).
Wear it with
Light hiking clothes, like those from the brands Gramicci or Wild Things, or city clothes. The magazine Popeye sees them as a gateway to the “sandal hike.”

Good to know

See also: Birkenstocks — The Birkenstock and its contoured cork footbed, the city boy's other sandal.

47

Boots

work boots · moc toe boots · hiking boots · ワークブーツ · モックトゥ · アイリッシュセッター · 6インチ クラシックモック

Origin
Two families: American hunting and work boots, and hiking shoes. In 1905, Charles H. Beckman founded Red Wing Shoes in Red Wing, Minnesota. In 2008 the brand added a more fashion-oriented “Heritage” line. In 1952, its #877 hunting boot gave rise to a moc-toe boot, with the upper stitched like a moccasin's: this is the Irish Setter line. Red Wing points out that it was designed for hunters before being adopted by workers. The Timberland boot came out in 1973. Its success led the Swartz family, owners of the Abington Shoe Company, to focus on their own brand. The company was renamed The Timberland Company in 1978. The American maker Russell Moccasin says it has had a workshop on the banks of the Fox River, in Berlin, Wisconsin, since 1898.
The city boy way
Cut. A 6-inch (about 15 cm) moc-toe boot, or an old-fashioned hiking shoe, low or mid-height.
Fabrics. Oiled full-grain leather (the intact surface of the hide), rough-out leather (worn flesh side out) or nubuck; rubber sole, white or lugged.
Colors. Copper, orange and brown, the classics; pastels, blue or dusty pink, as a touch of color.
Details. Wedge sole (a single block, with no separate heel), like Red Wing's Traction Tred. Goodyear-welted construction, which allows the sole to be replaced, and triple stitching. For hiking, a vulcanized sole (baked rubber) or one from the maker Vibram.
Wear it with
Relaxed pants, with the old-fashioned hiking shoes selected by the magazine Popeye. With the work boot, loose-fitting clothes.

Good to know

Accessories

48

Bandana

bandana · bandanna · バンダナ · carré de coton

Origin
The bandana comes from India, where silk and cotton handkerchiefs, called bandhani, were dyed. It spread to the United States in the late 18th century: snuff takers preferred colored handkerchiefs, which hid stains. Between 1800 and 1830, the printed cotton square was in fashion in the West. Its pattern was often paisley, made of curved droplets of Indian origin. It became the necktie of workers: blacksmiths, farmers, sailors, cowboys, miners. In the 1930s, American miners wore red bandanas as neckerchiefs. The “Fast Color” bandanas (colorfast, meaning they don't bleed) produced from the 1940s to the 1970s serve as models for Japanese brands. According to the American retailer Standard & Strange, the Japanese brand Kapital draws on them for its cotton squares made in Japan. They are woven with a selvedge, a finished edge that doesn't fray.
The city boy way
Cut. A flat square, folded into a triangle or a band. It is tied around the neck or on the head, or used as a furoshiki, the Japanese square of cloth knotted into a bundle. About 50–55 cm per side, up to 70 cm for large sizes.
Fabrics. Light cotton, with a selvedge at Japanese brands; in winter, a wool-knit variant.
Colors. Red or yellow: it is the number one accessory for adding a touch of color, according to fashion YouTuber Percia Verlin. Also indigo and natural dyes.
Details. Classic paisley, or revivals of old “Fast Color” patterns. Also Japanese techniques: katazome (stencil dyeing), shibori (tie-dyeing), boro (mended patchwork).
Wear it with
Tied around the neck with a T-shirt or a work shirt, or on the head: an inexpensive accessory to liven up a neutral outfit.

49

Baseball cap

baseball cap · ball cap · 6-panel cap · キャップ · ベースボールキャップ

Origin
In 1860, the Brooklyn Excelsiors baseball team wore the forerunner of the baseball cap: rounded top, long visor, button on the crown. The magazine Popeye also dates its beginnings to around 1860. At the time it was a wool cap with eight panels, the sewn pieces of fabric that form the top. In 1920, Ehrhardt Koch founded the E. Koch Cap Company, the future New Era, in Buffalo, New York. In the 1940s the cap moved to six panels, for a better fit; the visor became standard, stiffened with latex. In 1954, Harold Koch modernized New Era's fitted cap under the name 59Fifty. In 1980, the brand began selling souvenir caps to fans: the cap left the ballpark.
The city boy way
Cut. Six panels, curved visor, a soft and fairly low crown (the part that covers the head), adjustable with a strap at the back. One size. Classic visor length, about 6.5 cm at the French maker Laulhère, longer at some Japanese brands.
Fabrics. Wool, in the spirit of old-time ballfields. Cotton twill (a diagonal weave), including chino; madras, a checked cotton; denim; indigo-dyed cotton.
Colors. Faded, classic tones: navy, beige, brown, green.
Details. Logos of defunct teams, minor leagues (the lower divisions of American baseball) or places. Leather or fabric strap; green under the visor, as on caps from Ebbets Field Flannels, an American specialist in replicas of old caps.
Wear it with
An amekaji outfit, the Japanese take on “American casual”: oxford shirt, sweatshirt, chinos, workwear.

Good to know

Bucket hat

bucket hat · fisherman hat · バケットハット · chapeau bob

Origin
It is said to have appeared around 1900 among Irish farmers and fishermen, in wool felt or tweed, as protection from the rain. The modern bucket hat derives from the olive cotton tropical hat issued to American soldiers during the Vietnam War. It entered fashion in the 1960s with the mods, a British subculture. In 1938, Jacques Spreiregen founded the hat brand Kangol in Cleator, Cumbria (England). The Kangol Bermuda Casual bucket hat became the signature of the rapper LL Cool J in his early days. In the 1980s, rappers adopted the bucket hat, which remained a street fashion classic into the 1990s.
The city boy way
Cut. A flat crown (the top of the hat), a short to medium brim, slightly sloping, about 5.5–6 cm. A soft shape, with no internal frame.
Fabrics. Washed cotton, heavy organic cotton canvas, technical nylon, rayon and cotton, or hand-crocheted cotton.
Colors. Khaki, olive, navy, black, beige; discreet prints (camouflage, small patterns).
Details. Small embroidered logo, drawcord or inner tie to adjust the size, small pocket.
Wear it with
Relaxed summer or outdoor outfits. In a podcast about hats, the website of the magazine Popeye notes that these history-laden kinds of headwear, the bucket hat among them, are also judged by the way they are worn.

Good to know

Short cuffed beanie

watch cap · fisherman beanie · beanie · ワッチキャップ · ニットキャップ · bonnet marin

Origin
As early as the 15th century, the Welsh town of Monmouth produced the oldest known type of knitted wool cap. From the 18th century on, the wool cap was the everyday headgear of sailors, fishermen and hunters. Its English name, “watch cap,” comes from the watch, the turn at guard duty kept aboard ships. The Japanese brand Buzz Rickson's makes an exact reproduction of the 1941 US Navy model, in worsted wool.
The city boy way
Cut. Short and worn high on the head, almost like a skullcap (a small cap fitted to the skull), with a single or double cuff.
Fabrics. Wool, including the pure wool of US Army surplus; merino; indigo-dyed cotton; acrylic at the entry level.
Colors. Navy, olive, black, khaki; also bright colors (orange, red) as an accent.
Details. Ribbing (raised vertical lines of knit stitches), cuff, a small label at most; a period label on military reproductions.
Wear it with
Work or military jackets, sweatshirts, parkas; in winter, in place of the cap.
