52

Beret

beret · béret basque · ベレー帽 · newsboy cap · casquette gavroche · ハンチング

Origin
According to archaeology and art history, headwear close to the beret has been worn in Northern Europe since the Bronze Age. Commercial production of the Basque beret began in the 17th century around Oloron-Sainte-Marie, in Béarn (southwestern France). The Beatex-Laulhère factory claims records going back to 1810; the Laulhère brand describes itself as “since 1840.” In 1889, the French mountain troops, the Chasseurs Alpins, were the first soldiers to adopt the beret. In 1924, King George V approved it for the British Royal Tank Regiment. In the 1980s, Kangol berets made their way into hip-hop, with Grandmaster Flash, Run-DMC, LL Cool J and Slick Rick.
The city boy way
Cut. A soft Basque beret in wool felt (fibers matted together, not woven), worn tilted or pushed back. A variant: the newsboy cap, with panels and a small visor. Top disc about 28 cm across; one stretch size, from 53 to 59 cm head circumference at Laulhère.
Fabrics. Felted merino wool, naturally water-repellent: water beads up on its surface. Silk and cotton for a summer newsboy cap.
Colors. Black, navy, and natural or muted tones: camel, khaki, mustard, burgundy.
Details. Satin inner lining, a small discreet label; six or eight panels for the newsboy cap.
Wear it with
Every day, until it feels natural: a person interviewed by the magazine Popeye describes getting used to it simply by wearing it. With knitwear, work jackets, coats. Fashion YouTuber Percia Verlin places it, along with the newsboy cap, among kinds of headwear a little more “ornate” than the baseball cap.

Good to know

Visible socks

crew socks · ribbed socks · ソックス · 靴下 · リブソックス

Origin
The invention of a knitting machine, in 1589, sped up sock making. Socks were then made of silk, cotton and wool, until nylon revolutionized production in 1938. In 1895, Franz Falke-Rohen founded Falke in Schmallenberg (Germany); the company built a new sock factory in 1920. On March 10, 1968, Naomasa Ochi founded Dan Socks, the future Tabio, in Japan. The brand opened its first store abroad in London, in 2002.
The city boy way
Cut. Ribbed (with raised lines of knit stitches), with retro sport stripes, or plain and thick: made to be seen. They reach just below the calf, and up to the knee for wool military models.
Fabrics. Cotton, including lisle, a smooth, lustrous twisted cotton, and combed cotton; thick military wool; hard-wearing cotton and nylon.
Colors. Gray with black loafers, a pairing chosen by the magazine Popeye. Olive, red or sport stripes as a touch of color; white with stripes for a sporty feel.
Details. Ribbing, retro triple stripe, reinforced heel and toe, a small motif at the heel, like the paisley motif of the Japanese brand Kapital.
Wear it with
Loafers and cropped or wide pants that let the sock show; the thick models with boots or work shoes.

Good to know

See also: Loafers — Gray socks show most with loafers and ankle-length pants.

54

Round glasses

round glasses · round frames · panto · Boston frames · 丸メガネ · ボストン

Origin
The round frames of this style are often inspired by 20th-century models from American opticians and manufacturers, reissued or reinterpreted by Japanese workshops. In 1899, Hyman Moscot, who had come from Eastern Europe through Ellis Island, sold ready-made glasses from a pushcart on Orchard Street, in New York. He opened his first store at 94 Rivington Street in 1915; Moscot has remained a family business. American Optical was founded in 1833; the brand dates its Original Pilot model, designed for the US military, to 1958. The AR model from the New York eyewear maker Tart Optical, sold from 1950 to 1952, has been reissued by Julius Tart Optical. In Japan, the eyewear maker Kaneko Optical was founded in 1958 in Sabae (Fukui), where it has three workshops. In 2009, the Japanese eyewear designer Yuichi Toyama launched his first label, USH, renamed YUICHI TOYAMA. in spring 2017.
The city boy way
Cut. Round lenses, or panto (round, with a flattened top), in prescription glasses as well as sunglasses. The magazine Popeye cites the artist David Hockney's large round glasses among iconic frames. The lens size, meaning the width of one lens, varies by model.
Fabrics. Acetate (a plastic made from cellulose) or thin metal.
Colors. Tortoiseshell, black, blond, tobacco and soft shades.
Details. On Julius Tart's AR reissue: a keyhole bridge, arch-shaped above the nose. A seven-barrel hinge, the metal rings that make it pivot.
Wear it with
Every day, as the piece that defines the face. The optician Yusuke Miyakawa, quoted by Popeye, advises choosing a frame with an eye on the style one aspires to, even if that means aiming a little high. Fashion YouTuber Percia Verlin points out that there is no need to spend a fortune.

55

Canvas tote

Boat and Tote · tote bag · canvas tote · ボート・アンド・トート · トートバッグ

Origin
The American verb “tote” (to carry, to haul) is attested in Virginia as early as 1677, and the phrase “tote bag” in 1900. In 1912, the hunter and fisherman Leon Leonwood Bean founded L.L.Bean in Freeport, Maine. In 1944, the brand launched a heavy canvas bag for carrying blocks of ice. This first “ice bag” became the Boat and Tote, still sewn by hand in the brand's workshops in Maine. In 2016, its Brunswick factory employed more than 450 people. In March 2026, for the model's 82nd anniversary, L.L.Bean released a “Tall Small” size. It has the base of the small (S) and the height of the medium (M), or 32 × 24 × 13 cm, so it carries better on the shoulder.
The city boy way
Cut. A structured tote that holds its shape, with a reinforced base and thick handles; bucket-shaped at SHIN+NA, a Los Angeles brand. L.L.Bean offers four sizes: S (8 liters), M (17 liters), L (35 liters) and XL (56 liters).
Fabrics. Very heavy cotton canvas at L.L.Bean: 24 ounces, a measure of the canvas's weight. Cotton denim at Everybody.World, a Los Angeles basics brand; canvas and leather at the French leather goods maker Bleu de Chauffe.
Colors. Ecru body, colored handles and base (navy, green…); many colorways at L.L.Bean Japan.
Details. Double stitching, short or long handles, monogram, zip-top version. Pockets and reversible models at Everybody.World and SHIN+NA.
Wear it with
Carried by hand, or on the shoulder with long handles. Fashion YouTuber Percia Verlin sews patches onto hers to add a touch of color.

Good to know

56

Porter bags

Porter Yoshida & Co. · Porter Tanker · Porter Force · ポーター · 吉田カバン · タンカー

Origin
In 1935, Kichizo Yoshida founded the workshop Yoshida Kaban Seisakusho, the forerunner of the Japanese bag maker Yoshida & Co. Its house brand, PORTER, was born in 1962. In 1983 came the TANKER series, which has become a classic. Its fabric is inspired by the US Air Force MA-1 flight jacket, and its lining is a “rescue” orange. In 2019, for its 35th anniversary, the series went back to the sage green of 1983, with stamped metal zipper pulls and an orange pouch. In May 2024, the Tanker switched to a nylon made entirely from plants, derived from corn and castor beans. This nylon was developed with the synthetic fiber maker Toray. The series also gained easier closures, removable pockets and metal parts whose paint wears off less.
The city boy way
Cut. Utilitarian shapes: waist bags, shoulder bags, pouches, 3-way bags (carried by hand, on the shoulder or on the back), backpacks. From the very small, like the Tanker keychain, to the large laptop backpack.
Fabrics. MA-1-style nylon for the Tanker; nylon woven like oxford shirt cloth and coated with acrylic, for the Force.
Colors. Tanker: black, green or blue. Force: navy, black or olive green. Orange interior.
Details. Removable pockets. On the Force, the pocket and the body are deliberately in slightly different shades, as on military surplus.
Wear it with
The Tanker waist bag is worn in front, loaded with pouches, rather than across the body. That is the advice of Koji, manager of the vintage clothing store danjil in Machida (Tokyo), in the Japanese webzine Houyhnhnm.

Good to know

Porter is a brand; the small shoulder bag, or sakosshu, is a shape. According to Japanese Wikipedia, it is a small flat bag worn across the body, which comes from cycling. It has no gusset, the fold that gives a bag depth. Porter makes several, including the Force Shoulder Pouch (15 × 18 cm), also featured in the Small shoulder bag sheet.

See also: Small shoulder bag — The small shoulder bag, of which Porter's Force Shoulder Pouch is an example.

Small shoulder bag

sacoche · shoulder pouch · crossbody bag · musette · サコッシュ · ショルダーバッグ

Origin
The Japanese word サコッシュ (sakosshu) comes from the French “sacoche,” which first meant a saddlebag. In Japan, it refers to a small flat bag without a gusset (the fold that gives a bag depth), worn across the body. It comes from competitive cycling, where it is used to carry food and drink during races. In March 2021, the magazine Popeye ran an article on Miyagawa Sports, a Tokyo sports shop that has been open for more than 50 years. Its hand-sewn bags of this kind are well known to the magazine's readers. Orders came in from all over the country after a bag made for the stylist Koichiro Yamamoto.
The city boy way
Cut. A small, flat pouch: about 15 × 18 cm for 1 liter, like Porter's Force Shoulder Pouch.
Fabrics. Coated nylon at Porter, canvas at SHIN+NA, a Los Angeles brand, and vegetable-tanned leather (tanned with plant extracts) at the French leather goods maker Bleu de Chauffe.
Colors. Understated tones: navy, black, olive green.
Details. Adjustable strap, front pocket. Orange lining and removable inner pockets on the Porter Force. At Miyagawa, a simple but solid construction, according to Popeye.
Wear it with
Worn crossbody, every day. Fashion YouTuber Percia Verlin prefers a bag worn across the body to one carried on the shoulder.

Good to know

See also: Porter bags — Porter's Tanker and Force series, where the Force Shoulder Pouch comes from.

Simple watch

wristwatch · Casio F-91W · Timex Weekender · field watch · チープカシオ · 腕時計

Origin
Two families come together here: cheap mass-market watches and military-inspired field watches. In 1854, the firm Benedict & Burnham created the Waterbury Clock Company, from which Timex descends. The Timex brand appeared in 1950; the name had been tried out as early as 1945 on a small batch of nurses' watches. In 1881, Kintarō Hattori opened the K. Hattori shop in Tokyo, the origin of Seiko. Seiko released the Laurel, the first Japanese wristwatch, in 1913, and launched Seiko 5 in 1963. In 1969, its Astron was the first quartz wristwatch to go on sale. The Casio F-91W came out in June 1989, the first model Ryūsuke Moriai designed for Casio. Wikipedia presents it as the best-selling watch in the world, but without citing a source. The watchmaker Hamilton presents its Khaki Field Mechanical as a faithful reproduction of a 1960s military watch.
The city boy way
Cut. An unpretentious watch. Either digital, in resin, in the “cheap Casio” spirit. Or three hands and a legible dial, in a 1960s spirit (Timex Marlin, Hamilton Khaki Field). A case from 34 to 40 mm.
Fabrics. Resin at Casio, steel; nylon, fabric or leather strap.
Colors. Black, cream or chocolate dials; colorful nylon straps.
Details. The F-91W runs on a battery rated for seven years. The nylon straps chosen by the magazine Popeye fit straight lugs (where the strap attaches to the case) no more than 18 mm apart.
Wear it with
Popeye deliberately pairs a cheap Casio with a high-end nylon strap from the brand Rimonta. Its “GEEK WATCH” series picks watches because they are fun, not for their prestige.

Keychain

key ring · keychain · key holder · carabiner · キーホルダー · キーリング · カラビナ

Origin
Wikipedia credits Samuel Harrison with inventing the key ring, in the 19th century. In the late 19th century, German and Austrian mountaineers adopted the carabiner, a metal ring with a spring-loaded gate. Its German name, Karabinerhaken, means “carbine hook”; its use is mentioned as early as 1879. The idea that the climber Otto Herzog invented it in the 1910s is a myth. Mini carabiners have become popular keychains.
The city boy way
Cut. A simple ring, a carabiner, or a small leather or nylon key holder. The one from the Japanese brand Hender Scheme measures 3 × 8.5 × 1.2 cm and holds three keys.
Fabrics. Cowhide at Hender Scheme, nylon for the Tanker keychain from the Japanese brand Porter, metal.
Colors. Natural or black for leather; bright colors are possible, as an accent.
Details. Removable ring; miniature replicas of pieces from the American brand L.L.Bean, such as its boots or its tote, as a nod to America.
Wear it with
On a simple ring, the magazine Popeye allows a cluster of charms. The carabiner clips onto a belt loop or a bag.

色

Chapter 05

05

Colors

Navy, khaki, ecru, denim: a base of muted colors, meaning colors that are not very bright. And, to liven it all up, a small bright touch.

The principle

A muted base, a bright touch

City boy is not a black-and-white style.

The term “city boy” refers to the ideal reader of Popeye, a Japanese men's magazine founded in 1976 by the publisher Magazine House. The base colors of this style are navy blue, khaki and beige, olive, ecru, gray, brown and denim.

But an outfit that stops there soon turns drab, warns the Japanese vintage clothing store RushOut on its blog. A small area of bright color livens it up: a bandana, a beanie, socks, a bag.

In short. Almost all of these shades go with one another, which makes it easier to put an outfit together without overthinking it.

About the color codes

The swatches in this chapter give a visual reference, with their on-screen color code (such as #1F2A44). They are typical shades, chosen for illustration, not official references. A single name, “olive” or “beige,” covers a whole range of shades.

The base colors

The color chart

Blues

Navy blue

ネイビー · 紺 (kon)

The quintessential base color: blazer, sweater, sweatshirt, work pants. Popeye paired it with gray as early as its 2012 relaunch (“gray and navy,” for “a boy on the verge of adulthood”). In 2021, it recommended it with white and gray, all worn “tastefully.”

Role. Dark base color, often used instead of black.

With. gray, white or ecru, light blue, tonal navy (several shades of navy together).

Season. Year-round; in summer, preferably with white.

Reference ≈ #1F2A44

See the looks

Light blue

サックスブルー (sakkusu burū) · 水色 (mizuiro)

The blue of the Oxford shirt or the striped shirt. Popeye treats it as a classic: the blue shirt appears in its 2013 city boy ABC. In 2021, the magazine slipped “the usual blue striped shirt” under a winter coat.

Role. Light color on top, most often the shirt.

With. navy, white, green pants, beige or khaki, denim.

Season. Year-round, including winter under a coat.

Denim

デニム · インディゴ

Jeans are everywhere. Popeye also likes denim “more faded than usual” (2025). Fading that comes from wear, stronger at the knees and thighs, is seen as a virtue.

Role. Color of the pants, and of the denim work jacket.

With. white, gray, navy, beige.

Season. Year-round; with a white T-shirt in summer; faded in spring.

Reference ≈ #3E5C82

Greens and earth tones

Olive green

オリーブ · アーミーグリーン

The green of military fatigue pants and field jackets. It is the pants color Percia Verlin sees “over and over and over again.”

Role. Color of the pants, or a statement piece such as the field jacket.

With. a blue top, brown, white, dark denim.

Season. Year-round; Popeye paired “brown & olive” in spring 2025.

Reference ≈ #5B5E3A

Ivy green

アイビーグリーン

A dark green, associated with the Ivy style of American universities and distinct from military olive. In 2021, Popeye ran the headline: “Apparently, I'm haunted by Ivy green.”

Role. Signature color of a single piece, ideally a sweater or sweatshirt.

With. light blue, ecru, gray, khaki.

Season. Fall and winter.

Reference ≈ #2F4F3A

Khaki and beige

カーキ · ベージュ

The color of chinos and light work pants. “Khaki” here has its English meaning, a sandy beige; in French, the word usually means a greenish brown. Percia Verlin counts beige pants, “khaki specifically,” among the bottoms that keep coming back. For the Japanese site WardRove, beige is the safest choice for wide chinos.

Role. Color of the pants.

With. light blue, navy, white, brown shoes.

Season. Mostly spring and summer (chinos, shorts); Popeye also ran a “Beige Book” in its fall 2018 issue.

Reference ≈ #C8B79A

See the looks

Camel and coyote

キャメル · コヨーテ

Sandy browns, warmer than beige. Popeye lists both in its ABCs: “Coyote Color” in 2012, “Camel” in 2022.

Role. Coat or sweater, for an earthy touch.

With. navy, ecru, gray.

Season. Fall and winter.

Reference ≈ #A67B4B

Brown

ブラウン · 茶 (cha)

The brown of leather shoes (derbies, boat shoes, loafers) and, in fall, of whole garments. In 2018, Popeye ran the headline: “classic brown, with a light touch.”

Role. Leather shoes and accessories; a fall piece.

With. beige, olive, navy socks.

Season. Fall and winter for clothes; year-round for shoes.

Reference ≈ #6B4A2F

Neutrals

White and ecru

白 · 生成り (kinari, ecru)

The white T-shirt under the shirt, white pants, the blue and white of summer. WardRove advises pushing white toward ecru, an off-white, to avoid an outfit that looks too studied.

Role. The light in the outfit: a visible inner layer, summer pants.

With. denim, navy, green, beige.

Season. Mostly summer; as an inner layer, year-round.

Reference ≈ #EFE8D8

Heather gray

グレー · 杢グレー (moku gurē)

The gray of the college sweatshirt and of New Balance sneakers. Heathering blends fibers of different colors, which gives a nuanced gray.

Role. Mid-tone neutral: sweatshirt, flannel pants, shoes.

With. navy, denim, white.

Season. Popeye devoted a winter feature to it in 2014; the sweatshirt is worn year-round.

Reference ≈ #A7A9AC

Black and charcoal

黒 · チャコール

Present, but to anchor the outfit rather than dominate it. The store RushOut points out that the style is not limited to black, white and gray, and WardRove advises softening black into charcoal, a very dark gray.

Role. An anchor (shoes, pants), in moderation.

With. white, gray, one bright color.

Season. Popeye wrote about “winter black” in 2020; year-round for shoes.

The detail that changes everything

The bright touch

Against this muted background, a small area of color changes everything. Percia Verlin sees the bandana as the accessory most often used to add red or yellow. The store RushOut also mentions the bag, sneakers, beanie and socks.

In short. The bright color stays a small area. A whole piece in a strong color, such as a green or orange sweatshirt, is worn with neutrals.

Red

赤 (aka)

The first color Percia Verlin mentions for the bandana. In 2022, Popeye also said it wanted a bright red hoodie like the one worn by Elliott, the young hero of the film E.T.

Role. A bright touch, on a small area.

With. navy, denim, white, olive.

Season. Year-round.

Reference ≈ #B3261E

Yellow, yellow-green, orange

イエロー · オレンジ

The most common bright touches in the outfits shown by Japanese fashion guides: a yellow bag, yellow sneakers, a yellow-green beanie. POPEYE Web, Popeye's website, also mentions sweatshirts in bold “Gatorade-like” colors, after the sports drink. It sees these colors as typical of clothes made in the United States.

Role. Accessory, shoes, beanie, or a bold-colored sweatshirt.

With. neutrals: navy, gray, beige, black.

Season. Mostly spring and summer.

えんじ色 (enji-iro) · ピンク

Rarer, but embraced. In a 2024 issue, Popeye highlighted “enji,” a deep carmine red that is the color of Tokyo's Waseda University. Pink is the P entry in its 2022 ABC.

Role. An occasional colored piece.

With. gray, navy, beige.

Season. In spring (2024) and in fall and winter (2022).

Pairs and trios

The combinations that keep coming back

Twelve combinations keep coming back in the pages of Popeye, in Percia Verlin's video, and in guides published by Japanese stores and websites. They make good starting points.

Blue on top, green on the bottom

A blue shirt or top, green pants, often fatigues. It is the combination Percia Verlin sees most.

Source: Percia Verlin, YouTube, 2024.

Gray and navy

The palette that suits “a boy on the verge of adulthood,” according to Popeye's issue on classics, in fall 2012.

Source: Popeye, November 2012.

White, gray, navy

Sportswear worn tastefully, for spring.

Source: Popeye No. 888, 2021.

The blue and white of summer

A white T-shirt and jeans: for Popeye, the great classic of summer style.

Source: Popeye No. 891, 2021.

Brown and olive

One of the keywords of the spring 2025 issue devoted to the finer points of clothes and how to wear them.

Source: Popeye No. 936, 2025.

Navy head to toe, lit up with white

A single-color outfit, where a white layer brings in the light.

Source: the Japanese online store prips, 2024.

Tonal blues and white

Several shades of the same blue with a white accent; or else a white shirt, navy and denim.

Source: prips, 2024.

White and green

Relaxed green pants with a crisp white shirt.

Source: prips, 2024.

Brown and beige

Brown gives the outfit structure, beige lightens it.

Source: prips, 2024.

Gray and indigo

A gray shirt with jeans rather than black pants, to keep things relaxed.

Source: prips, 2024.

Earth tones, broken up by a neutral

Beige, khaki, olive and brown together, but separated by a white layer and black or dark brown shoes. That way, the outfit does not look like a construction worker's.

Source: WardRove.

A neutral base and a bright touch

A sober base (navy, khaki, beige) and a small bright area: bandana, bag, sneakers, beanie, socks.

Source: RushOut.

A safeguard for beginners

The site WardRove advises sticking to three colors per outfit, to keep a clean look. This advice comes from a 2025 guide aimed at people aged 30 to 50. It is not a Popeye rule, but it is a good way to start.

The seasons

A synthesis, not a rule. Popeye does not publish a color chart by season. What follows brings together article titles from its spring, summer, fall and winter issues.

  1. 01

  2. 02

    Blue and white, a white T-shirt and jeans (2021); pale shirts, shorts.

  3. 03

    Fall

    Classic brown with a light touch and the “Beige Book” (2018), Ivy green (2021), camel, tweed and checks.

シルエット

Chapter 06

06

Silhouettes

More than the pieces themselves, it is the proportions that make the city boy: volume, but volume by choice.

The principle

No rules, just proportions

No source sets an official city boy silhouette.

Popeye, a Japanese men's magazine founded in 1976 by the publisher Magazine House, made the “city boy” its ideal reader. It works by example (street photos, fashion shoots), never by rules. The eleven typical silhouettes in this chapter therefore group published examples; they are not rules.

What they share is roominess, but a considered roominess. In 2022, Popeye declared the end of oversize (deliberately too-large clothes) worn without a second thought.

In short. The collar and shoulders stay where they belong; the volume comes from the cut of the garment.

Words for it

The vocabulary of proportions

Japanese fashion guides describe silhouettes with letters and a handful of precise words. Here they are, explained.

A-lineAライン
The top is neat or close to the body, and the bottom widens like the letter A. This comes from wide pants, or from a long top that draws the eye downward.
I-lineIライン
Straight and close to the body from top to bottom, much like a suit. It is more or less the opposite of the city boy, who relaxes this line.
Y-lineYライン
The volume is at the top (long coat, down jacket, loose shirt or T-shirt), and the bottom is slim.
O-lineOライン
A rounded, barrel-shaped fullness. For RushOut, a Japanese vintage clothing store that publishes advice on its blog, it is the foundation of the city boy look. By contrast, a Japanese stylist's site reserves it for people who take care of their face and feel confident in their looks. A foundation for some, a demanding line for others: it is a true marker of the style.
X- and H-linesXライン · Hライン
Two more recent terms: X for a defined waist, H for a straight, roomy silhouette. Some guides link the H-line to the O-line.
Big silhouette, oversizeビッグシルエット · オーバーサイズ
A garment cut or chosen roomier than the fitted size. W. David Marx, an American author based in Tokyo, traced the history of American style in Japan in Ametora (2015). In a 2024 essay, he credits Akio Hasegawa, Popeye's fashion director from 2012 to 2018, with the “big silhouette” look of the late 2010s. In 2022, the magazine put an end to oversize by default.
Yurutto, loose silhouetteゆるっと · ルーズシルエット
“Loose,” “relaxed.” For the Japanese store JEANS FACTORY, pulling everything together into a wide, relaxed silhouette is the key to the city boy style.
Wide pants, baggy pantsワイドパンツ · バギーパンツ
Pants that are wide along their whole length; “baggy” comes from the word bag.
Balloon pantsバルーン
Roomy at the thigh, tapering toward the ankle. This is the cut recommended by Percia Verlin, a fashion YouTuber whose video “City Boy starter pack” (April 2024) was the starting point of this monograph. She wants pants that are wider, “more balloon shaped,” with pleats (folds sewn in at the waist).
Nukekan抜け感
Literally “a sense of letting go”: leaving a little air (roominess, soft fabric, a slight shift in tone) in an otherwise polished outfit. It is not sloppiness. For the Japanese fashion site WardRove, sloppiness means never having put your outfit in order. Nukekan means relaxing after you have.
Konarekanこなれ感
Ease: the outfit looks like what the person wears every day, not a costume. WardRove defines it as a state in which nothing looks out of place.
Layeringレイヤード · 重ね着 (kasanegi)
Visible layers: a T-shirt under the shirt, a shirt under the sweater or vest. Popeye looks closely, right down to how much white T-shirt shows.
Length丈 (take)
The length of a garment. In 2018, Popeye ran a section on pant length.
Ankle length7～8分丈 · アンクル丈
So-called “7/8” pants, which show the ankle, and therefore the sock, without having to be rolled up.
The “three necks”3首 (mikubi)
Showing the neck (open collar), wrists (sleeves pushed up) and ankles (hems rolled up) makes an outfit lighter. In Japanese, the wrist and ankle are called the “neck of the hand” and the “neck of the foot,” hence the name.
Tuck inタックイン
Tucking the top into the pants. POPEYE Web, the website of the magazine Popeye, recommends tucking in a loose shirt while leaving it some volume around the waist.
Size balanceサイズバランス
The balance between top, bottom and shoes; a theme in its own right for Popeye in 2025.
Sweater tied across the chestたすき掛け (tasukigake)
A sweater knotted diagonally across the torso, like the Japanese sash called a tasuki.

Sources: かめたくルーム (menswear blog); RushOut (the vintage store's blog); UPGRADE FASHION (a stylist's site); Popeye No. 900 “実用とシック” (released March 9, 2022), table of contents on magazineworld.jp; JEANS FACTORY (store), spring city boy guide; Japanese Wikipedia, “バギーパンツ”; Percia Verlin, “City Boy starter pack (Japanese Americana),” YouTube, April 29, 2024; WardRove, “抜け感・こなれ感とは？”; Japanese Wikipedia, “重ね着”; Popeye October 2018, No. 858 (released September 7, 2018), table of contents on Fujisan; チェンジングミー (stylists' site), “抜け感とは！？”; POPEYE Web, “若きシティボーイに必要な服。” (issue 912, 2023); Popeye No. 936 (released March 7, 2025), table of contents on magazineworld.jp; Popeye No. 906 “シティボーイのABC”, fall–winter 2022, table of contents on magazineworld.jp.

Examples, grouped

Eleven typical silhouettes

01

The loose shirt, tucked in

ビッグシャツのタックイン

A loose shirt, in oxford cloth or stripes, tucked into wide pants (pleated chinos, work pants, jeans): the volume is there, but held in at the waist.

Proportions. A loose top held in at the waist, a loose bottom; the whole outfit doesn't billow.

The pieces. Oxford button-down shirt, Chinos, Wide pleated trousers, Straight or wide jeans, Thick-soled derbies, Loafers.

Size. For a shirt already cut loose, POPEYE Web advises going about one size down. The volume comes from the cut, not from a size that is too big.

Avoid. Letting a very loose shirt billow over pants that are just as loose. RushOut tucks the shirt in “so the silhouette isn't too baggy.”

See the looks

Sources: POPEYE Web, “若きシティボーイに必要な服。”; RushOut (blog), outfit No. 9; RushOut (blog), outfit No. 1.

02

The loose shirt, worn untucked

オーバーサイズシャツ（裾出し）

The variation: a wide shirt that flares toward the hem, designed to be worn over the pants. Percia Verlin contrasts it with the slim shirt made to be tucked in.

Proportions. A wide, long top that covers the belt; a straight or wide bottom.

The pieces. Loose shirt worn untucked, US Army fatigue pants (OG-107), Chinos.

Size. Try before you buy. For Percia Verlin, the fit of a shirt is “in a lot of ways the most important thing.” So she advises looking for one in person, at a thrift store.

Avoid. Wearing a slim dress shirt untucked when it was made to be tucked in: the cut has to be designed to be worn over the pants.

See the looks

Sources: Percia Verlin, YouTube video, April 29, 2024.

03

The O-line: a vest over the shirt

Oラインシルエット（ベスト×シャツ）

A rounded silhouette: a shirt, a sleeveless vest on top, loose pants; the shirttail shows below the vest.

Proportions. Volume at the top and bottom; the vest gives the torso structure, the shirttail adds ease.

The pieces. Sweater vest, Fishing vest, Down vest, Loose shirt worn untucked, Retro running sneakers.

Size. Neither too tight nor too big: a little roomier than a fitted size, without going all the way to oversize, according to RushOut.

Avoid. Too much oversize tips the outfit into streetwear, the fashion of the street, RushOut warns.

See the looks

Sources: RushOut (blog); RushOut (blog), outfit No. 3; JEANS FACTORY.

04

The A-line: a neat top, wide pants

Aライン（ワイド／バルーンパンツ）

A simple top (Breton shirt, T-shirt, shirt) and wide pants, ideally pleated or balloon-shaped. With this cut, even khaki pants avoid looking like a uniform.

Proportions. The volume sits below the waist; the top stays neat.

The pieces. Breton striped shirt, Heavyweight T-shirt, Wide pleated trousers, US Army fatigue pants (OG-107).

Size. Choose pants cut wide rather than straight pants a size too big. Percia Verlin looks for something “a little bit wider, more balloon shaped.”

Avoid. Basic chinos, which look like a uniform according to Percia Verlin. On narrow shoulders, the A-line can exaggerate a slight frame, a Japanese menswear blog warns.

See the looks

Sources: かめたくルーム; Percia Verlin, YouTube video, April 29, 2024; Popeye No. 925 “ぼくと服と東京の暮らし。” (released April 9, 2024), table of contents on magazineworld.jp.

05

Layering

レイヤード（白T×シャツ×ニット／スウェット）

Visible layers: a white T-shirt under an open shirt, a shirt peeking out beneath a sweater, or a sweatshirt worn as a middle layer in spring.

Proportions. Layers of slightly staggered lengths (neckline, hem, cuffs); moderate roominess so they stack.

The pieces. Heavyweight T-shirt, Oxford button-down shirt, Crewneck sweater, Cardigan, Crewneck sweatshirt, Wide pleated trousers.

Size. Choose the outer layer roomy enough to cover without squeezing.

Avoid. Layering without paying attention to what shows: Popeye is particular about exactly how much white T-shirt peeks out.

See the looks

Sources: prips, guide of June 6, 2025; Popeye April 2025, No. 936, table of contents on Fujisan; POPEYE Web, “若きシティボーイに必要な服。”; Popeye April 2020 (released March 9, 2020), table of contents on Fujisan.

06

Wide shorts and tall socks

シャツ×ショーツ×ハイソックス

A shirt, often striped, fairly wide cotton or nylon shorts and tall, clearly visible socks. On the feet, Clarks (suede shoes with crepe soles), derbies or sneakers. It is the summer outfit, somewhere between boyhood and a polished look.

Proportions. A loose top, wide shorts at or just above the knee, the leg cut by the tall sock.

The pieces. Shorts, Visible socks, Clarks Wallabees and desert boots, Thick-soled derbies, Baseball cap.

Size. Fairly wide shorts; the top can be compact or loose, depending on the balance you're after.

Avoid. Ignoring how the shorts and socks work together in fabric and color: Popeye made it a topic in 2025.

See the looks

Sources: JEANS FACTORY; Popeye April 2025, No. 936, table of contents on Fujisan; prips, guide of June 6, 2025; RushOut (blog), outfit No. 7.

07

Cropped loose pants

7～8分丈のゆるいパンツ／ロールアップ

Loose pants that stop above the ankle, or are rolled up, to show the sock; often with a neat shirt.

Proportions. A wide leg and a high hem: the sock becomes part of the outfit.

The pieces. Wide pleated trousers, Visible socks, Loafers.

Size. Length matters more than width: Popeye ran a section on pant length in 2018.

Avoid. Thin socks with chunky sneakers, according to WardRove. And don't treat it as an absolute rule: Popeye also pays attention to the “break,” the fold that longer pants make over the shoe.

See the looks

Sources: RushOut (blog), outfit No. 6; チェンジングミー; Popeye No. 858 “みんなのマイ・ウェイ。” (released September 7, 2018), table of contents on magazineworld.jp; POPEYE Web, “若きシティボーイに必要な服。”; WardRove, “メンズ靴下の色は何に合わせる？”.

08

A single work or military piece

ワーク／ミリタリーの一点投入

A blue work jacket, an olive field jacket or straight fatigue pants. The piece is paired with ordinary clothes (white shirt, navy sweater, jeans), not with a full matching outfit.

Proportions. A short, boxy jacket that ends at mid-hip; fatigues straight from top to bottom; cargo pants (with large thigh pockets) of moderate width.

The pieces. Work jacket, US Army fatigue pants (OG-107), M-65 field jacket, Cargo pants.

Size. For cargo pants, WardRove recommends a moderately roomy, fairly straight cut, not a very wide one.

Avoid. Wearing it all at once (field jacket, bulky cargo pants and heavy boots): it looks like an outfit for work or the mountains.

See the looks

Sources: WardRove, “カーキコードとは？”; Popeye No. 888 (released March 9, 2021), table of contents on magazineworld.jp; Percia Verlin, YouTube video, April 29, 2024; Popeye No. 900 “実用とシック” (2022), table of contents on magazineworld.jp.

09

The long coat over several layers

ロングコート×フーディ×ワイドパンツ

A wool coat, a single-breasted trench coat or a balmacaan (a coat with a small turn-down collar), thrown over a hoodie. Below, wide pants or track pants, and understated shoes.

Proportions. One large vertical mass (buttoned up, a trench coat looks like “a big tent,” says Percia Verlin); layers showing at the collar; neat footwear.

The pieces. Trench coat, Balmacaan coat, Hoodie, Tracksuit, Wide pleated trousers.

Size. A coat cut roomy from the start. Back in 2016, Popeye was already asking where those “huge clothes” came from.

Avoid. Weighing down the bottom half too: the Japanese online store prips keeps “the footwear sleek.”

See the looks

Sources: prips, guide of June 6, 2025; Percia Verlin, YouTube video, April 29, 2024; Lach Thomson, “The Rise of the City Boy,” Yokogao Magazine; Popeye No. 834 “風が吹いたらコートを、カフェ・オ・レにはセーターを。” (released September 10, 2016), table of contents on magazineworld.jp.

10

Urban outdoor

アーバンアウトドア

A technical rain jacket, fleece, vest or fanny pack, mixed with city clothes (shirt, chinos, wide pants). As early as 2012, Popeye treated it as a staple of city dress.

Proportions. A technical top, often roomy; wide or cycling-inspired pants; technical sneakers.

The pieces. Anorak, Fleece jacket, Down vest, 60/40 mountain parka, Retro running sneakers.

Size. No precise rule: the examples mostly show roomy cuts.

Avoid. A head-to-toe mountain outfit in the city, according to WardRove.

See the looks

Sources: Popeye November 2012 (released October 10, 2012), table of contents on Fujisan; Popeye No. 943 “山から街まで着たい服。” (released October 9, 2025), table of contents on magazineworld.jp; JEANS FACTORY.

11

Relaxed Ivy

現代風アイビー（紺ブレ×チェックシャツ×ワイド）

The vocabulary of Ivy, the style of students at America's Ivy League universities (navy blazer, oxford or check shirt, chinos). Here it is worn loose and casual, sometimes with sneakers.

Proportions. A fairly boxy jacket, inherited from the softly structured Ivy jacket; wide pants.

The pieces. Relaxed blazer, Flannel check shirt, Oxford button-down shirt, Chinos, Canvas sneakers, Loafers.

Size. No rule in numbers: the volume comes from the cut.

Avoid. Copying proper, fitted Ivy: for JEANS FACTORY, roominess is what makes the city boy.

See the looks

Sources: JEANS FACTORY; English Wikipedia, “Ivy League (clothing)”; Lach Thomson, Yokogao Magazine.

Attention to detail

The art of layering

Layering is a subject in its own right at Popeye, which examines it very closely. The magazine looks at the shirt peeking out beneath a sweater, how much white T-shirt shows at the neck of a sweatshirt, how the shorts go with the socks.

In spring, while it is still cool, POPEYE Web recommends an “anonymous” sweatshirt, with no distinguishing marks, that also works as an underlayer.

See the layered looks

The question that keeps coming up

What size should you buy?

Should you go up one or two sizes?

No, not as a matter of principle. None of the magazines, guides and stores cited in this chapter makes it a rule. They converge on a different idea: choose roomy cuts, not sizes that are too big. Adjust to the original cut, sometimes by going one size down. And try things on.

  1. 01

    Neither too tight nor too big

    A little roomier than the fitted size, without going to extreme oversize.

    RushOut

  2. 02

    Sometimes one size down

    For a cut that is already roomy, go about one size down.

    POPEYE Web

  3. 03

    A reason for every size

    No more oversize by default: every choice of size has to be justified.

    Popeye No. 900, 2022

  4. 04

    Clean roominess

    Shoulders that don't droop, a torso with room but not sloppy, fabric that doesn't pull when you move.

    WardRove

  5. 05

    Forget about size

    The Japanese brand Graphpaper does away with the notion of size as far as possible, so that its clothes fit every body type.

    Graphpaper

The takeaway. What separates intentional roominess from clothes that simply don't fit is what stays fitted: the collar and the shoulders, where they belong.

Sources: RushOut; POPEYE Web; Popeye No. 900; WardRove; Graphpaper, “Concept” page of its website.

はじめの一歩

Chapter 07

07

Getting started

There is no need to buy everything, or to buy everything new. Ten pieces are enough to start, and most can be found second-hand for a few dozen euros. Here is where to begin, how much to budget, where to look in France and what is best avoided.

The mindset

Choose little, choose well

Popeye, a Japanese men's magazine founded in 1976 by the publisher Magazine House, made the “city boy” its ideal reader. For its 50th anniversary, in 2026, it defines him as someone who knows how to enjoy the city. Faced with endless choices, the city boy knows how to “edit”: to sort through things and keep what he needs.

In this anniversary issue, fashion comes first. That is “not because it is the most important thing,” the editors explain, but because it helps you enjoy the city freely. In other words: a small wardrobe of classics, rather than a complete outfit bought all at once.

Percia Verlin, a fashion YouTuber whose video “City Boy starter pack” (April 2024) was the starting point of this monograph, offers the most useful method. Spot a piece at a brand, then type its exact name into second-hand sites: it's cheaper, and better for the environment.

The takeaway. Start with the basics, wear them often, then add one piece at a time. It is also the best way to discover your own proportions before investing in an expensive piece.

In three steps

1. Start from the list. The ten pieces below form a base, to be filled out little by little.

2. Look second-hand first. Use the exact model name, on the resale sites Vinted (the European second-hand clothing app), eBay or Grailed, or in thrift stores.

3. Try things on. Especially shirts and pants: the fit matters more than the brand.

one piece at a time!

Sources: POPEYE Web (the website of the magazine Popeye), introduction to No. 951, June 8, 2026; Percia Verlin, “City Boy starter pack (Japanese Americana),” YouTube, April 2024.

The starter wardrobe

Ten pieces to start, then a few for variety

The first eight pieces come from the model wardrobe that Popeye published in this anniversary issue, in June 2026. Added to them are the work jacket and the cap, two classics of the style that Percia Verlin often mentions. Check them off as you go.

Level 1 · The first ten pieces

  • Oxford shirt — sky blue or white, loose, to wear untucked or tucked in.
  • Chinos — heavy, fairly wide, even pleated (folds sewn in at the waist), to avoid the uniform look.
  • Jeans — straight or moderately wide, never skinny; raw (never washed) or faded.
  • Heavyweight T-shirt — white or gray, boxy, fairly short.
  • Crewneck sweatshirt — heather gray or navy, in heavy cotton.
  • Hoodie — plain, with a hood that holds its shape.
  • Crewneck sweater — in rustic wool, worn like a sweatshirt.
  • Canvas sneakers — white or off-white, in a classic shape.
  • Work jacket — blue, with three pockets, worn open over a sweater.
  • Cap — six panels and a soft crown, in faded tones.

Level 2 · For variety

  • Olive fatigues — the piece Percia Verlin says she sees “over and over and over again,” ideally with a blue top; also sold as baker pants. New, expect around €100–300 from the classic brands Stan Ray, orSlow or Buzz Rickson's; second-hand, search for “og107,” the reference number of the US Army fatigues.
  • Wide pleated trousers — for the roomy silhouette, with casual pieces.
  • Big shirt — wide, especially toward the hem, worn untucked.
  • Breton shirt — in heavy cotton, the Breton way, or as a loose striped T-shirt.
  • Retro running sneakers — gray New Balance, or Karhu and Diadora for a change.
  • Loafers and visible socks — gray socks that show beneath pants cut at the ankle.
  • Navy blazer — soft, worn with a T-shirt or light-wash jeans.
  • M-65 jacket or mountain parka — the US Army field jacket or the parka, for spring and fall.
  • Canvas tote — structured, with thick handles.
  • Short beanie and bandana — the cheapest touch of color.
  • Duffle coat — the last classic on Popeye's list, for winter; it has no entry on this site.

Sources: POPEYE Web, No. 951, “Almost Always,” June 8, 2026; Percia Verlin, YouTube video, April 2024; entries in Chapter 04.

How much to budget

Three rough budgets

Here are three ways to buy the ten Level 1 pieces. For new clothes, the ranges cover an entry-level model and a high-end model, sold by the brand or a retailer. For second-hand, they use the prices of the Vinted listings cited in the Chapter 04 entries.

The takeaway. The gap between A and B comes almost entirely from buying second-hand. Second-hand, jeans, chinos or a sweatshirt often cost a quarter of the new price, or less. The most sensible approach is probably to mix: second-hand to test cuts, new for the pieces worn every day.

Where to buy in France

Stores, websites and French brands

Places to try things on

  • Kiliwatch, a vintage store in Paris (64 rue Tiquetonne, 2nd arrondissement). It mixes vintage with new Japanese or American denim (Edwin, Japan Blue, Momotaro, Lee, Wrangler). Handy for trying several cuts of jeans in one place.
  • Centre Commercial, a clothing store in Paris, at 2 rue de Marseille (10th arrondissement) and 26 rue de Charonne (11th arrondissement). It carries denim jackets from the Japanese brands orSlow and Big John, and down jackets from the Japanese brand Nanga. Its neighboring store, Centre Commercial Outdoor (10 rue de Marseille), is devoted to outdoor gear.
  • Courir, a chain of stores in France, with a website: New Balance, Converse, Vans, Timberland and Clarks shoes.
  • Strictly, an online store based in Bordeaux, in southwestern France: M-65 jackets from the brand Alpha Industries.
  • Doursoux, a military surplus store in Chennevières-sur-Marne (Val-de-Marne, outside Paris), with an online store.
  • Opticians that sell glasses from the Japanese brand Yuichi Toyama: L'Ingénieur Chevallier (17 rue des Pyramides, Paris 1st), Carlotti (40 rue Saint-Sulpice, Paris 6th), Jonathan Optic (17 rue des Rosiers, Paris 4th), E. Jandot (35 rue Franklin, Lyon 2nd).

Online, in euros

The online retailer Zalando carries Levi's, Polo Ralph Lauren, GANT, Brooks Brothers, New Era, Patagonia and Teva; Courir also sells online. BonneGueule, a French menswear advice site, sells its own clothes. L'Exception, a French online store, sells sweatshirts. Largeot & Coltin sells French workwear online. Cultizm, a German online store, sells Japanese reproductions (orSlow, Fullcount, Japan Blue) and Carhartt WIP. Dickies, Alpha Industries, Karhu, Sebago and Red Wing also have their own European stores. In pounds sterling: Clutch Cafe, a London store (Buzz Rickson's, The Real McCoy's, Jelado), and the online store of the brand Stan Ray.

Second-hand

Thrifting smart

  1. 01

    The exact name

    Percia Verlin advises spotting a model at a brand, then typing its exact name into eBay or Grailed. The method also works on Vinted and Etsy. Typing “pantalon og107” (French for “og107 pants”) brings up real fatigues. “dickies 874” finds chinos for €15–30, and “champion reverse weave” sweatshirts for €10–20.

  2. 02

    Vinted first

    Well-known models are plentiful there. Expect €15–60 for a pair of Levi's 501s and €200–300 for Paraboot Michael derbies. Timberland 3-Eye boat shoes range from €30 to €300. A vintage Scottish Shetland sweater goes for €30–70. Searches that are too vague bring up the wrong things: “bob vintage” (“bob” is French for bucket hat) turns up Bob Marley and SpongeBob, known in French as “Bob l'éponge.”

  3. 03

    Label Emmaüs

    Label Emmaüs is the nonprofit online store of the Emmaüs charity shops in France. Stock is limited, but prices are low. Lacoste polo shirts range from under €10 to €70, sailor sweaters from €5 to €30. A Champion sweatshirt costs a few euros.

  4. 04

    Thrift stores and surplus

    Percia Verlin recommends the nearest military surplus store, which often has real fatigues. She also says bandanas can be found in any thrift store. Surplus Le Marsouin, a military surplus store in the Bouches-du-Rhône, in southern France, that sells online, offers the French Army's F2 fatigues. Old but never worn, they cost about €30; they are, however, cut short.

  5. 05

    Read the label

    OG-507 military pants, in polyester and cotton, are not OG-107s, the American fatigues in cotton sateen. “Mohair” sold by a fast-fashion chain is often synthetic. A “Down Parka” can be filled with synthetic insulation. Check the fabric content before buying.

  6. 06

    What not to buy worn

    A well-worn Birkenstock sandal has taken the shape of someone else's foot. By contrast, Norwegian-welted derbies or Goodyear-welted boots are still good buys if the leather is sound, even with a worn sole. Both ways of stitching the sole allow it to be replaced.

Sources: Percia Verlin, YouTube video, April 2024; Vinted and Label Emmaüs listings cited in the Chapter 04 entries; Surplus Le Marsouin.

Sizes and proportions

Finding the right size

The general rule is in Chapter 06: choose roomy cuts rather than sizes that are too big, and keep the collar and shoulders where they belong. But every model fits differently. Here is the sizing advice given by manufacturers, by a store and by Popeye. “Loopwheel” refers to a heavy jersey knitted as a tube on old machines.

Sizing advice, model by model
PieceAdviceWho says so
Paraboot Michael derbiesHalf a size below your usual shoe size.Paraboot, the manufacturer
G.H. Bass Larson loafersRuns large: go down about half a size.G.H. Bass, the manufacturer
Spring Court G2 sneakersBetween two sizes, take the larger one.Spring Court, the manufacturer
Alpha Industries M-65 jacketRuns very large: take one or two sizes down.Strictly, an online store based in Bordeaux
Merz b. Schwanen loopwheel T-shirtRuns small and shrinks: go up at least one size.Merz b. Schwanen, the manufacturer
100% cotton loopwheel sweatshirtExpect about 2 cm of shrinkage in length.Loopwheeler, a Japanese sweatshirt brand
Flannel shirtOne size up, to fit a zip-up hoodie underneath.Popeye, 2024
Rugby shirtOne size up, to wear it over a shirt.Drake's, a London brand
Pants with loafersCut at the ankle and turned up once, to show the sock.Popeye

In short. When buying second-hand, the measurements matter more than the size on the label. For pants, the waist and the leg opening; for a jacket, the shoulder width. Measure the garment laid flat, then compare with one you already like.

Sources: product pages from Paraboot, G.H. Bass, Spring Court, Merz b. Schwanen and Loopwheeler; Strictly; POPEYE Web; Drake's.

Avoid

Beginner mistakes

  1. 01

    Oversize by default

    “Wearing oversized clothes without a second thought is over,” writes Popeye: every choice of size needs a reason. Popeye No. 900, 2022

  2. 02

    Chinos that look like a uniform

    For Percia Verlin, standard-cut chinos have nothing interesting about them. Choose them wider, pleated or in a balloon cut that tapers at the ankle. Percia Verlin's video

  3. 03

    The slim shirt, tucked in

    The city boy shirt is loose, whether it is worn untucked or tucked in. Percia Verlin contrasts it with the slim shirt made to be tucked in. And a shirt has to be tried on: its fit is what matters most. Percia Verlin's video

  4. 04

    The sweatshirt with shapeless pants

    Worn with shapeless sweatpants, a sweatshirt or hoodie looks like loungewear: the bottom half should stay neat. POPEYE Web

  5. 05

    Workwear that's too rugged

    Popeye advises lightening up workwear: aim for lightness rather than a laborer's look. POPEYE Web, 2026

  6. 06

    The textbook outfit

    Wearing the navy blazer too much by the book, as a full preppy uniform, the kind worn by students at American private schools. The idea is to dress it down. POPEYE Web

  7. 07

    Loafers without socks

    Popeye prefers visible gray socks with black loafers. POPEYE Web, 2022

  8. 08

    Overpaying for an accessory

    For Percia Verlin, a bandana at more than about €40 is already expensive for what is “essentially a cloth.” Percia Verlin's video

  9. 09

    The full costume

    In short. Lumberjack from head to toe, yacht-club sailor, old-time laborer: recreating a costume betrays the spirit of the style. The style mixes a piece from one world with a piece from another (see Chapter 03).

  10. 10

    Investing before trying

    In short. Before buying a Japanese reproduction for over €200, test the cut with a second-hand model. A pair of Levi's 501s for a few dozen euros on Vinted is enough to find out whether you like straight jeans.

Chapter 08

08

Glossary

Popeye, a Japanese men's magazine founded in 1976 by the publisher Magazine House, made the “city boy” its ideal reader. The style that bears the name speaks three languages: the magazine's Japanese, the English of American clothing and the technical vocabulary of the workshop. Here are 128 words to help you find your way, with a link to the relevant entry where there is one.

From A to Z

The words of the style

60/40
A fabric blending cotton and nylon, introduced in 1968 by the California brand Sierra Designs for its mountain parka. The name gives the ratio: 60% cotton, 40% nylon. 60/40 mountain parka
ABC of the city boy (The) シティボーイのABC
A manifesto feature in Popeye, laid out like an alphabet book. It was the theme of the first issue of the relaunched magazine, in 2012; it came back in 2013, 2014 and 2022.
Aloha shirt アロハシャツ
An open-collar Hawaiian shirt. The term “aloha shirt” first appeared in an advertisement published in Honolulu in 1935. Hawaiian shirt
Amekaji アメカジ
Japanese abbreviation of “American casual”: casual American clothing (jeans, chinos, sweatshirts, sneakers, varsity jackets, boots, bandanas, military surplus) and the way it is worn. Amekaji
Ametora アメトラ
“American traditional”: the classic American wardrobe, Ivy and preppy. It is also the title of the book Ametora (2015) by W. David Marx, an American author based in Tokyo, which traces the history of American style in Japan.
Anorak アノラック
A jacket pulled on over the head. The word comes from the Greenlandic “annoraaq”; it did not appear in English until 1924. Anorak
Baker pant ベイカーパンツ
The civilian name, popularized in Japan, for the US Army utility pants with large patch pockets. It is not a military term: soldiers spoke of “fatigues” (work uniform). Baker pants
Balloon (balloon cut) バルーン
A “balloon” shape: roomy at the thigh, tapering toward the ankle. Percia Verlin, a fashion YouTuber whose video “City Boy starter pack” (April 2024) was the starting point of this monograph, associates it with city boy pants. Wide pleated trousers
Balmacaan ステンカラーコート
A single-breasted coat with a small turn-down collar and raglan sleeves, which run in one piece up to the collar. It is named after an estate near Inverness, in Scotland. In Japan it is often called a “soutien collar coat.” Balmacaan coat
Bandana バンダナ
A large square of printed cotton, often with a paisley pattern, of Indian origin. In the 19th century, it was the “necktie” of American laborers, farmers, sailors and cowboys. For Percia Verlin, it is the most common accessory for adding a touch of color. Bandana
BEAMS ビームス
A store opened in February 1976 in Harajuku, a Tokyo neighborhood: about 25 m², designed like a Californian student's bedroom. It became one of Japan's three big select shops (stores that pick and mix several brands), along with SHIPS and United Arrows.
Bermuda shorts
Shorts that stop just above the knee. Their invention is credited to the manager of a tearoom in Bermuda, in 1914. Vogue magazine was using the term “Bermuda shorts” as early as 1948. Shorts
Big silhouette ビッグシルエット
A very roomy cut. According to W. David Marx, this look of loose sweatshirts and sportswear was born at Popeye in the late 2010s. It was launched by Akio Hasegawa, the magazine's fashion director from 2012 to 2018.
Blake, Goodyear
Two ways of stitching the sole of a dress shoe; both allow a worn sole to be replaced (resoling). Loafers
Bleu de travail
Blue workers' clothing, jacket and pants, whose name appeared in France in the 19th century. The jacket is what English speakers call a “chore coat.” Work jacket
Boat and Tote ボート・アンド・トート
A heavy canvas tote introduced in 1944 by the American brand L.L.Bean for carrying blocks of ice. It has become a classic of Americana, the traditional American wardrobe. Canvas tote
Boxy
A square cut: a wide body and shoulders with no slope, which rounds out the silhouette. Used mostly of sweatshirts and T-shirts. Crewneck sweatshirt
Brutus ブルータス
A magazine launched at Magazine House in 1980 by Yoshihisa Kinameri, former editor-in-chief of the weekly Heibon Punch. It is Popeye's big brother.
Chambray シャンブレー
A light cotton cloth whose name comes from Cambrai, in France. The US Navy authorized it in 1901; later adopted by American workers, it gave rise to the expression “blue collar.” Chambray shirt
Cheap Casio チープカシオ
Japanese nickname for inexpensive Casio watches, such as the F-91W. Simple watch
Cheap chic チープシック
Elegance achieved with well-made, practical and affordable clothes. It is the title of an American book by Caterine Milinaire and Carol Troy, Cheap Chic, and a recurring feature in Popeye (2013, 2024). Cheap Chic
Herringbone (HBT)
“Herringbone twill”: the herringbone weave of US Army work uniforms during World War II. It was replaced in 1952 by the cotton sateen of the OG-107. US Army fatigue pants (OG-107)
Chino チノパン
A cotton twill (a fabric with fine diagonal lines) of military origin and, by extension, the beige or khaki pants made from it. Chinos
Chore coat
A short work jacket with patch pockets. In its blue French version, it is the jacket of the bleu de travail. Work jacket
City boy シティボーイ
A cultured young city dweller who pays attention to the details of his life. It is Popeye's label (“Magazine for City Boys”) and, by extension, the style that goes with it. The term was already in fashion before 1976: Popeye did not invent it.
City boy would do it this way (A) シティボーイならこうするね
A recurring phrase in Popeye used to give advice on fashion, decorating your room or everyday life.
City girl シティガール
The female counterpart, present in Popeye (the issue “シティガールたちよ！”, meaning “Calling all city girls!”, 2018). According to the magazine, city girls enjoy wearing men's clothes just as much as the boys do.
Coach jacket コーチジャケット
A light nylon jacket worn by coaches on the sidelines of American sports fields in the 1960s–1970s; hence its other name, “stadium jacket.” Coach jacket
Band collar バンドカラー
A straight, standing band that circles the neck with no folded-over part. Loose shirt worn untucked
Dead stock デッドストック
Old stock that has never been worn: a new garment, but one made in another era.
Desert boot デザートブーツ
A two-eyelet suede ankle boot on a crepe sole, introduced in 1950 by the English brand Clarks. Its creator, Nathan Clark, drew on styles he had seen during his military service in Burma. Clarks Wallabees and desert boots
Diguru ディグる
From the English “dig”: to spend a long time searching thrift stores, flea markets or record bins for the right piece.
Double knee ダブルニーパンツ
Work pants with knees reinforced by a second layer of canvas. Work pants and painter pants
Easy pant イージーパンツ
Pants with an elastic or webbing-belt waist, descended from the climbing pants launched in 1982 by the California brand Gramicci. Elastic-waist pants
Enji-iro えんじ色
A dark carmine red, close to burgundy.
Fade, iro-ochi フェード／色落ち
Fading. 色落ち refers to the process (the dye wearing off), フェード to the resulting look, often sought after in vintage clothing.
Fatigues ファティーグパンツ
Military work clothing, and above all the straight green US Army pants with large patch pockets. According to Percia Verlin, it is the city boy piece you see most often. US Army fatigue pants (OG-107)
Flannel ネル
A brushed wool or cotton fabric, soft and warm: the fabric of the check shirt. Flannel check shirt
Furugi 古着
Second-hand clothing, vintage. In Japan, used American clothing was imported in bulk from the postwar years on. Vintage and thrift
Gorpcore ゴープコア
A trend that emerged in 2017: wearing technical outdoor clothing (down jackets, fleece, hiking shoes) in the city. “GORP” is the name of hikers' trail mix. Heavy Duty and outdoor
Gusset
A diamond-shaped piece of fabric sewn into the crotch for freedom of movement, as on Gramicci climbing pants. Elastic-waist pants
Guernsey
The wool sweater of the fishermen of the island of Guernsey, worn by British Navy sailors in the 19th century. Crewneck sweater
Heather 杢
A mottled effect created by blending fibers of different colors, like the gray of a sweatshirt.
Heavy Duty ヘビーデューティー
The name of Japan's outdoor clothing boom in the 1970s. Its leading figure was the illustrator Yasuhiko Kobayashi, with his book “ヘビーデューティーの本” (“The Heavy Duty Book,” 1977). Heavy Duty and outdoor
Heavy Duty Ivy ヘビアイ
A mix of outdoor clothing and Ivy (mountain parka and oxford shirt). Yasuhiko Kobayashi presented it in 1976 as a parody of Ivy rules; readers took it seriously. Heavy Duty and outdoor
Heibon Punch 平凡パンチ
A weekly launched in 1964 by Heibon Shuppan, the former name of Magazine House. It passed one million copies in 1966 and made Ivy its style of reference.
Hot-Dog Press ホットドッグ・プレス
A magazine launched in 1979 by the Japanese publisher Kodansha, a direct competitor of Popeye.
Ivy アイビールック
The style of students at Ivy League universities, on the US East Coast, brought to Japan in the 1960s: button-down shirt, three-button blazer, cotton pants, loafers. Ivy and Take Ivy
Japanese Americana
An English-language label for the Japanese reinterpretation of the American wardrobe. Percia Verlin uses it as a synonym for city boy, in the very title of her video.
Jazz kissa ジャズ喫茶
A café where people listen to jazz, often on vinyl; Popeye devoted pages to them in 2016.
Just size ジャストサイズ
The “right size,” fitted. In 2022, Popeye asked that every choice of size, roomy or fitted, have a reason behind it.
Kasanegi, layered 重ね着／レイヤード
Layering clothes so that each layer stays visible.
Khaki coded カーキコード
A 2026 trend: earthy colors (khaki, beige, olive) and pieces such as the safari jacket, the field jacket or cargo pants. It is more military and closer to workwear than gorpcore.
Kinari 生成り
Ecru: a natural, unbleached white, softer than pure white.
Kissaten 喫茶店
A quiet, Japanese-style coffee house, which appeared in the early 20th century and came back into fashion in the 2020s.
Kodawari こだわり
Personal exactingness, an almost obsessive concern for getting the detail right.
Kon-bure 紺ブレ
Japanese abbreviation of “navy blazer.” Relaxed blazer
Konarekan こなれ感
Ease: the outfit looks effortless, and nothing looks out of place.
L.12.12
The reference number of the first Lacoste polo shirt: L for Lacoste, 1 for the piqué fabric, 2 for short sleeves, 12 for the twelfth prototype, the one that was chosen. Polo shirt
LifeWear magazine
Uniqlo's free magazine, launched in 2019 under the direction of Takahiro Kinoshita. As Popeye's editor-in-chief from 2012 to 2018, he had relaunched the magazine around the city boy before joining Uniqlo.
A-line Aライン
A trapeze-shaped silhouette: the lower half is wider than the upper half.
I-line Iライン
A silhouette that is straight and close to the body from top to bottom.
O-line Oライン
A rounded silhouette, roomy overall. The blog of RushOut, a Japanese vintage clothing store, presents it as the foundation of the city boy look.
Y-line Yライン
A Y-shaped silhouette: volume at the top, a slim bottom.
Ankle length アンクル丈
Pants that stop above the ankle (seven-eighths length).
Loopwheel 吊り編み
A knit made on old machines, which produces a heavy tubular jersey with no side seams; prized for sweatshirts and T-shirts. Crewneck sweatshirt
M-65
The US Army field jacket issued from 1965, with a hood rolled into the collar. M-65 field jacket
Made in U.S.A. catalog メイド・イン・USA
A 1975 catalog: 274 pages of American goods, with the addresses where they could be bought. It was produced by the future founders of Popeye; the magazine paid tribute to it in June 2026.
Magazine House マガジンハウス
The Tokyo publisher of Popeye, Brutus, Olive and an·an, founded in 1945 in the Ginza district. It was called Heibon Shuppan from 1954 to 1983.
Marinière (Breton shirt) バスクシャツ
The blue-and-white striped knit top of French Navy sailors, regulation issue since 1858. In Japan, it is also called a “Basque shirt.” Breton striped shirt
Men's Club メンズクラブ
A Japanese men's magazine founded in 1954 under the name Otoko no Fukushoku. For many years, it was the mouthpiece of the Ivy style and the VAN brand.
Mikubi (the three necks) 3首
The neck, wrists and ankles: baring them (open collar, rolled-up sleeves, short pants) makes an outfit lighter. In Japanese, the wrist and ankle are called the “neck of the hand” and the “neck of the foot,” hence the name.
Miyuki-zoku みゆき族
The “Miyuki tribe”: young people in Ivy clothes who gathered on Miyuki Street, in Tokyo's Ginza district, around 1964. The Tokyo police rounded some of them up in September 1964, ahead of the Olympic Games.
Moc toe モックトゥ
A boot with a moccasin toe. The archetype is the 1952 hunting boot by the American brand Red Wing. Boots
Nasukon 茄子紺
“Eggplant navy”: the purplish navy that navy blue fabric takes on with wear.
Normcore ノームコア
Unisex fashion made up of ordinary clothes, with no distinguishing marks. The trend forecasting collective K-HOLE introduced the word in 2013. For K-HOLE, it was first of all an attitude: “finding liberation in being nothing special.” Normcore
Nukekan 抜け感
Letting go: a little breathing room in a polished outfit (roominess, soft fabric, a shift in tone), without tipping into sloppiness.
Nuptse ヌプシ
A short, puffy down jacket by the American brand The North Face, often cited as the archetype. Down jacket
OCBD オックスフォードシャツ
“Oxford cloth button-down”: a button-down collar shirt in oxford cloth, a pillar of the Ivy style. The American brand Brooks Brothers began selling it in 1900. Oxford button-down shirt
OG-107
The US Army work uniform in olive green cotton sateen, specified in November 1952 and worn until 1989. Its pants are the city boy's fatigues. US Army fatigue pants (OG-107)
Olive オリーブ
Popeye's sister magazine. It became a title in its own right in June 1982, with the slogan “Magazine for City Girls.” From 1983, it was “Magazine for Romantic Girls”; the last issue came out in 2003.
Oversize オーバーサイズ
A garment roomier than the fitted size, leaving air between the body and the fabric.
Oxford bags
Very wide trousers worn by Oxford students in the mid-1920s, the ancestors of wide pleated trousers. Wide pleated trousers
Painter pant ペインターパンツ
The work pants of American painters and carpenters. The brand Stan Ray has been making them in Texas since 1972. Work pants and painter pants
Penny loafer ローファー
A loafer with a slotted strap. In 1936, the American brand G.H. Bass launched its Weejuns, inspired by the shoes of Norwegian farmers and fishermen. Loafers
Pleats (tucks) タック
Folds sewn in at the waist of pants, which add room at the hips and thighs; “2タック” means two pleats. Wide pleated trousers
Fleece フリース
A light synthetic pile fabric, developed in 1979 by the American textile mill Malden Mills and the outdoor brand Patagonia to imitate wool. Fleece jacket
Popeye ポパイ
A men's magazine founded by Magazine House in 1976, subtitled “Magazine for City Boys.” Its name plays on “pop eye”: an eye on pop.
POPEYE Web
The website of the magazine Popeye, launched in March 2021.
Preppy プレッピー
The style of students at private preparatory schools in the northeastern United States: a younger, sportier version of Ivy (polo shirt, rugby shirt, boat shoes). Preppy
Quiet luxury
Discreet luxury: understated elegance, top-quality materials, no logos.
Raglan
A sleeve that runs in one piece up to the collar, named after Lord Raglan, a British general in the Crimean War. Balmacaan coat
Regular furugi レギュラー古着
“Ordinary” second-hand clothing, often American and cheap, as opposed to rare vintage. Vintage and thrift
Ripstop
A fabric reinforced with a grid of stronger threads, which stops a tear from spreading.
Roll up ロールアップ
Rolling up pant hems or sleeves to show the ankle or wrist.
Sacoche サコッシュ
A small flat bag worn across the body, which comes from the musette bags handed to riders in cycling races; the Japanese word comes from French. Small shoulder bag
Sashi-iro 差し色
“Inserted color”: a small bright touch in a neutral outfit (bag, sneakers, beanie, socks).
Cotton sateen
A cotton weave with a smooth, slightly shiny surface. It is the fabric of the OG-107 pants, weighing 8.5 ounces per square yard, or about 290 g/m². US Army fatigue pants (OG-107)
Sax blue サックスブルー
A light blue with a slight gray cast, the color of the oxford shirt.
Select shop セレクトショップ
A store that picks and mixes pieces from several brands, the way an editor puts together a magazine. Japanese examples: SHIPS (1975), BEAMS (1976), United Arrows (1989).
Selvedge セルビッチ
The clean, finished edge of fabric woven on old, narrow looms; it shows when jeans are rolled up. Straight or wide jeans
Twill
A weave that forms fine diagonal lines on the surface of the fabric; chino and denim are both twills. Chinos
Shibukaji 渋カジ
“Shibuya casual”: the American-inspired fashion of young people in Tokyo's Shibuya district in the 1980s–1990s. It spread the word “amekaji.” Amekaji
Smock
Another name for the anorak, a garment pulled on over the head. Anorak
Snap スナップ
A street photo of a well-dressed passerby. As early as 1963, Men's Club launched a column of this kind; according to W. David Marx, it was probably the first in the Japanese press.
Snap-T
A Patagonia fleece with a stand-up collar that closes with snaps, cut from Synchilla, the brand's own fleece. Fleece jacket
Stadium jumper スタジャン
The collegiate jacket with a team letter, also known as a varsity jacket.
Standard 定番／スタンダード
A classic piece that never goes out of style: a central idea in Popeye's features.
Style Sample
An issue of Popeye devoted to the outfits of passersby photographed in the street. It has come back regularly since the 2010s.
Sumiguro 墨黒
“Ink black”: a faded black that shades into charcoal, the result of wear.
Sweatshirt スウェット
A fleece-backed cotton top born in 1920 as a college football practice jersey, in Alabama. Crewneck sweatshirt
Take 丈
The length of a garment: pants, top or coat.
Take Ivy
A 1965 film, then a photo book, shot on American campuses by a team from the Japanese brand VAN. It is the bible of the Ivy style in Japan. Ivy and Take Ivy
Tanker タンカー
A line of bags from the Japanese brand Porter, launched in 1983, in a nylon inspired by the American MA-1 flight jacket. Porter bags
Tasukigake たすき掛け
A sweater or other garment tied diagonally across the chest.
Top-sider デッキシューズ
The boat shoe, with a non-slip sole, invented in 1935 by the American Paul Sperry. Boat shoes
TPO
“Time, Place, Occasion”: the rule set out in 1963 by Kensuke Ishizu, founder of the VAN brand. It says you should dress for the time, the place and the occasion.
Trucker Gジャン
Levi's 1962 denim jacket, known as the Type III, after the Type I (1905) and the Type II (1953). Denim jacket
Tuck in タックイン
Tucking the top into the pants, even a loose shirt, to keep the waist visible.
Unfashion アン・ファッション
“Anti-fashion”: clothes born of work, a culture or a place, outside of fashion. It was the theme of Popeye's October 2014 issue.
Urban outdoor アーバンアウトドア
Outdoor clothing and gear worked into city dress; a Popeye theme since 2012. Heavy Duty and outdoor
VAN
A Japanese brand founded by Kensuke Ishizu (the company dates from 1954), which brought Ivy to Japan. It went bankrupt in April 1978. Ivy and Take Ivy
Vulcanized (sole)
A vulcanized rubber sole, typical of canvas sneakers such as the Converse All Star. Canvas sneakers
Wallabee ワラビー
A Clarks suede shoe, constructed like a moccasin on a crepe sole. Clarks Wallabees and desert boots
Watch cap ワッチキャップ
A knit sailor's beanie, designed for US Navy lookouts standing watch. Short cuffed beanie
Whole Earth Catalog
An American counterculture catalog. According to W. David Marx, Yasuhiko Kobayashi and Jirō Ishikawa, of the Heibon Punch editorial team, discovered it in New York in 1969. It inspired the Made in U.S.A. catalog, and then Popeye.
Wide pants, baggy ワイドパンツ／バギーパンツ
Pants that are wide along their whole length; “baggy” comes from the word “bag.” Wide pleated trousers
Yellow Pages イエローページ
A directory of recommended stores that Popeye publishes in its features, laid out like a phone book.

Definitions based on the sources of Chapters 01 to 06: tables of contents and articles from the magazine Popeye; the author W. David Marx; Japanese online fashion guides, including the site WardRove, the blog of the vintage store RushOut, the menswear blog かめたくルーム and the stylists' site チェンジングミー; Japanese, English and French Wikipedia; the piece entries. The Japanese spellings are those used by these sources.

出典

Chapter 09

09

Sources

Where the facts, quotes, prices and images in this monograph come from; what remains uncertain; and the common misconceptions it corrects.

Method

How these sources were gathered

Public pages only. All sources are public pages, read without an account, without logging in and without getting around a paywall. For a partly paywalled article, only the public part is used.

Faithful quotations. Quotes are checked word for word against the text of the original pages. Quotes from English sources keep their original wording; quotes from Japanese sources are translated, followed by the original Japanese.

Facts and interpretations. Every fact points to a dated source. When a passage is interpretation, the text says whose it is: a quoted author or the monograph itself. Information reported by a single weak source is presented as uncertain.

Prices. Prices are given as rounded ranges in euros, as a rough guide. They are converted from the currency shown by each shop, excluding sales, then generously rounded. Real prices change quickly and vary by shop and country. A price quoted in an old issue of Popeye keeps its date.

Images. Descriptions state only what is visible. Names, places, brands and credits are given only when they are written on the original page. The photos belong to their authors and are gathered here for strictly personal use.

Limits. The style's reception in the West (Reddit forums, TikTok, magazines such as GQ or Highsnobiety) is less documented here than its Japanese history. Only facts read on the source pages themselves are included.

Keep in mind

What remains uncertain

  • The month of Popeye's first issue: June 1976 according to author W. David Marx, Japanese Wikipedia and the publisher Magazine House; July 1976 according to English Wikipedia, which probably goes by the month printed on the cover.
  • The date of the “Heavy Duty Ivy Party declaration”, a text by the illustrator Yasuhiko Kobayashi in the magazine Men's Club: November 1976 according to Kobayashi, September 1976 according to Marx.
  • The “concept” behind Popeye's 2012 relaunch, which supposedly described a white boy from the New York suburbs. Only the Japanese fashion blog God Meets Fashion (2016) reports it.
  • The origin of the term “city boy” in the Japanese magazine Takarajima (January 1975): a single second-hand source makes this claim, a blog published on the note.com platform.
  • Popeye's editors-in-chief between 1980 and 2012: public sources do not name them.
  • Circulation: the figures disagree. Accounts give 700,000 or over 800,000 copies at the peak; 40,000, 100,000 or 150,000 in the 2010s. The sources cite no official figure.
  • The spelling of some names: the given names of two members of the 1976 team, Matsuyama and Baba, are written two ways depending on the source (松山剛 or 松山猛, 馬場佑介 or 馬場祐介). The pronunciation of the given name of Nakamura, vice president of the store SHIPS, remains uncertain.
  • Two doubtful stories about Popeye's founding. According to Japanese Wikipedia, the US tourism office supposedly backed the launch. As for secret funding by the CIA, Marx himself presents it as a rumor.
  • Second-hand anecdotes. Kensuke Ishizu, founder of the brand VAN, reportedly exclaimed in a Uniqlo store: “This is what I wanted to do!” According to a Japanese blog published on note.com (2020), a 2019 recruitment video supposedly said that Popeye's editorial team had no women. The magazine's Instagram account is said to be followed mostly from outside Japan.
  • Conflicting founding dates: VAN (1951, 1954 or 1955, depending on what is counted), SHIPS (1975, according only to Osamu Shigematsu, founder of United Arrows), the end of the US military OG-107 fatigues (1981 or 1989), and the brands Saint James (1850 or 1889), Paraboot (1908, 1910 or 1927) and Laulhère (1792, 1830 or 1840).
  • The vocabulary of silhouettes: no Japanese source clearly defines the “balloon” cut (“バルーン”). The typical silhouettes and the season-by-season color summary are groupings made by this monograph, not Popeye categories.
  • Prices: the euro ranges are rough guides. Some shops do not show their prices in euros, even when visited from France: the brand Stan Ray gives them in pounds, J.M. Weston in dollars, even on its French page. Prices quoted by Popeye date from the article, and second-hand listings change constantly.
  • Images: the archive scans of Popeye were put online by third parties. The lookbook contains no Popeye look from the 1970s, nor from the 1982–2009 period. The covers taken from the publisher's website, magazineworld.jp, are low resolution.

Misconceptions

Corrections

Good to know

These points contradict claims in circulation, including in Percia Verlin's “City Boy starter pack” video, the starting point of this monograph.

  • Popeye did not invent the term “city boy.” Percia Verlin's video says it did. In fact, “City Boys” was a fashionable expression in the 1970s. It was even the title that Jirō Ishikawa, a founding member of the magazine, wanted to give it, according to Marx in the Bandana newsletter (2024). “Magazine for City Boys,” on the other hand, has indeed been Popeye's slogan since 1976.
  • No source says to “size up one or two sizes.” The blog of the Japanese vintage clothing store RushOut recommends a fit that is “neither too tight nor too oversized.” POPEYE Web, the magazine's website, even suggests “one size down” for a cut that is already loose. In 2022, Popeye asked that every choice of size have a reason. What matters is loose cuts, not clothes that are too big.
  • Take Ivy was first a film, shot in 1965 on American campuses by a team from the Japanese brand VAN. The well-known photo book came afterward.
  • “Baker pant” is not a military name. The official name of these US Army pants was “utility trousers,” and soldiers called them “fatigues.” The American site Heddels, devoted to denim and workwear, sees “baker pant” as an invention of Japanese fashion.
  • Heavy Duty Ivy was a parody. Kobayashi presented this mix of outdoor clothing and Ivy style as a mockery of the Ivy rules. It was the readers who took it seriously.
  • Takahiro Kinoshita did not “single-handedly” create the city boy style. Yet that is what the streetwear site Hypebeast claims in its “Hypebeast 100” list (2015). As Popeye's editor-in-chief from 2012 to 2018, he revived a word, a slogan and codes that had existed since the 1970s.
  • The automatic captions of Percia Verlin's video mangle names: “unique glow” for Uniqlo, “Ptibato” for Petit Bateau, “Lule Laberoy” for Le Laboureur, “Carhoe” for Karhu, “workware” for workwear, “fatiques” for fatigues. In this monograph, the names are corrected based on the description Percia Verlin posts on YouTube.
